docs.title: The Persianate World
docs.text:
A player wiki for The Persianate World, a 1337 mod for Europa Universalis V (1.4.7) that rebuilds the post-Ilkhanid Iranian world and the lands around it: its succession, its administration, its people, and the political settlement everyone in it was trying to escape.

Abū Saʿīd died in November 1335 and the house of Hülegü died with him. What the base game makes of this is two "hordes" on the map and a generic collapse. What actually happened is one of the strangest political experiments in medieval history: an empire whose army, treasury, chancery and provinces all survived, but whose sovereignty evaporated, because the one rule everyone agreed on was that only a descendant of Chinggis Khan could reign, and the supply of plausible descendants was running out.

This mod is about that world. Not the collapse as flavor, but the collapse as a system.

docs.title: What changed in 1.4
docs.text:
For players coming back from the summer builds. The mod now targets Europa Universalis V 1.4.7, and it has grown well beyond the Iranian plateau: the last version of this wiki (June) described a government type, two estates and the Erānzamīn succession. This page lists what is new or different since then, with a link to the page that explains each item.

Much of this is recent and has not yet been played through. Known issues and systems in testing says which parts.

docs.title: What the 1.4 engine changed for the mod
docs.text:
• Estate power now comes from pops. Literate urban Iranian and Arab noble pops form the Dīwān; other Muslim noble pops form the Amirs; the Amirs' weight also scales with the share of tribesmen in the realm. Building up cities and literacy strengthens the pen; a large tribal population strengthens the sword. See the Dīwān estate and the Amirs estate.
  • Political influence is a currency the mod now uses. The Chinggisid Regency costs −20% political influence gain, sworn governorates pay their regent in it, the Dīwān of the Realms adds +10% to its gain, and several privileges and actions are priced in it. See the closing section of estate privileges.
  • Cavalry is split into light and heavy. Amirs ride heavy; the tribes ride light until the Qizilbash. Amir Cavalry levies 30% of amir nobles and the tribes 10% of tribesmen, while peasant and Dīwān levies are cut by 90%. See the military system.

docs.title: The Persianate state
docs.text:
• Five chancery reforms instead of one: Persianate Bureaucracy, Mamluk Government, The Delhi Dispensation, Rasulid Chancery and Timurid Empire. Egypt and Delhi now start as Persianate Sultanates. See government reforms and periphery sultanates.
  • New reforms: Ilkhanate Governorate, Amīr Sultanate, The Gurkani Regime, The Īlāt Compact, Sword of The Sharia. A sultanate with no answer to the legitimacy question carries Unsettled Legitimacy (−0.6 legitimacy a month).
  • The Amirs keep private regiments through the Right to Retinue, and the crown can Summon the Amirs' Tümens. See the Amirs estate.
  • The privilege catalogue has more than doubled, and the Maẓālim court now has 18 crown decrees, 17 estate petitions and 52 cases. See estate privileges and the Maẓālim court.
  • Buildings: the iqṭāʿ now decays into Unaudited Iqṭāʿ and Tuyul unless audited; six estate-built waqf endowments; Qanāt Networks, forty of them damaged at the start in Khurāsān and Balkh. There are three Dīwāns of the Realms in 1337 (Tabrīz, Delhi, Cairo), not one. See buildings, goods and materials.
  • Goods: tar is gathered at Baku, horses are no longer food and are cheaper to move, glass is no longer needed to build a town, trade range is +300 worldwide, and Herāt has a market.
  • Persia as a formable now requires the legitimacy wager and the Matter of Tork settled; Iran o Toran is a new formable.

docs.title: The succession of Erānzamīn
docs.text:
• The Erānzamīn organisation has its own panel: the Five Seats, the Khans in Custody, a Notables tab, and four roles for its 73 members. See the Erānzamīn organisation.
  • Contenders are Muslim realms seated in the region. Christian realms are members but not contenders; the ṭarīqa orders and the amirs of Ulus Chaghatay stand outside the contest.
  • Conquest is immediate. A contender who takes a place by siege or occupation annexes it on the spot, and a province capital carries its province. Victory now requires Shiraz as well as the other four seats. See the succession of Erānzamīn.
  • The victory is a single outcome followed by a branch on the Türk–Tāzīk axis: Integrate into the Dīwān or Invite Turkic Settlers.
  • Custody of the Ulus: sworn governorates pay the regent +0.05 legitimacy and +0.10 political influence each, and defending them is a choice. See the Borrowed Mandate and the Ilkhanate Governorate.
  • The Matter of Tork was rebuilt. Its paths now stack and the disaster closes with a proclamation; the march became the Great Raid; it fires at 750,000 Turco-Mongol tribesmen and more than 240 locations. The Farr and Ghāzī audits were renumbered throughout. See the Matter of Tork, the Farr Under Examination and the Burden of the Sword.

docs.title: The Shia world
docs.text:
• The Commonwealth of Martyrs is the Sarbadars' own government, with the Sufyānī and Shaykhī estates, and the Sarbadar Phenomenon runs from the first day. See the Commonwealth of Martyrs.
  • Shia Islam was rebuilt: four aspect slots and eleven aspects, and new establishments in the school slot. Seven landless ṭarīqa orders exist in 1337, among them Ardabil, and an order can rise, capture a court and be crowned. See ṭarīqa orders and the Shia rework.
  • Yemen is divided between the Rasulids at Taʿizz and a new Zaydi Imamate at Ṣaʿda, an organisation whose members swear bayʿa, pay zakāt and answer the Imam's wars. See the Zaydi Imamate and Yemen.

docs.title: The steppe
docs.text:
• Borjigin hordes get the yam (+33% proximity efficiency and eight more governors), Darugha's Seats, and ulus grants to princes. The flat loss of horde unity at a khan's death is replaced by a poll with four outcomes, and Jochi and Chagatai choose their khans by the scored Törü. See hordes.
  • Ulus Chaghatay is an organisation: the Chagatai khan and fifteen Amirs of the Ulus, who owe him a 5% qubchur. Four new countries are carved out of the khanate. Base's scheduled Timur is switched off. See Ulus Chaghatay, and the next section for what has been built on it since.

docs.title: The steppe, November 2026
docs.text:
Everything in this section was built after the wiki's last revision and is largely untested in play; see Known issues. The numbers are collected on Ulus and regency numbers.

  • Weight decides the ulus. A realm's weight is now 40% military strength, 30% tax base, 20% its ruler's abilities and 10% prestige. The amirs can raise a khan when the three greatest of them outweigh the khan four times over, or when the begs hold half the power in his realm. The panel shows what each house's weight and kingmaker score are made of. See Ulus Chaghatay.
  • Pledges. A house can pledge its whole tümen to another, or be asked to; the khan can ask the lesser lords to stand with the seat. A pledged house drops out of the reckoning for the khan and rides in its patron's wars. Allies and patrons outside the ulus count as well, to a limit, and an outsider can Back an Amir of the Ulus.
  • Rise Against the Khan. An amir among the three likeliest kingmakers need not wait for a funeral once a bar is met. If he wins he takes the khan; if he loses he pays in silver and land, and perhaps with his head.
  • Lead a Raid. Amirs and regents raid their neighbours for plunder and captives. Raiding unbelievers is a ghazā; raiding one's own faith without a cause costs prestige.
  • Client kings. Badakhshan and Karategin are no longer vassals of Chagatai. They sit in the ulus as Persianate courts with their own status and reform. The ground of a tümen that has lost its whole army is disposed of by whoever broke it: taken, raised again as a tümen, or given to a client king.
  • The Amirs' Regency is complete: four stages, a legitimacy gap that drains each month and is filled by victories and largesse, the regent's three actions on the disaster's own panel, the houses' Claim the Khan and Back the Khan's Purge, the cadet who takes a tümen when its chief flees, and three endings: the Khan Triumphant, the Ṣāḥib-qirān and the Bulqaq, with the Breaking of the Chaghatay after it. See The Amirs' Regency.
  • The Ṣāḥib-qirān is the mod's Timur: whoever ends the regency with a khan in keeping, a wife of the line and five years of standing. Loyal houses beside his own seat are annexed, the rest of the loyal become Sworn Amirs, and his realm rides out under his house's name. What holds it together is his fortune, which drains at peace and is filled by victory and by dividing the plunder. The Timurids can no longer be formed by decision. See The Ṣāḥib-qirān.
  • Chaghatay culture. The khan's seat, the western tümens and the carved domains are Chaghatay, not Mongolian: Turkic-speaking, Muslim in the west, still of the steppe. Temür's house is the Barlas dynasty, no longer filed under the Borjigin. See Demography and cultures.
  • Steppe privileges. Hordes that begin from the base horde setup start with Hereditary Tümens and Bound to the Tümen in place of two manorial privileges. A Kurultai may stand wherever the ruling people is of the steppe, and the tribes sit in a horde's parliament. See Hordes.
  • The Beglerbeg's Regency. When the Golden Horde's Törü elects a beg over the princes, he no longer becomes a khan of an invented dynasty. He rules through a kept khan under a disaster of his own, in which princes with shares declare themselves khan, and which ends with a khan of the line, the office made hereditary, or the khanate partitioned. See The Beglerbeg's Regency.

docs.title: The periphery
docs.text:
• Rise of the Ottomans is now Shattered Rum. The beyliks become Persianate Sultanates and choose between the ghazā, the Seljuk claim, or remaining a march; the Seljuk Inheritance leads to a Sultanate of Rum. See Shattered Rum.
  • The Kurdish emirates have their own government, the Iranic Tribal Polity, with Zagros infantry and +50% levies in defence. See Kurdish emirates.

docs.title: The map and its people
docs.text:
• Population in Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus and Afghanistan is calibrated to Mustawfī's register of 1340: the Persia region rises from about 4.0 to 13.3 million, the Caucasus from 1.9 to 4.7 million, the Khorasan region from 3.8 to 5.7 million, and Tabrīz is a city of a quarter of a million. Eighty-five more places between the Euphrates and the Pamirs are ranked as towns or cities.
  • There are no Hazara in 1337, Sistan and the lower Helmand are Khorasani, the Neguderi are Mongol, and Türkmen pastoralists are seeded across the Jazira. The Mongol elites who had become Persian in everything but lineage have a culture of their own, Persianized Mongol.
  • Accepted and tolerated cultures are set for 83 realms on the first day, by population weight. The Jews of Iran and Yemen are no longer typed as slaves.
  • No war is under way inside Erānzamīn at the start, and the base game's swarms of Jalayirid and Gurgan vassals are gone. The Dīwān and Amirs estates exist from day one.

See demography and cultures, and countries and tags for the changed map.

docs.title: The Amirs estate
docs.text:
The men of the sword: the state does not own an army, it borrows theirs.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The amirs' private regiments and the Summon the Amirs' Tümens action were added for 1.4 and have not yet been confirmed in a played campaign. They are described here as designed.

The Amirs are the military service aristocracy of a Persianate state. Together with the Dīwān they take the place the nobility holds in a European realm. In game they appear on the estate panel as The Amirs Estate.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: An amīr is a commander. In the post-Ilkhanid world the word covers the Mongol noyans and their heirs, the chiefs of the Turkic and Mongol tribal followings, and the warlord houses (Chobanid, Jalayirid, later Qara Qoyunlu, Aq Qoyunlu and Timurid) who made and unmade khans. What they share is a household of armed retainers and a claim on the iqṭāʿ, the assignment of a district's revenue in place of a salary. The umarāʾ are a service order whose rank is in principle revocable, not a landed nobility by right of descent; the long drift of the revocable grant into hereditary property is the political story of the estate, and the privilege list follows it step by step.

docs.title: Who belongs to it
docs.text:
Since 1.4 an estate's power comes from the pops that belong to it.

A noble pop is an amir pop when:

Condition Detail The state has a chancery The owner carries the Niẓām al-Mulk Chancery flag (Persianate Bureaucracy and the other chancery reforms listed on the Dīwān page). It is not a dīwān pop The Dīwān test is applied first; literate urban Iranian and Arab nobles go to the pen. Religion Muslim, unless you hold The Open Muster Rolls, which opens the corps to every creed.

Non-Muslim noble pops stay in the base Nobility, which the Persianate Bureaucracy reform holds at −90% power. From time to time (about 1% a year) a Muslim Persianate Sultanate with such pops is petitioned to open the rolls.

Tribesmen are not amirs. They form the separate Tribes estate, which the mod strengthens: each tribesman pop carries a power weight of 1 (the base game's is 0.25) and the estate is taxed at 1 per pop (base 0.01). The two are linked, as the next table shows.

docs.title: Where its power comes from
docs.text:
Source Effect Pops Each amir noble pop carries the standard noble weight (25 per pop). Tribal Power Base (any chancery state) Amirs power rises with the share of your population that is tribesmen: +250% for every 10% Base values of any chancery state +30% Amirs power Amirs Base Values for any civilized nation (Persianate Sultanate) +5% Amirs power, +40% target satisfaction Amirs With a Mission +2.5% target satisfaction while at war Privileges and laws See below and Estate privileges

The tribal population is the real foundation of the estate. A realm that has absorbed large pastoral populations has powerful amirs whether or not it has granted them anything; one that settles or loses its tribes weakens them more surely than any decree.

docs.title: Tax and the estate's own modifiers
docs.text:
The Amirs are assessed at 25 per pop: a quarter of a base-game noble (100) and an eighth of a dīwān man (200). They are paid by the state far more than they pay it. They have dynasties, run no bank, and supply mercenary captains.

The estate's effects scale with its satisfaction and with how far its power stands above or below the engine's thresholds; the figures are the listed strengths.

Satisfied Amirs Powerful Amirs Weak Amirs Levies +25% levy combat efficiency, +10% levy size −10% levy size +5% levy size Morale +15% land morale −20% land morale Cavalry +10% heavy and light cavalry power +5% heavy and light cavalry power Loot +50% Manpower −25% +10% Tax efficiency −15% Control −7.5% max urban, −15% max rural Decentralization +0.2 per month Amirs' own max tax +25% (the iqṭāʿs are being recalled)

Note the shape: you want the amirs content, not strong. Satisfaction gives you the army; power takes the countryside, the manpower pool and the tax register.

docs.title: The pen and the sword
docs.text:
Under the Persianate Bureaucracy reform amir characters may lead armies and may not sit in the cabinet; the reverse holds for the Dīwān. The privilege Umarāʾ at the Dīwān admits them to the cabinet (and is the condition one of the Matter of Tork outcomes checks for); Tāzīk Command of Arms lets chancery men command. Amir privileges almost all push the Turk vs Tazik value toward Turk.

At game start every Persianate Sultanate receives two amir characters of the country's own culture with strong military ability.

Where a country has an Amirs estate, its noble pops raise amir cavalry levies in place of the base game's mailed knights; the units themselves are covered under the military system. Several privileges raise the size of the amirs' and the tribes' levies.

docs.title: Retinues: the amirs' own regiments
docs.text:
1.4 lets an estate keep a private army bought from its own treasury. The amirs gain that right through the privilege Right to Retinue, which both Persianate starting templates hold from 1337.

To call those regiments under the royal standard, use Summon the Amirs' Tümens in the estate actions panel.

Requires An Amirs estate, the Right to Retinue, and at least one regiment the amirs have not yet raised Legitimacy −10 Political influence −15; reduced to −5 when the Dīwān holds more estate power than the Amirs Amirs −10% satisfaction Cooldown Three years

The discount is the point of the design: a chancery strong enough to outweigh the camp turns the muster into a matter of the registers; a weak one has to beg and pay for it.

docs.title: The law on the umarāʾ
docs.text:
A law category, Rights of the Persian Nobility, is open to any country with an Amirs estate.

Policy Favoured by Effects Curtail the Umara Dīwān Amirs: −5% target satisfaction, −10% power, −20% levy size; tribes levy size −10%; tax efficiency +50%; max control +5%; Tazik +0.05 per month Rights of the Umara Amirs Amirs: +10% target satisfaction, +10% power, +10% levy size; Turk +0.05 per month Amir Autonomy Amirs Amirs: +30% power, +5% target satisfaction, +20% levy size; tribes levy size +10%; tax efficiency −20%; max control −5%; decentralization +0.1 and Turk +0.1 per month

docs.title: The amirs before the court
docs.text:
In the Maẓālim court the amirs answer for land seizure, illegal tolls, forced billeting, phantom horsemen on the muster rolls and private justice. Convictions cost them 10–25% satisfaction and often a quarter to two fifths of the estate's treasury, which goes to yours. They can also petition: to fortify the borders, to expand the cavalry, and to have the summer pastures written into the register.

The Dīwān's petition Audit Iqta Holders takes a fifth of the Amirs' treasury if it passes.

docs.title: Estate events
docs.text:
While the Amirs hold at least 25% of estate power, three events can come up on the Persianate flavour pulse:

Event Choices Demands of the Sword (only without Amīr al-Umarāʾ) Grant Amīr al-Umarāʾ and gain 15% Amirs satisfaction, or refuse and lose 20% Contented Amirs +10% Amirs satisfaction Amir Encroachment In a location the Amirs dominate: allow it and lose 10% control there, or uphold the centre and lose 5% Amirs satisfaction

docs.title: The estate after the Matter of Tork
docs.text: The Matter of Tork can end with the Turco-Mongol order dissolved. The estate does not disappear; its charter changes. The tribal privileges (Tribal Hosts (Yurt), Tribal Autonomy Rights, Umarāʾ at the Dīwān, Amir-Held Commands, Iqtaʿ Commutation) are withdrawn from the list, and where the order was removed by force the three Dehqan Revival privileges take their place. See Estate privileges for the entries.

docs.title: Playing with the Amirs
docs.text:
• Keep them satisfied and keep their power moderate. War, the Iqtāʿ Grant and the Right to Retinue raise satisfaction cheaply; Tribal Hosts and Soyurghal Grants raise power steeply.
  • Count your tribesmen. The Tribal Power Base outweighs most privileges, so conquest of pastoral country is a political decision about your own court.
  • If you mean to use the retinues, build the Dīwān's power above the Amirs' first; the political influence saved on each summons is ten points.
  • An amir-heavy realm fields large cavalry levies on a thin tax base and a dark countryside. That is a workable state, and historically the usual one, but plan your income around it.

See also: Dīwān estate, Estate privileges, The Maẓālim court, Turk vs Tazik, Matter of Tork, The military system, Hordes.

docs.title: The Amirs' Regency
docs.text:
He has the name of khan. We have the khan.

New — largely untested in play

The regency was built in November 2026. Its onset, the panel and the regent's actions have been run in spot tests with debug tools; no campaign has yet been played from a khan's death to an ending. Every number on this page is a first setting. See Known issues.

A man without the blood of Chinggis could not be khan, so the amir who held the army kept one. Qazaghan of the Qara'unas killed Qazan Khan in 1346, raised first an Ögedeid and then the Chaghatayid Bayan Quli at his own camp, and ruled the western ulus in their names for twelve years. He was murdered on a hunt in 1358 by the son-in-law of a man he had slighted. His son assumed he had inherited the ulus with the tümens and was driven out within the year; no single beg replaced him, and each amir made war on his neighbours as he saw fit. In 1360 and 1361 Tughluq Temür, khan of the eastern half, rode into Transoxiana and for two years there was one khan again. In 1370 Temür of the Barlas took Balkh, married into the line, set a khan on the felt and received the oath of the amirs.

Beatrice Manz's reading, which the mod follows, is that the conqueror was the product of those twenty-four years and not of the calendar. The Amirs' Regency is that sequence as a disaster carried by whichever state holds the khan of Ulus Chaghatay: four stages, a measure of the regent's standing that only victory and gold can fill, and three ways out.

docs.title: How it begins
docs.text:
There are two ways in.

When Who becomes regent The legitimacy gap starts at The amirs raise a khan A khan dies, one of the two bars is at its line 30 to 80 days after his successor is seated, and a man of the line exists to enthrone The amir with the highest kingmaker score — or a darugha of the old seat who outscores every amir 50 Rise Against the Khan An amir wins the war The amir who rose 35

The regent takes a prince of the line into his keeping: the youngest boy at the court of any member, failing that the least able grown man; if the line has nobody left, a cadet is found. The leadership of the organisation moves to the regent's state, which takes the reform Beglerbeg's Regency, and the disaster begins there. The regent gains 10 prestige (The Amirs Raise a Khan); every other player in the ulus is told (The Amirs' Regency). Pledges to the old khan lapse. The qubchur the amirs send the seat is halved for as long as a regent holds it.

If the khan's successor is a child and no bar is met, there is no Amirs' Regency: the realm has an ordinary regency (A Boy on the Felt, −5 horde unity) and both bars stand a third lower at the next succession.

docs.title: The old seat answers
docs.text:
The khan's old realm keeps its ruler and is asked once (A Khan Not of Our Making):

Option Result A khan is a khan. −10 horde unity. It stays in the ulus as an Amir of the Ulus under the amirs' khan. Its subjects nearer the regent's capital than its own pass to the regent A beg's captive is no khan of ours. +10 horde unity. It leaves the ulus as the eastern khanate. Every member whose capital lies nearer its own than the regent's follows it out as its vassal (an AI member at once; a player is asked in Two Khans). It holds Restore the Ulus on the regent, which does not expire while the regency lasts. Regent and khan take −100 opinion of each other ("Two khans of one ulus")

This is where Moghulistan comes from. From the 1337 roll the houses nearer Almaliq are the Dughlat, Issyk-Kul and Dzungaria.

docs.title: What the regent carries
docs.text:
Source Effect on the regent's state Beglerbeg's Regency (reform) +0.10 monthly horde unity, −0.10 monthly prestige, −20% political influence gain, −3% maximum control The Amirs' Regency (disaster) −0.02 monthly horde unity, −5 subject loyalty The Regency Under Strain −0.03 monthly horde unity and −0.03 monthly prestige for each stage reached (so −0.12 each in the fourth) The keeper's office +20% political influence gain, which cancels the reform's penalty, and +0.75 / +0.50 / +0.25 political influence a month in the first, second and third stage. Nothing in the fourth

A regent's state counts as a khan's for the horde systems: it keeps the yam, the darugha seats and the right to grant shares (see Hordes).

docs.title: The four stages
docs.text:
The disaster's panel shows The Stage of the Regency and a clock, Toward the next stage, that runs from 0 to 100.

What moves the clock Amount Each month the nobles hold 50% or more of estate power in the regent's realm, or the three greatest amirs together weigh at least as much as the regent +1 Each month neither is true and the crown holds more power than the nobles in his realm −0.5 The kept khan dies and another is enthroned +10 The regent dies +15 The regent loses a war, or an outsider takes his capital +10 The regent chooses to rule without a khan +25 Recall the Darughas −15 Marry into the Line −20 A share granted to a prince of the line (Grant a Share of the Ulus) −10 The khan's purge fails The next stage at once

Unchecked, a stage lasts 100 months.

Stage What it opens I. The Beglerbeg's Peace One beg rules through a khan. No member may make war on another. The regent may set a kinsman over an amir house and the house must accept II. The Amirs Fall Out −10 horde unity for the regent. Members may make war on one another with a casus belli. Every house takes −100 opinion of the keeper ("Keeps the khan who is ours as much as his") unless it is his subject, has pledged to him, or is both lighter than he is and his ally. Every house takes −100 opinion of every other house ("The amirs have fallen out") except its allies, its lord or subject, and the house it is pledged to or that is pledged to it: what is left standing is the blocs. Claim the Khan and Press the Feud open. A house may refuse an imposed kinsman. A kinsman who is the better soldier may seize a tümen III. The Shock from Outside −10 horde unity. The regent's three strongest independent neighbours outside the ulus, and the eastern khanate if there is one, hold The Ulus in Disarray on him for ten years (land is cheap for them). Members may leave the ulus. Whoever takes the regent's capital in war takes the khan. No kinsman can be imposed. A chief beaten by an invader may flee and a kinsman submit in his place IV. The Ṣāḥib-qirān At the turn the amirs are measured once more: if an amir not of the line now has a higher kingmaker score than the regent, the khan goes to him. Whoever holds the khan gains 15 prestige (The Lord of the Conjunction). The endings are now counted

docs.title: The office hardens
docs.text: Each time a stage turns with the legitimacy gap at 60 or more, the regent gains a step of The Beglerbeg's Office, to three steps (The Office Hardens). Each step gives +5% crown power and +0.03 monthly horde unity and prestige, which undoes one stage's worth of strain, and is meant to raise his heir's standing against the best rival by 10%. All of it goes with the khan: a state that loses him loses the office.

docs.title: The legitimacy gap
docs.text:
A beg has no blood to rule by, only deeds. The gap is a measure from 0 to 100 of how well the regent's deeds cover for the blood he lacks. It starts at 50 and counts as filled at 60 or more.

It drains each month Stage I / II / III / IV 0.15 / 0.30 / 0.45 / 0.60 No khan in keeping × 2 Any amir's effective weight is greater than the regent's × 1.5 It is filled by A great battle won +4 A siege won +2 A war won (a raid counts) +10 Distribute Largesse +10 A war lost, or the capital taken by an outsider −15 Choosing to rule without a khan Halved at once

Only real engagements count: skirmishes do not fill it. The panel shows the gap, its monthly drain, and the running count of months filled or empty.

docs.title: The regent's actions
docs.text:
These three are on the disaster's own panel. Recall the Darughas is offered to whoever leads the ulus, but it is reached from the regency's panel.

Action Requires Effect Recall the Darughas A nobles estate; not already in force For ten years Darughas Recalled: −15% nobles' estate power, −10% nobles' target satisfaction. At once: −15% nobles' satisfaction, −10 stability, the clock −15. The seats themselves stand Marry into the Line A living khan in keeping; the ruler not already a son-in-law of the line The ruler takes a wife of the khan's house and stands as güregen. +10 prestige; every member gains +15 opinion of us; the clock −20. It is required of a Ṣāḥib-qirān, and it lets the house raise a khan of its own daughter's blood when a kept khan dies Distribute Largesse — The gap +10. Nobles +5% satisfaction. Every member gains +25 opinion of us (fading within about two years). For two years: +10 subject loyalty (Largesse Remembered), +3 weight in the ulus, and no house that took the silver can Claim the Khan

docs.title: What the houses can do
docs.text:
These are on the Ulus Chaghatay panel, with the pledges and raids described on the ulus page.

Action Who and when Effect Claim the Khan An amir at peace, from stage II, who has not taken the regent's largesse within the last two years The casus belli Take the Khan on the regent for ten years; the goal is his capital. If the claimant then loses a war to the regent, his own house may put him aside Press the Feud An amir at peace, from stage II, who has pledged or been pledged to The casus belli Feud of the Tümens for five years on a house that stands in a different bloc and with which we have no truce. Land is dear in the peace Back the Khan's Purge An amir, at any stage, while the kept khan is a grown man with military skill of 50 or more Three chances in ten that the khan kills the regent's house and rules (The Khan Triumphant); an even chance if his military skill is 70 or more. If he fails (The Khan's Hand Is Stayed) the regency moves to its next stage at once, the regent loses 10 horde unity, and three times in four the khan is put to death

docs.title: Deaths
docs.text:
The kept khan dies (The Khan Is Dead). The regent chooses:

Option Requires Result Find another of the blood. A man of the line to raise; 20 political influence Another prince is enthroned. The clock +10 My daughter's son carries the blood of Chinggis. The house has married into the line; 10 political influence A child of the in-law line is enthroned and the ruler stands as güregen There will be no khan. — −20 horde unity. The gap is halved at once and drains twice as fast; the clock +25. If the gap is under 60 and no man of the line is left to raise, this ends in the Bulqaq

The regent dies. His heir inherits the state but not the khan. Thirty to eighty days after the accession the amirs are polled, and the clock moves +15. The heir keeps the khan only if his kingmaker score is at least 80% of the best rival's (The Khan Stays, +5 horde unity). Renown died with his father, which is half of why heirs lose. Otherwise the best rival takes the khan and the leadership (The Khan Comes to Us, +10 prestige), the regency moves to stage II if it was still in stage I, and the dispossessed house loses 10 horde unity and holds Take the Khan on the new regent.

The regent is murdered (The Beg Is Murdered). Rolled once a year:

Rivals whose kingmaker score is at least half the regent's Chance One or two 2% Three or more 4%

The chance is doubled if the nobles' satisfaction in his realm is under 40%. There is no roll in the twelve months after he wins a great battle.

The regent's state is destroyed. The amirs are polled again and the strongest takes the khan, or finds another.

docs.title: An amir house's succession
docs.text:
When the chief of an amir house dies, whoever leads the ulus is asked (An Amir's Succession):

Option Result The son holds what the father held. The house gains +30 opinion ("Confirmed our succession") That tümen is the khan's to give. A kinsman of the same house replaces its ruler. It costs 15 political influence, or 30 for a regent, and the house takes −75 opinion. From stage II there is an even chance the house refuses: it then holds Take the Khan on the regent and he loses 10 prestige. From stage III nobody can be imposed

docs.title: The cadet takes the tümen
docs.text:
In 1360 Hajji Beg, chief of the Barlas, fled before Tughluq Temür; a young kinsman, Temür, stayed, submitted and was confirmed over the tribe. A tümen was the house's, not the chief's. The same can happen to any amir house that has a grown man of the ruler's dynasty at court.

Trigger From stage III: the house loses a war to an invader from outside the ulus or to the regent, or its capital falls to one The Chief Looks to the Road The house rose against the khan and lost, and its chief survived; or it claimed the khan and lost to the regent The same event, at any stage From stage II, at peace: a kinsman has at least 15 more military skill than the chief The Tümen Talks — 3 chances in 100 a year, 12 in 100 for six years after a coup has succeeded anywhere in the ulus

If the chief rides out, the kinsman becomes ruler with 5 renown. Confirmed by an outsider, the house becomes that invader's tributary if the war between them can be closed; confirmed by the holder of the khan (or by the khan after a failed rising) no subject tie is made, and the new chief is sworn to him for five years. Each gains +40 opinion of the other. A house goes through this at most once in ten years, and a chief who stood his ground is not asked again for two.

The old chief leaves alive. Within one to three years he returns for his tümen (7 chances in 10: The Old Chief at the Edge of the Pastures, where the kinsman yields or refuses) or dies on the road (3 in 10). The first tümen in a regency to change chiefs by a coup earns its new chief 5 more renown and the house 10 prestige.

docs.title: Taking the khan by force
docs.text:
From stage III, when a country at war with the regent takes his capital:

The captor Result The eastern khanate, or any realm whose ruler is of the line The Khan Triumphant by the sword A member of the ulus The khan and the leadership pass to him (The Khan Is Ours, +15 prestige, +3 renown) Anyone else The khan's household flees: the clock +10, the gap −15

At any stage, a regent who loses a war to a realm whose ruler is of the line has met the Khan Triumphant by the sword.

docs.title: How it ends
docs.text: Ending Condition Result The Khan Triumphant (the purge) Back the Khan's Purge succeeds The kept khan becomes the ruler of the state that held him. The reform ends. The Khan Triumphant for twenty years: +20% crown power, −15% nobles' power, +0.10 monthly horde unity. +25 horde unity. The begs cannot raise another khan for fifteen years The Khan Triumphant (the sword) A realm of the line beats the regent in war, or takes his capital from stage III (One Khan Again) The victor's realm leads the ulus, re-entering it if it had left and bringing home the members who followed it east. The same modifier, unity and fifteen years Ṣāḥib-qirān Stage IV; a living khan in keeping; the ruler has a wife of the line; the gap at 60 or more for five years running The ulus becomes one man's realm. See The Ṣāḥib-qirān Bulqaq The gap empty for three years running; or the clock full in stage IV with the gap under 60; or the regent rules without a khan, no man of the line is left, and the gap is under 60 −25 prestige for the regent and the reform ends. The organisation is dissolved and every member stands alone, at −10 horde unity. The eastern khan, if there is one, holds Restore the Ulus on each of them

docs.title: The Breaking of the Chaghatay
docs.text:
The Chaghatay were an army with households. After a Bulqaq what is left in the pastures is the tümens' families and herds, and the neighbours come for them.

  • Claims. Every country bordering a former member holds Break the Tümens on it for 25 years.
  • The prize, once in a game. The first independent country not of Chaghatay culture and not itself a former member that holds, with its subjects, half the pastures the thirteen Chaghatay realms held in 1337 is asked what becomes of them (The Tümens Are Ours to Dispose Of):
Option Result Divide them among our own, hearth by hearth. In every such pasture we own, the Chaghatay tribesmen, soldiers and nobles become people of our own culture at once. The Tümens Distributed for 30 years: +20% manpower, +15% levy size. +50 prestige Let them keep their captains and their name, and ride for us. They keep their culture. The Tümens in Our Service, permanently: +10% levy size, +5% land morale, +1 cultures capacity. +25 prestige
  • The dissolution. Every year, in each old pasture held by a country not of Chaghatay culture, there is one chance in ten that its Chaghatay tribesmen, soldiers and nobles pass into the ruler's own people. Townsmen and peasants are untouched.

The same claims and the same prize open without a Bulqaq if a Ṣāḥib-qirān's army is lost (see his page).

docs.title: Playing it
docs.text:
As the regent. You are paid in political influence early and charged in horde unity and prestige later, and the gap drains four times faster in the last stage than in the first. Fight: battles, sieges and won wars are the only free fillers, and a raid counts as a war. Marry into the line early; it sets the clock back, and the last stage requires it. Largesse costs a year's income and buys ten points, two years of goodwill and two years in which no house that took it can claim the khan. Build crown power in your own realm: while it exceeds the nobles' and the three greatest amirs do not outweigh you, the clock runs backwards. Reach each stage's turn with the gap at 60 and the office hardens. Have an heir who is a soldier; he must reach four fifths of the best rival's score with none of your renown.

As an amir under a regent. Renown is only earned while a regency lasts, so this is when a name is made. From stage II you can claim the khan, but the capital only delivers him from stage III. A regent with no army, or one some house already outweighs, is the one to move against. If you would rather have a khan than this regent and the kept khan is a soldier, back his purge.

As the old khan. Defying keeps your claim and takes the eastern houses with you; beat the regent in any war and you lead the whole ulus again.

As a neighbour. Stage III hands the regent's three strongest neighbours a ten-year claim with cheap land. A Bulqaq hands every neighbour one.

See also: Ulus Chaghatay, The Ṣāḥib-qirān, Ulus and regency numbers, The Beglerbeg's Regency, Hordes, Custody of the Ulus, Known issues.

docs.title: The Beglerbeg's Regency
docs.text:
The khan reigns. We shall see to the rest.

New — untested in play

This is the newest system in the mod. It loads; it has not been played. Every number on this page is a first setting, shared with the Amirs' Regency. See Known issues.

When Berdibek Khan was killed in 1359 the line of Batu ran out, and the Rus chronicles call the twenty years that followed the Great Trouble. The man who mattered through most of it was Mamai, a commander married into the khan's house and not a Chinggisid. He could not be khan, so he kept one: a succession of princes was raised at his camp, coin was struck in their names, and the orders carried his seal. In 1378 Tokhtamysh, a prince of the line with a share of his own in the left wing, declared himself khan, and by 1380 he had beaten Mamai and joined his share to the khanate. A generation later Edigü held the same office for twenty years, and the khanate that came out the other side was no longer one realm.

The Jochid ulus was not an organisation of tümens. It was one realm, and the rivals of a beg who ruled it were its own princes. So this is a separate disaster from the Amirs' Regency of Ulus Chaghatay. The two share an idea and their numbers, but here the khan does not pass from house to house: a rival raises himself and fights for the throne.

docs.title: How it begins
docs.text:
At a khan's death the succession law may seat a man who is not of Chinggis's line. On the Golden Horde (GLH) The Törü of the Ulus scores every noble of the realm beside the princes, and a capable beg in a realm where the nobles hold much of the power can outscore them (see Hordes).

When that happens on a Steppe Horde whose throne a Chinggisid has held, outside Ulus Chaghatay, he does not become khan. Thirty to eighty days after his accession:

  • he takes a prince of the line into keeping — the youngest boy in the realm, failing that the least able grown man, and if every man of the line is ruling a share of his own, a lesser prince is found;
  • his state takes the reform Beglerbeg's Regency (+0.10 monthly horde unity, −0.10 monthly prestige, −20% political influence gain, −3% maximum control);
  • the disaster The Beglerbeg's Regency begins (−0.02 monthly horde unity, −5 subject loyalty) with the event The Beglerbeg.

Before this change the same accession cost 20 horde unity and seated a khan of an invented dynasty. A horde that never had a Chinggisid on its throne is not affected, and if no man of the line is left alive anywhere in the realm the older outcome There Is No One Left to Raise applies instead.

docs.title: The legitimacy gap
docs.text:
The regent's standing among the begs and the princes is a measure from 0 to 100 on the disaster's panel. It starts at 50 and counts as filled at 60 or more.

It drains each month Stage I / II / III / IV 0.15 / 0.30 / 0.45 / 0.60 No khan in keeping × 2 A prince with a share has a larger army than the regent × 1.5 The regent has a wife of the line × 0.75 It is filled by A great battle won +4 A siege won +2 A war won +10 A war won against a prince who had claimed the throne A further +10 Distribute Largesse +10 Marry into the Line +5 A war lost −15 A new khan raised after the old one dies −10 The regent dies and his heir takes over −15

When the kept khan dies there is one month with none, and the next month another prince is raised (Another Khan).

docs.title: The four stages
docs.text:
The clock runs from 0 to 100 in each stage.

What moves the clock Amount Each month the nobles hold 50% or more of estate power in the realm +1 Each month the crown holds more power than the nobles −0.5 A war lost +25 The khan's attempt to rule fails +25 The regent dies +20 Recall the Darughas −15 Stage What it opens I. The Beglerbeg's Peace One beg rules through a khan and the princes are quiet II. The Princes Stir Every prince with a share takes −60 opinion of the regent ("A beg rules in the khan's place"). Each year the strongest of them may declare himself khan III. The Shock from Outside Every independent neighbour with an army more than half the size of the regent's holds The Ulus in Disarray on him for ten years. Each prince with a share has an even chance of breaking away at once IV. The Office or the Shares The endings are counted

docs.title: A prince declares himself khan
docs.text:
From stage II, once a year, while some prince of the line holds a share and no claimant is already in the field:

Chance Base 10% Stage III or IV +10% The legitimacy gap under 30 +15% Within two years of Distribute Largesse The total × 0.25

The prince with the largest army breaks with the regent, ceases to be his subject and holds Restore the Ulus on him for fifteen years (A Prince Declares Himself Khan). An AI prince declares war at once; a player prince is told (The Felt Is Ours to Take) and chooses his moment. If the regent wins that war the claim is dead.

docs.title: The khan tries to rule
docs.text:
Once a year, while the kept khan is a grown man with military skill of 50 or more:

Chance Base 6% The legitimacy gap under 30 +8% Stage III or IV +4%

If he tries, he succeeds three times in ten, or one time in two if his military skill is 70 or more (The Khan Rules). If he fails (The Khan's Friends) the clock moves 25 toward the next stage and three times in four he is put to death. Unlike in Ulus Chaghatay, nobody outside needs to back him.

docs.title: The regent's actions
docs.text:
All three are on the disaster's panel.

Action Effect Distribute Largesse The gap +10. Nobles +5% satisfaction. Every prince with a share gains +25 opinion of us. For two years a prince is a quarter as likely to declare himself khan Marry into the Line Needs a living khan in keeping. The ruler takes a wife of Chinggis's house: +10 prestige, the gap +5, and it drains a quarter slower while this ruler lives. His heir must marry again Recall the Darughas For ten years −15% nobles' estate power and −10% nobles' target satisfaction; at once −15% nobles' satisfaction and −10 stability; the clock −15

A landless prince can also be given a share with the character action Grant a Share of the Ulus (see Hordes). It buys him off at the price of giving him a base: a prince with a share is the one who can declare himself khan.

docs.title: The regent dies
docs.text: His heir keeps the khan and the stage (The Beglerbeg's Heir): the gap loses 15, the clock moves 20, and the wife of the line was the dead man's. If instead the succession seats a prince of the line, the regency is over without a blow (The Line Returns, +10 horde unity, the reform ends).

docs.title: How it ends
docs.text:
Ending Condition Result The Khan Triumphant The kept khan's attempt succeeds; or a prince who declared himself khan beats the regent in war (A Khan of the Line) A khan of the line rules and the beglerbeg is put to death. If it was a prince's war, his share and the khanate are one realm again under him. The reform ends. The Khan Triumphant for twenty years (+20% crown power, −15% nobles' power, +0.10 monthly horde unity) and +25 horde unity The House Holds Stage IV, a living khan in keeping, and the gap at 60 or more for five years running The disaster ends; the khan and the reform stay. +20 horde unity, +15 prestige, and The Office Is the House's permanently (+0.05 monthly horde unity, +0.02 monthly prestige). At the ruler's death his heir begins the regency again from the first stage, with the gap already at 60 The Partition The gap empty for three years running; or the clock full in stage IV with the gap under 60 Every share becomes an independent khanate under its prince, at −60 opinion of the regent. He keeps what he holds directly, with no khan and no office: −30 horde unity, −25 prestige, and The Khanate Partitioned for twenty years (−0.05 monthly horde unity and prestige)

There is no Ṣāḥib-qirān here. Mamai's and Edigü's power was the Horde's own army and never became a following that could leave.

docs.title: Playing it
docs.text:
As the beglerbeg. The danger is a prince with a share and an army. Each share you leave standing is a possible claimant from stage II and an even chance of secession at stage III; each one whose army is larger than yours drains your standing half as fast again. Largesse every two years keeps the princes quiet and fills the gap. Marry into the line as soon as you hold a khan. Keep the crown stronger than the nobles in your own realm and the clock runs back; recall the darughas if the begs are what is driving it. Win wars: a lost one costs fifteen points and a quarter of a stage. The aim is to reach the fourth stage and hold the gap at 60 for five years.

As a prince with a share. If you are of the line and the man at the great camp is not, the yearly roll may raise you. Win the war and you rule the whole khanate with your share joined to it.

As the khan of the Golden Horde, before any of this. The regency starts when the Törü elects a beg. Read the line of succession: if a darugha or a great noble stands above your sons, the next accession is his.

See also: Hordes, The Amirs' Regency, Ulus Chaghatay, Ulus and regency numbers, Known issues.

docs.title: The Borrowed Mandate — Custody of the Ulus
docs.text:
One ulus, one khan, one steward — and it will be us.

The Mongol political order rested on one rule: only a descendant of Chinggis Khan could reign. When the Hülegüid line ran out, the great amirs did not break the rule; they kept it and hollowed it. Ḥasan-i Kūchak the Chobanid ruled through the princess Sati Beg and then through Sulaymān; Ḥasan-i Buzurg the Jalayirid through Muḥammad and Jahān Temür. Coin was struck and the khuṭba read in the khan's name while the amir held the seal. It worked for about twenty years, and it failed in two ways that were both on display between 1336 and 1357: rivalry — the Jalayirid–Chobanid wars were fought over whose khan was the khan — and expiry, as khans died and each replacement was a little less convincing than the last. In 1356 Shaykh Uvays quietly stopped minting a khan's name at all. A generation later Tīmūr made the arrangement permanent by ruling as gūrkān, son-in-law of the line.

The Borrowed Mandate is the disaster that audits the regent, the third of the legitimacy trials beside the Proof of Fortune and the Burden of the Sword.

Proof of Fortune Burden of the Sword Borrowed Mandate The claim the king bears the farr sword of the faith steward of the khan Under audit the ruler's fortune the realm's deeds the fiction itself How it fails the houses stop believing the umma stops believing rival khans, and dead ones

docs.title: The regency
docs.text:
The Chinggisid Regency cannot be chosen from the reform menu. The only way in is the opening event of the Succession of Erānzamīn — Find us a Borjigin to enthrone — or to start as the Chobanids (CHB) or Jalayirids (JAL), who hold it from the first day with Sati Beg and Muḥammad Khan as their kept khans. Only a member of the Erānzamīn organisation can hold it.

It is the cheapest legitimacy in the game, and it comes with a ceiling.

Effect of the reform Value Monthly legitimacy +0.5 Tribes levy size +15% Tribesmen population growth +20% All estates' target satisfaction +7.5% Tolerated and accepted culture upkeep −66% Monthly prestige −0.2 Political influence gain −20% Maximum control −3% Cabinet efficiency −10% Monthly drift toward decentralisation +0.10 Monthly drift toward Türk +0.10

Every act is issued in the puppet's name and has to be laundered through him first; the chancery never quite reaches full stride. While it lasts, a regent also cannot be asked the Matter of Tork and cannot form Persia — he rules in another man's name.

docs.title: When the audit starts
docs.text:
The disaster begins as soon as a realm holds the Chinggisid Regency, and it happens once per realm: however it ends, it never returns. It opens with the event The Borrowed Mandate, which lays out the two truths below.

While it runs, the disaster itself costs:

Effect Value Monthly legitimacy −0.10 Dīwān rebel growth +0.005 per month

That is the price of keeping the mask on. The heavier costs come from the two axes.

docs.title: The mandate is indivisible — the Duel of Khans
docs.text:
Each month a census counts the rival custodies standing: every other member of the Erānzamīn organisation that either

  • holds the Chinggisid Regency itself, or
  • is ruled by a Borjigin outright.

Subjects count as well as independent realms. In 1337 that means, at the least, the other great regent (Chobanid for the Jalayirids and the reverse) and Gurgan (GRG) under Ṭoghā Temür — the actual Borjigin sovereign of Khurasan, against whom every regency's fiction is junior — plus any other Borjigin-ruled member and every house that answered the opening question with a puppet of its own.

While any rival stands you carry The Duel of Khans, sized by their number:

Per rival custody (up to eight) Value Monthly legitimacy −0.10 Antagonism received +2.5%

Three rivals plus the disaster's own drag take −0.40 of the regency's +0.5. Every rival that falls — annexed by you, annexed by someone else, driven out of the regency, or replaced by a non-Borjigin ruler — gives a tenth back the next month.

A rival that you annex by force while the disaster runs is also a kill, and kills unlock the apparatus below faster than waiting does.

When the count reaches zero the Sole Custody clock starts. It needs 24 unbroken months; a single new rival — an AI that takes up a puppet, a Borjigin inheriting somewhere — resets it to nothing.

docs.title: The mandate is mortal — the charade
docs.text:
The kept khan is a character at your court and he will die. Each time, The Khan is Dead asks whether to end the fiction (−100 legitimacy, −25 stability, Amirs −30%, Tribes −30%, Dīwān +5%) or to enthrone another. Each enthronement deepens The Charade Continues by one step: −0.15 monthly legitimacy, −5% Amirs and −10% Dīwān target satisfaction per step. After three enthronements no fourth is offered, and the next death leaves only the full-price exit. The details are on the situation page.

The disaster panel counts this as the charade out of 4. The count starts at 1 with your first khan and rises by one with each replacement.

docs.title: The panel
docs.text:
The disaster panel shows three tracks:

Track Reads You want Rival custodies standing the monthly census 0 Sole Custody — months held months at zero rivals, out of 24 24 The charade — successions survived out of 4 as low as you can keep it

docs.title: The apparatus
docs.text:
Six actions belong to the disaster. Most of the maintenance tools are gated on the contest going your way: you earn the fiction by winning the duel, or by outlasting the field as it kills itself. Gold costs scale with the size of your economy; the figure given is the multiplier.

Action Requires Costs Cooldown Effect Press the Custody at least one rival; at peace — 1 year pick any rival custody from the roll and receive the Succession of Erānzamīn casus belli against it for 10 years. Unlike Press Claim on the situation panel, the target need not be a neighbour — the picker is also the plainest list of who the other khans are Demand Fealty at peace 5 political influence, paid win or lose 2 years call an independent Ilkhanate Governorate to swear; see below Proclaim the True Custody at least one rival standing, and either one kill or no more than three rivals left — 5 years +5 prestige; The True Custody Proclaimed for 5 years: +0.05 monthly legitimacy and +0.025 monthly prestige, multiplied by your kills (up to four) Secure the Khan's Household once only gold ×12 — The Khan's Household Secured for the rest of the disaster: +0.05 monthly legitimacy, +5% stability investment The Khan's Name on Every Coin two kills, or no more than two rivals left gold ×6 5 years The Khan's Name in Silver for 5 years: +0.10 monthly legitimacy, +15% minting income Summon the Kuriltai of Confirmation Sole Custody held 24 months; once only — — opens the fork below

All of these modifiers are tools of the disaster and are cleared when it ends.

docs.title: Demand Fealty and the sworn governorates
docs.text:
The demand goes to a governorate that is a member, is nobody's subject, and has not been asked by anyone in the last six months. The governor decides:

The governor… Result accepts becomes your sworn governorate; you send robes and gifts — gold equal to your tax base, which he receives; you lose 10 legitimacy (a sole ruler would not have to ask) and gain 10 prestige refuses nothing changes hands but the 5 political influence already spent; you are told Fealty Refused

An AI governor is likeliest to accept when it is weak or at war, and likeliest to refuse when it has an army of its own.

Governorates also come to a regent unasked — through their own Declare Fealty and through a periodic event that presses them to choose among the strongest regencies (see the Ilkhanate Governorate). However they arrive, while you rule as a Chinggisid Regency each sworn governorate is worth +0.05 monthly legitimacy and +0.10 monthly political influence (Sworn Governorates). The oath is thin — the governor still collects his own taxes and keeps his own horsemen — but each one is a witness that the custody is real. Two of them cancel a rival khan.

A sworn governorate does not drag you into its wars. When one is attacked by anyone but you, The Governorate Calls: ride to it and join the war as a defender, or leave it to its own walls at a cost of 5 legitimacy and its resentment.

docs.title: Sole Custody — the Kuriltai of Confirmation
docs.text:
Winning the custody war buys nothing durable; the fiction still expires. What it buys is the right to decide what the regency becomes.

Choice What happens The Quiet Crown — the Shaykh Uvays move the Chinggisid Regency is dropped on your own terms: −25 legitimacy instead of −100; Dīwān +10%, Amirs −10%. You are now free to take a crown in your own name from the reform menu, the Matter of Tork can be asked of you, and Persia is no longer barred. Until you adopt a new answer you carry Unsettled Legitimacy (−0.6 monthly legitimacy), so have the next reform ready The Restored Yarliq — wed the golden line the regency is replaced by The Gurkani Regime and you gain the permanent The Restored Yarliq: +0.25 monthly legitimacy, +0.05 monthly prestige, Amirs and Tribes target satisfaction +5%, a monthly drift toward Türk; Amirs +10%, Tribes +10% satisfaction. The khan is your house now and the puppet-death cycle ends. This is the Mongol endpoint, and deliberately not Persia

docs.title: Endured — The Long Regency
docs.text:
If the disaster has run 300 months and the charade stands at 2 or more — the fiction has survived a succession and twenty-five years — you are offered a weaker, dated fork:

Choice What happens Institutionalise it −10 legitimacy; the regency becomes The Gurkani Regime Drop it a late Quiet Crown at a survivor's price: −50 legitimacy Ride on the disaster closes its books, but you remain a regent and khans keep dying

docs.title: The Fiction Expires
docs.text: If the regency is lost with none of the above to explain it — the mask taken off at a khan's death, by choice or because no further enthronement was credible — the disaster ends in public failure. On top of the −100 legitimacy of the exit itself, the realm is forced into the Amīr Sultanate, the honest version of what the regency always was, and carries The Mask Came Off permanently: −0.05 monthly prestige, −1 diplomatic reputation. As things stand the Amīr Sultanate does not by itself lift Unsettled Legitimacy, so the fallen regent nets roughly −0.45 legitimacy a month until he moves on to a better answer.

docs.title: What the endpoints are
docs.text: Reform In brief The Gurkani Regime the capped, stable version of the borrowed mandate: +0.2 monthly legitimacy, Tribes levy size +20%, tribesmen growth +10%, estates +5%; −0.1 monthly prestige, −10% political influence gain, −2% maximum control, −10% cabinet efficiency. No more successions to survive and no rivals to outbid. Land held by a Gurkani realm is immune to the succession's sword rule, and the regime is one of the gates to Iran o Turan Amīr Sultanate rule by the army's assent: +0.15 monthly legitimacy, Amirs power +25%, Amirs levy size +20%, Amirs seated in the cabinet, cavalry and manpower bonuses. No farr claimed, no khan needed — and, for a realm that arrives here by failure, no relief from Unsettled Legitimacy. See Government reforms

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Count your rivals before you count your legitimacy. +0.5 looks generous until the disaster (−0.10) and three rival khans (−0.30) are subtracted. A regent with four or more rivals is losing legitimacy from the first month.
  • Annex, do not merely beat. Only a rival that ceases to exist — or ceases to be a regent — leaves the census. Vassalising a rival regent does not remove him. Annexing him yourself is a kill, and kills are what unlock the denunciation and the coinage early.
  • Gurgan is the long pole. Ṭoghā Temür is a rival by blood, not by reform, and he is on the far side of Iran from Tabriz and Baghdad. Sole Custody is not possible while a Borjigin rules any member.
  • Collect governorates. At 5 political influence a try, sworn governorates are the cheapest legitimacy available to a regent, and each also brings political influence. Defend them when they call, or accept the 5-legitimacy fine.
  • Buy the Household early. It is the one tool with no gate, and it pays for the whole length of the disaster.
  • Decide before the third khan. After three enthronements the charade costs −0.45 a month and the next death is a forced −100. Reach the Kuriltai, or reach the 25-year mark, before that.
  • The Quiet Crown is a ramp, not a home. It is the only orderly road from the regency to the farr, the ghazā, a Tāzīk victory or Persia. Take it with legitimacy to spare and a reform in mind.

See also: The Succession of Erānzamīn, The Erānzamīn organisation, The Ilkhanate Governorate, Farr — the Proof of Fortune, The Burden of the Sword, The Matter of Tork, Government reforms, Ulus Chaghatay.

docs.title: Buildings, goods and materials
docs.text:
The pen writes the land onto the register; the sword takes it off again.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The Unaudited Iqṭāʿ and Tuyul tiers, the waqf endowments' yearly reassessment and the qanāt pair were built or rebuilt for 1.4 and their numbers are a first draft. The Kāshī Guild currently has inputs but no output defined (see below).

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
A Persianate state in 1337 is held together by two kinds of paper. One is the chancery's own: the dīwān with its registers, audits and provincial branches, the institution every dynasty from the Buyids to the Ilkhans inherited and none could rule without. The other is the paper by which the chancery gives land away: the iqṭāʿ, a registered assignment of a district's revenue to an amīr in return for his cavalry, and the waqf, a pious endowment that puts property beyond the reach of tax collector and confiscation alike. Both began as instruments of the state and both tended, over generations, to become the private property of the people they were issued to. Underneath all of it lies the water: the qanāt, the underground channel that makes the plateau farmable and that has to be dug out again after every war.

This page is the reference catalogue for every building the mod adds or changes, followed by the changes to goods, construction costs and markets.

docs.title: The Dīwān chain
docs.text:
Three chancery buildings and the court. All require the Persianate Sultanate government and are removed if the country leaves it. Nobles staff them.

Building Where Requirements Limit Local Dīwān Town, city or megalopolis that is not the capital Local control above 10% One per province Regional Dīwān The capital, if it is a city or megalopolis. An empire-rank realm may also seat one in a city in each area that has none Duchy rank or higher One per site Dīwān of the Realms The capital, if it is a city or megalopolis Kingdom rank and one of: Türk–Tāzīk axis at 50 or more toward Tāzīk; the Restore Persian Bureaucracy action taken; empire rank One Royal Court The capital (town or larger) None beyond the government One

docs.title: Local Dīwān
docs.text:
The provincial chancery branch: the wālī's secretariat, with the tax rolls, the land registers and the qāḍī's records of endowment and contract.

  • Acts as a proximity source of 30 (a governor's seat gives 80), so control radiates outward from it.
  • +10 maximum literacy for local nobles and burghers; +0.75 local Dīwān estate power; draws nobles, clergy and burghers to the town.
  • Upkeep: 0.3 paper, 0.1 books, 0.1 fine cloth.
  • On completion: a small Farsi noble pop settles, the realm moves +1 toward Tāzīk, the Dīwān gains 3% satisfaction and the Amirs lose 2%.
  • It can only be demolished once local control has fallen below 30%, and doing so costs 5% Dīwān satisfaction.

docs.title: Regional Dīwān
docs.text:
The chancery of a middling realm, of the kind the Injuids ran from Shīrāz, and under an empire the regional office of a great provincial city.

  • Proximity source of 66; +10 maximum literacy for local nobles and burghers; +0.33 local Dīwān estate power.
  • When it stands in the capital it also gives the country +1.5% maximum control, +5% crown power, +15% Dīwān estate power and +1.5% tax efficiency.
  • Upkeep: 0.5 paper, 0.2 books, 0.2 fine cloth.
  • On completion: a Farsi noble pop and +2.5 toward Tāzīk.
  • Building the Dīwān of the Realms in the same city replaces it.

docs.title: Dīwān of the Realms
docs.text:
The Dīwān al-Mamālik, the central chancery of a kingdom or empire: the office of the Juvaynīs and Rashīd al-Dīn.

Effect (country-wide) Value Maximum control +4% Crown estate power +20% Dīwān estate power +50% Tax efficiency +4% Monthly political influence gain +10%

It also gives +1.0 local Dīwān estate power in the capital. Upkeep is 0.8 paper, 0.3 books and 0.3 fine cloth. Founding it settles a Farsi noble pop in the capital and moves the realm +5 toward Tāzīk. The requirements only apply to building it: once standing it stays until the city stops being the capital or the government changes.

docs.title: Royal Court
docs.text: The bārgāh, the audience hall and household. It gives +2% cabinet efficiency, +10% crown power and a slow monthly drift toward absolutism, and it is expensive to keep: 1 paper, 1 fine cloth, 0.5 books, 0.15 furniture, 0.1 glass and 0.05 tools.

docs.title: Where the chanceries stand in 1337
docs.text:
Building Location (owner) Dīwān of the Realms Tabrīz (Chobanids, CHB), Delhi (DLH), Cairo (Mamluks, MAM) Regional Dīwān Baghdad (Jalayirids, JAL), Damascus (MAM), Daulatabad and Multan (DLH) Local Dīwān Aleppo and Alexandria (MAM)

Within Erānzamīn itself there is exactly one Dīwān of the Realms, at Tabrīz, and one Regional Dīwān, at Baghdad. Everyone else builds from nothing.

docs.title: Iqṭāʿ Grant
docs.text:
A chancery-registered grant of a rural district's revenue to an amir, who settles there with his household and retinue.

Who builds it The crown. Estates cannot Where Rural settlements only Requirements Persianate Sultanate; the Amirs hold the Iqtāʿ Grant or Hereditary Tuyul privilege; local control below 60% Levels Up to 3 Cost Very cheap (about half a month's income) Upkeep 0.1 horses, 0.2 weaponry, 0.2 leather, 0.2 cloth, 0.1 fine cloth, 0.05 paper Demolition Only when local control is above 80%; costs 5% Amirs satisfaction

Effects:

  • +20% local levy size, more local noble pops (a flat +0.1 plus a share scaled to population) and +10% local noble growth.
  • +1.0 local Amirs estate power, −5% local maximum control, −10 maximum noble literacy, and a slight permanent drag on Dīwān satisfaction. These are carried by a separate location modifier, "Offsetting Iqta Grant Effects", so read both tooltips. They are designed to scale with the level of the grant.
  • The building tooltip shows a tiny manpower bonus. It is cancelled by the same modifier and is there only so the AI will build grants; an iqṭāʿ gives levies and no manpower.
  • On completion: a noble pop of your primary culture and religion settles and the realm moves very slightly toward Türk.

Both standard Persianate starting setups begin with the Iqtāʿ Grant privilege already held, so most countries can register grants from the first day.

The Amirs Ask for Land. In the first year, and every ten years after while fewer than fifteen of your locations carry a grant, the Amirs petition for land. Accepting gives them the Iqtāʿ Grant privilege if they lack it, registers three grants at once and free of charge in eligible rural locations, and adds 10% Amirs satisfaction. Refusing costs 15% Amirs satisfaction and pleases the Dīwān by 5%. The AI always accepts.

docs.title: Unaudited Iqṭāʿ and Tuyul
docs.text:
The Amirs build these themselves on top of an existing grant. They are how a revocable assignment turns into a patrimony.

Unaudited Iqṭāʿ Tuyul Built by The Amirs estate The Amirs estate Needs An Iqṭāʿ Grant in the location; local control below 30% An Unaudited Iqṭāʿ in the location; the Hereditary Tuyul or Soyurghal Grants privilege. Replaces the Unaudited Iqṭāʿ Local Amirs power +0.5 +1.5 Local maximum control −15% −30% Local levy size −10% no change Amirs' satisfaction equilibrium +1% each +2% each On completion −0.25 toward Türk; Dīwān −1%, Amirs +1% −0.5 toward Türk; Dīwān −2%, Amirs +2% You may demolish it when Local control is above 70% (Amirs −5%) Local control is above 90% (Amirs −10%)

The first Unaudited Iqṭāʿ in the realm announces itself with the event The Audit That Never Came. The remedy short of raising control is the maẓālim court's Decree: Reopen the Audit, which forces about a quarter of the unaudited grants back onto the register at a quarter of the usual resentment, moves the realm +0.5 toward Tāzīk and gives +5 legitimacy. It cannot touch a Tuyul.

docs.title: Waqf endowments
docs.text:
Waqf buildings are raised by the estates, not by you. They appear only in a Persianate Sultanate that holds the Muṣādara Right privilege: the endowment is the shelter against confiscation, so it exists only where confiscation does.

Building Estate Where Grand form unlocked by Aʿyān Waqf Dīwān Towns and cities Inviolable Endowments Urban Waqf Burghers Towns and cities Charter of the Bazaar Awqāf Clerical Waqf Clergy (Muslim countries) Anywhere, including rural Sanctity of the Endowments

Each has up to ten levels and gives its estate +0.25 local power. The Grand form of each replaces the ordinary one once the charter privilege is granted.

What they cost you is worked out once a year for the whole realm. For each estate the game adds up, over every location holding its waqf, the location's tax base × the estate's local share of power × the waqf's level (grand levels count double), and expresses the total as a percentage of the country's tax base. That percentage sets the size of a country modifier:

Per point of share Aʿyān ("Tax Lost to Waqf Exemptions") Urban ("The Bazaar Endowments") Clerical ("The Clerical Endowments") The estate's maximum tax −0.5% −0.5% −0.5% Estate enrichment +0.25% +0.25% +0.25% Loan capacity −0.5% −0.5% −0.5% Tax efficiency −0.2% none none Clergy estate power +0.25% +0.25% +0.25%

In addition:

  • Each ordinary waqf level pays its estate 0.1 gold a month, each grand level 0.2.
  • The same share shelters the estate's treasury from you: muṣādara and corruption fines take that much less, up to a ceiling of 90%.
  • The first endowment in the realm fires the event Given to God, Forever.

Getting rid of them. Demolishing a waqf costs the owning estate 2.5% satisfaction (5% for a grand one) and the clergy 1% (2%). While the matching charter is in force the endowments cannot be demolished at all. The maẓālim court's Decree: Reclaim the Illegal Waqf dissolves the waqf in roughly a fifth of the locations that have one, at a quarter of the usual resentment and with +5 legitimacy, but it is only available while you hold the Muṣādara Right and no charter has been granted to any estate. The charters are attractive (each gives its estate +10% satisfaction equilibrium and +0.025 monthly legitimacy) and that is the trap.

docs.title: Qanāts
docs.text:
The mod adds three kinds of land to the map: Qanat Farmlands (165 locations on the plateau), Seasonal Irrigation (190 locations) and Crumbling Qanats (defined, but no location starts as one).

Land Population capacity Food Development growth Supply limit Qanat Farmlands 65 +22% +4% 2 Seasonal Irrigation 80 +28% +6% 3 Crumbling Qanats 45 +10% +2% 0

On top of the land sit two buildings:

Qanāt Network Damaged Qanāt How it appears Present at the start in every Qanat Farmlands location owned by a member of the Erānzamīn organisation, except those with a Damaged Qanāt. Can be built elsewhere on qanāt land Present at the start in forty locations of the Khurāsān–Balkh belt, among them Merv, Marv al-Rūdh, Qūchān, Bojnord, Esfarāyen, Maymana, Sheberghān, Kunduz and Baghlān. Cannot be built Levels Up to 3 1 Population capacity +5 −15 Food +2% −10% Development growth +0.66% −4% Supply limit +0.33 −1.5 Maximum RGO size none −5% Upkeep 0.3 masonry, 0.1 tools none

A Damaged Qanāt cannot be demolished. It goes away in two ways: the location grows past 50 development on its own, or you build a Qanāt Network over it.

Building a Qanāt Network takes ten years. It is cheap to commission and the cost is the wait and the upkeep. It needs local control above 30% and either a Türk–Tāzīk axis of at least 25 toward Tāzīk or the Dīwān's Land Registers privilege. Completing one removes the Damaged Qanāt, gives the peasants 3% satisfaction and moves the realm +1 toward Tāzīk. Neither building can be demolished, and the base game's irrigation building is removed from any location that has one of them.

In the current build the damaged belt is fixed at the start of the game. War and sack do not yet turn a working network into a damaged one.

docs.title: Goods, construction and markets
docs.text:
Naphtha and tar. Tar can now be gathered as a raw material, and the Absheron seeps at Baku produce it. A new first-age advance, Naphtha Gathering, permits the extraction; it sits directly after bronze working at a low research cost.

Horses. Horses no longer count as food, and their transport cost falls from 2 to 0.5: herds walk to market. Camels are left as the base game has them.

Building materials. Base output per worker is doubled for clay (0.02), stone (0.012) and lumber (0.01), and raised for sand (0.01).

Demand. Paper, books and fine cloth are demanded at 1.5 times the normal rate in the Persia, Khurāsān and Fertile Crescent regions. Tribesmen now buy modest amounts of tea, salt, weaponry, cloth, tools and jewelry, eat more wheat and millet, and buy no lumber or leather on the market.

Construction costs. Glass is no longer needed to build the common town buildings (temples, madrasas, hospitals, markets and the rest) or a market centre; masonry of equal value replaces it. A caravanserai is built from masonry, livestock and horses and no longer needs lumber or camels.

Trade range. Every country in the world has +300 trade range.

Markets in 1337. Herāt has its own market. In the north the Kazan market sits at Bolghar instead, and the base game's markets at Sarāy-Jük and Chimgi-Tura are removed.

Start of game. Every Erānzamīn member's farmland and Seasonal Irrigation locations begin with the base game's irrigation building.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Build a Local Dīwān in every province you mean to keep. It is the only building here that raises control at a distance, and each one nudges the realm toward Tāzīk.
  • Register iqṭāʿ grants where control is poor anyway. A grant costs 5% maximum control in a place that had little, and gives 20% more levies there.
  • Watch for the Unaudited Iqṭāʿ. It needs control below 30%, so a Local Dīwān or a governor nearby is the prevention, and the decree is the cure. Do not grant Hereditary Tuyul or Soyurghal Grants unless you accept that the Tuyul tier will follow.
  • Decide early whether you will ever want to dissolve waqf. Once one charter is granted, the decree is closed to you until the charter is revoked.
  • Repair the Khurāsān qanāts if you hold them for the long term. Ten years is slow, but a Damaged Qanāt costs a location 15 population capacity and a tenth of its food.

See also: Dīwān estate, Amirs estate, Estate privileges, The maẓālim court, The military system, Türk vs Tāzīk, The Matter of Tork.

docs.title: The Commonwealth of Martyrs
docs.text:
Sar be-dār — "our heads on the gallows, rather than submit."

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

Estate power now comes from pop types, and the Shaykhī dervishes' weight was rebuilt for 1.4 with a per-location multiplier. Their share is designed to read about 30% at Sabzavār on day one; that figure, and everything keyed on it (preacher dispatch, the notables' takeover), has not been confirmed in a 1.4 game.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: In 1337 the men of Bāshtīn, a village in the Bayhaq district of Khurāsān, killed an Ilkhanid fiscal agent, took Sabzavār, and held western Khurāsān for forty-four years. The Sarbadār state was an uneasy partnership between local landed and urban leaders and the Shaykhiyya, the dervish organisation founded by Shaykh Khalīfa and built into a disciplined network of craftsmen and villagers by Shaykh Ḥasan Jūrī. Its Twelver piety was real and was expressed in the ordinary idioms of the age: devotion to the Prophet's house, expectation of the Hidden Imām, the Sufi bond of master and disciple. Under ʿAlī-yi Muʾayyad it took institutional form: Twelver coinage, and a letter to the jurist Muḥammad b. Makkī of Jabal ʿĀmil asking for a book of law, which he answered with al-Lumʿa al-Dimashqiyya. Historians disagree about how consistently Shīʿī or how egalitarian the state was; twelve rulers in under half a century, most of them removed by violence, suggests how unsettled the partnership stayed. The mod's Commonwealth of Martyrs models that partnership as a government type of its own, and extends it past 1381 as a counterfactual.

docs.title: Who starts as one
docs.text:
Only the Sarbadars (SRB). They begin with six locations around their capital Sabzavār, the Shaykhiyya as their religious establishment, a level-2 Dervish Khānaqāh and a Zūrkhāna in Sabzavār, and a lodge in each of two other locations. Their neighbours are Togha Temür's ordu in Gurgān, the Jauni Qurbān at Ṭūs and Nishapur, and the Kartids at Herat.

At the opening of the Succession of Erānzamīn, a Commonwealth has exactly one answer to "Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty": defiance. It gives +10 devotion, +10% Shaykhī and +5% Sufyānī satisfaction, and for the Sarbadars it fires Heads Pledged to the Gallows:

  • 500 gold (the liquidated estates of the expropriated amīrs);
  • five Dervish Corps regiments mustered at Sabzavār;
  • Revolutionary Zeal for 25 years.

Other Commonwealths can appear later: a Shia religious rising that has to name its own government may choose the Sabzavār answer, and a village-based ṭarīqa order that rises against its patron lands as a Commonwealth (see Ṭarīqa orders).

docs.title: How it differs from a sultanate
docs.text:
Persianate Sultanate Commonwealth of Martyrs Government power Legitimacy Devotion Political dyad Dīwān vs Amirs Sufyānī Notables vs Shaykhī Dervishes Succession Dynastic Dyarchic Election between the two wings The khuṭba question Must be answered with an Age 1 reform Not asked: coin is struck in the Hidden Imām's name Parliament The maẓālim court The Sarbadar Council Army core Amirs' levies, ghulāms The salaried Dervish Corps and town militia Rulers Regnal numbers No regnal numbering; the Imām is the only sovereign

The Commonwealth does not carry the unsettled-legitimacy penalty that sultanates suffer before choosing a legitimacy reform, and it cannot take those reforms.

docs.title: The Bāshtīn Proclamation
docs.text:
The founding reform is applied at start and defines the polity:

Effect Value Nobles estate power −50% Amirs estate power −75% Dīwān estate power −30% Shaykhī Dervishes levy contribution +75% Sufyānī Notables levy contribution +25% Burghers levy contribution +25% Peasants levy contribution −50% Tribes levy contribution −80% Dervish Corps build, maintenance and reinforcement cost −50% each Manpower +25% Land morale +10% Monthly devotion +0.05 Tolerance of the true faith +2 Pop promotion speed +150% Stability cost efficiency −10% Monthly legitimacy −0.10 Monthly drift towards Tāzīk +0.05

It also seats both wings in the cabinet and the council, fully enfranchises the peasantry, and lowers the control ceiling.

docs.title: The two wings
docs.text: Both estates start with a base target satisfaction of 40%. Each one's opinion of you falls as the other gains power, so the dyarchy cannot be made happy on both sides at once.

docs.title: Sufyānī Notables
docs.text:
