Sayyids, civic notables and the heads of merchant families: the men of the courts, the endowments and the ledgers. Their power is drawn from nobles pops living in cities and province capitals. Their characters have dynasties. They like stability, high control in the home region and a Tāzīk-leaning realm.

State Effects Satisfied +12% cabinet efficiency, +8% tax efficiency, +10% maximum control, +5% stability cost efficiency Dominant +25% cabinet efficiency, +15% tax efficiency, +15% maximum control, −10% policy change cost, −0.05 monthly devotion, drift towards centralization Collapsed −30% cabinet efficiency, −20% tax efficiency, −15% stability cost efficiency, +0.08 monthly devotion

docs.title: Shaykhī Dervishes
docs.text:
The armed brotherhood of the khānaqāh network. Their power is drawn from soldiers pops, which the Dervish Khānaqāh attracts and employs, so lodges are how the wing grows. Their characters have no dynasties. They gain +25 opinion while you are at war and +15 under a Shia ruler. They pay almost no tax.

State Effects Satisfied +20% land morale, +20% levy combat efficiency, +15% manpower, +0.04 monthly devotion, −50% Dervish Corps build cost Dominant +30% land morale, +25% manpower, +40% loot, +0.10 monthly devotion, +2 tolerance of the true faith, cheaper Dervish Corps upkeep, −20% cabinet efficiency, −20% tax efficiency, −10% stability cost efficiency, drift towards decentralization Collapsed −20% land morale, −15% manpower, −0.08 monthly devotion

docs.title: Privileges
docs.text:
Every privilege raises its own wing's power and target satisfaction. The starting set is marked (start).

Sufyānī privilege Power Main effects Sufyānī Civic Assembly (start) +40% +5% stability cost efficiency, +5% cabinet efficiency Sufyānī Waqf Administration (start) +50% +8% tax efficiency, −15% Shaykhī power, −0.03 monthly devotion Sufyānī Judicial Office +45% +10% maximum control, +8% stability cost efficiency Sufyānī Urban Militia +35% +30% burgher levies, +10% fort defence, −10% Shaykhī power Sufyānī Tax-Farming Rights +55% +15% tax efficiency, −5% maximum control, +50% privilege revocation cost Sufyānī Sayyid Pensions (Shia only) +40% +2 tolerance of the true faith, +0.03 monthly devotion, −10% Shaykhī power The Fixed Tax Register +30% +8% peasant satisfaction, −10% maximum estate tax, pops slower to join rebels Chancery of the Vow (after taking Nishapur) +35% +20% Dīwān power, +5% tax efficiency, +5% cabinet efficiency The Collaborators' Pens (after taking Nishapur) +30% +10% cabinet efficiency, −0.03 monthly devotion, −5% Shaykhī satisfaction Shaykhī privilege Power Main effects Shaykhī Dervish Corps (start) +50% +25–35% manpower, +15% land morale, +0.05 monthly devotion Shaykhī Mahdist Proclamation (start, Shia only) +60% +20% land morale, −0.025 monthly war exhaustion, +30% loot, +0.10 monthly devotion, −15% stability cost efficiency, −20% Sufyānī power Shaykhī Anti-Aristocratic Purges (start) +50% −50% Amirs power, −30% Nobles power, +10% tax efficiency Shaykhī Khānaqāh Network +45% +2 tolerance of the true faith, +0.03 monthly devotion, −10% cabinet efficiency, −10% Sufyānī power Shaykhī Dargāh Endowments +40% +2 tolerance of the true faith, +0.04 monthly devotion, +10% clergy power, −5% tax efficiency, −10% Sufyānī power Shaykhī Jihād Authority +55% −25% cost of war without a casus belli, +10% land morale, +0.07 monthly devotion, −5% stability cost efficiency The Saddled Horse Vigil +30% +0.10 monthly devotion, −5% stability cost efficiency The Martyrs' Rolls +30% +0.02 monthly devotion, +5% land morale; devotion from great battles (below) The Common Table +30% +25% pop promotion speed, +5% peasant and +3% burgher satisfaction, −5% Sufyānī satisfaction

docs.title: Devotion
docs.text:
Devotion replaces legitimacy as the Commonwealth's government power. Its sources beyond the reform, estates and privileges:

  • Conquest: +1 devotion for every location taken.
  • The Martyrs' Rolls: with the privilege, a great battle against a realm whose ruler is of Turkic, Mongol or Tatar culture gives +2 devotion if won and +4 if lost. (Minor skirmishes do not count.)
  • The Tenth of Muḥarram: a roughly annual ʿĀshūrāʾ commemoration. The street procession gives +5 devotion and favours the Shaykhīs; the sponsored majlis gives +2 and favours the Sufyānīs and burghers.
  • The Sarbadār Movement: +0.02 monthly devotion for members.
  • Custodian of the Threshold: +0.05 monthly devotion, permanently, for taking Mashhad.

docs.title: Revolutionary Zeal
docs.text:
The founding generation is a wasting asset. Revolutionary Zeal lasts 25 years and decays steadily to nothing over that time. At full strength:

Effect Value Manpower +50% Army maintenance efficiency +25% Regiment reinforcement speed +25% Land morale +20% Land morale recovery +10% Tax efficiency +10% Monthly prosperity and development (all locations) −0.001 each

While the zeal lasts and the Commonwealth is fighting a defensive war, The Vow Besieged adds a second, undecayed helping of every bonus in the table (and a further −0.0005 monthly prosperity and development). Because the surge is flat while the base withers, a late defensive war restores most of what the years have taken. A Commonwealth founded later by a rising also receives the full 25 years.

docs.title: Succession: the Dyarchic Election
docs.text:
A ruler serves until death. The council then chooses among up to five candidates drawn from the two wings.

Factor Weight Shaykhī candidate + his military skill Sufyānī candidate + his administrative skill Shaykhī candidate while the Commonwealth is at war +150 Sufyānī candidate while the Commonwealth is at peace +100 Any candidate + age and all three skills

In practice: die at war and a shaykh follows; die at peace and a malik follows.

docs.title: The Sarbadar Council
docs.text:
The Commonwealth's parliament seats the two wings, the clergy, the peasants and the tribes; nobles are barred. Each wing brings its own issues.

Issue Wing Result if passed Codify the Qāḍī Courts Sufyānī Codified Qāḍī Courts for 10 years: +10% maximum control, +5% stability cost efficiency Curb the Dervish Excesses (Shaykhī power above 55%) Sufyānī 8 years of −10% Shaykhī power; −15% Shaykhī and +15% Sufyānī satisfaction Negotiate the Amīr Settlement Sufyānī 15 years of +15% improve relations, +1 diplomatic reputation, +10% Amirs power; −10% Shaykhī satisfaction Endow a Great Madrasa Sufyānī 20 years of +8% research speed, +1 tolerance of the true faith, +10% clergy power Subsidize the Bazaar Caravans Sufyānī 10 years of +10% tax efficiency and +10% trade income Proclaim Jihād (at peace) Shaykhī 5 years of −25% no-casus-belli war cost, +10% land morale, +10% manpower; +10 devotion Purge the Surviving Amīrs Shaykhī 8 years of −25% Amirs and −15% Nobles power, +10% tax efficiency, −10% improve relations Mobilize the Dervish Corps Shaykhī 5 years of +20% manpower and +10% land morale Proclaim the Imām's Return Imminent Shaykhī 6 years of +0.10 monthly devotion, +20% land morale, −15% stability cost efficiency, −10% cabinet efficiency; +20 devotion, −15% Sufyānī satisfaction Excommunicate the Compromisers (Sufyānī power above 50%) Shaykhī −20% Sufyānī and +15% Shaykhī satisfaction, +10 devotion

The council also hears maẓālim cases against each wing, five apiece. Ruling against the notables costs them 15–25% satisfaction and usually seizes a quarter to two-fifths of their estate's gold for the wronged parties or the treasury. Ruling against the dervishes costs them 15–20% satisfaction and 5–10 devotion: the brethren hold no fortunes to confiscate, so the Commonwealth pays for disciplining its own base in fervour and is repaid in order.

docs.title: Buildings, units and the cabinet
docs.text:
Name What it does Dervish Khānaqāh Up to 5 levels, any settlement. Employs and attracts soldiers pops, gives local manpower and garrison, raises local Shaykhī power, and allows regiments to be recruited in the location. Consumes cloth and weaponry. Mission of the Liberated One level, built in your own land. Converts the location to Shia and lowers unrest; each month Sunni laborers, peasants and tribesmen there have a chance to convert by halves. Disappears if the location leaves Commonwealth rule. Dervish Corps Heavy infantry unique to the Commonwealth. Deals +30% and takes −30% morale damage, takes +15% strength damage, +2 initiative, light supply needs. Stronger in farmland, hills and mountains; −10% on grassland and sparse steppe. Charter of the Liberated Administrative cabinet action. Target an owned province that is at least half Shia and still has conquered locations: integration runs with a +8 integration speed bonus until every location is integrated.

The Zūrkhāna and the Shahr Militia are shared with the wider mod; see Buildings and the military system.

docs.title: Mashhad and Nishapur
docs.text:
Two conquests fire once each.

The Threshold of the Eighth Imam (Mashhad). All three choices grant Custodian of the Threshold (+0.05 monthly devotion, +1 tolerance of the true faith, permanent). Give the shrine to the notables or to the brethren for +25 devotion and +15% satisfaction for the chosen wing; or write to the jurist of Jabal ʿĀmil for +15 devotion and +15% clergy satisfaction.

The Old Metropolis (Nishapur). Seat the notables for +5 stability, +15% Sufyānī satisfaction and The Nishapur Chancery for 25 years (+5% cabinet efficiency, +5% tax efficiency); or convene the tribunal for 100 gold, +10 devotion, +10% Shaykhī satisfaction and −5 stability. Either way, taking Nishapur unlocks the two chancery privileges above.

docs.title: The reform path
docs.text:
A single line of later reforms turns the vow into a clerical state. Each requires the one before it and a Shia realm.

Reform Age Requires Main effects The Niyāba ʿĀmma Charter 2 Chancery of the Vow privilege Grants the chancery apparatus that the rest of the mod's administrative content keys on; cancels the −30% Dīwān power; +10% cabinet efficiency, +5% maximum control, +5% tax efficiency Usūlī Consolidation 2 The Charter +30% clergy power, +15% cabinet efficiency, +10% maximum control, +10% research speed, −15% Shaykhī power Marjaʿiyya 3 Usūlī Consolidation +50% clergy power, +20% cabinet efficiency, +15% maximum control, +0.20 monthly legitimacy, +3 tolerance of the true faith, −25% Sufyānī and −10% Shaykhī power Wilāyat-i Faqīh 4 Marjaʿiyya +75% clergy power, +25% cabinet efficiency, +25% maximum control, +0.15 monthly devotion, +5 tolerance of the true faith, −50% Sufyānī and −25% Shaykhī power, −10% manpower, −20% improve relations

The last step is a twentieth-century doctrine projected backwards; the mod's own text says so.

docs.title: The Sarbadar Phenomenon
docs.text:
A situation, active from the first day and for as long as any Commonwealth exists. It is visible to countries in the Erānzamīn region, the Middle East and Central Asia, and to anyone who has a cell.

Sarbadar Preachers are covert cells that appear in other rulers' cities. They can only take root in a city with Muslim pops, inside those same regions, that is not already Commonwealth-owned.

Every Commonwealth-owned city and every existing cell is a carrier. Each month, each carrier makes these rolls:

Roll Monthly chance per carrier Plant a cell in a random eligible city with a Zūrkhāna in the carrier's market 6% Plant a cell in a random eligible city in that market whose ruler has granted the Asnāf–Futuwwa Compact 4% Plant a cell in any random eligible city in that market 2%

There is also a long jump: each Middle Eastern or Central Asian realm in trade range of a market whose centre holds a cell or belongs to a Commonwealth has a 2% monthly chance of a cell in one of its cities. Cells spread cells, so an ignored infection compounds along the caravan roads.

What a cell does to its host:

  • −0.005 monthly control and +0.5 unrest in the location; pops there join rebels more readily;
  • steady conversion to Shia, plus a 2% monthly chance for each Sunni burgher or laborer pop that half of it converts.

A host can Crush the Cell by demolishing it, for three months' income and 10 stability. A cell dissolves by itself if a Commonwealth takes the city or the situation ends.

For rulers who are not a Commonwealth, the situation panel is also where Patronize An Order lives (see Ṭarīqa orders).

docs.title: Dispatch a Preacher
docs.text: A Commonwealth with Shaykhī power of at least 25% can plant a cell in a chosen foreign city once every 24 months, at no cost in gold. The cost is at home: each dispatch adds Preachers Sent Abroad, −5% Shaykhī power for 25 years, and these stack.

docs.title: The Notables Take the Council
docs.text:
If Shaykhī power falls below 10%, there is a 15% monthly chance of this event.

  • Let there be a sultanate. The Commonwealth becomes a Persianate Sultanate with the Persianate Bureaucracy reform, gains +10 stability and +20 legitimacy, and falls out of the Sarbadār Movement. If it was the last Commonwealth, the Phenomenon ends.
  • Summon the brethren home. −30% Sufyānī satisfaction, +15 devotion, −10 stability, and The Last Purge for 10 years (+15% Shaykhī power, +0.05 monthly devotion, −10% stability cost efficiency). The question can be asked again.

docs.title: The Sarbadār Movement
docs.text: An international organisation seeded at the start with the Sarbadars as its only member. Only independent Commonwealths can belong; members cannot resign, and a member that stops being a Commonwealth leaves automatically. Members get +0.02 monthly devotion and +5% land morale, and open their roads to each other in wartime. A Commonwealth founded by a Shia rising that chooses the Sabzavār answer joins at once; members can invite any other. The organisation has no leader and, for now, no actions of its own.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Spend the zeal. The first decade is when the Dervish Corps is cheapest and strongest relative to its neighbours. Nishapur and Mashhad are both a short march away and both pay permanently.
  • Stay attacked, not attacking, when you can. The Vow Besieged doubles the zeal only in defensive wars.
  • Build lodges for power, not only for recruits. The Shaykhī wing's weight comes from the soldiers pops that lodges draw in.
  • Count your preachers. Three dispatches are −15% Shaykhī power for a generation. The notables' takeover is the designed consequence of exporting the revolution too freely.
  • Time the succession. If you want a shaykh, be at war when the ruler is old.
  • Convert before you integrate. A Mission of the Liberated first, then the Charter of the Liberated once the province is half Shia.

See also: Ṭarīqa orders and the Shia rework, the Zaydi imamate, the Succession of Erānzamīn, Persianate Sultanate, the maẓālim court, Türk vs Tāzīk, countries and tags, known issues.

docs.title: Demography and cultures
docs.text:
The registers do not stop.

The mod replaces the base game's population of Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus, Khurasan and Transoxiana, redraws who lives where on the eastern marches, adds one new culture, gives the region a web of cultural attitudes, and sets every realm's accepted and tolerated cultures from the people it actually rules. None of it is a button you press; all of it is what you find when you open the population map on day one.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
In 1340 Ḥamd-Allāh Mustawfī of Qazvin, a career accountant of the Ilkhanid finance office, finished the Nuzhat al-Qulūb: a geography of the realm written by a man who had seen its tax registers. It goes district by district — the revenue assessed, the towns and their walls, the crops, the water, the legal school the people follow. It is the nearest thing to a census the fourteenth-century Middle East produced, and it describes a country of large cities and dense irrigated districts: Tabriz as the greatest emporium between Cairo and Delhi, Yazd and Kerman as industrial oases, Soltaniyeh as a living capital, Rey as a ruin.

The base game's Iran is built from a model that projects modern settlement backwards. It therefore finds people where they live today and misses them where they lived then: Rey is populous because Tehran now stands beside it; Tabriz, Shiraz and Kerman are market towns; there are almost no townsmen at all. The mod's population is calibrated to Mustawfī instead.

docs.title: How many people
docs.text:
Population of the mod against the base game, in the regions the calibration covers:

Region Base game Mod Persia (the plateau, Azerbaijan, the Caspian coast, Fārs, Kerman, Sistan, Baluchistan) 4.0 million 13.3 million The Caucasus 1.9 million 4.7 million The Khorasan region (Khurasan, Khwarazm, Transoxiana, Badakhshan) 3.8 million 5.7 million Iraq-i Arab and the Jazira 1.7 million 2.2 million

That is roughly 26 million people between the Euphrates and the Pamirs where the base game has a little over 11 million. The calibration must not be read as a buff: it is the denominator every other system in the mod is balanced against.

Three neighbouring passes follow the same method on a smaller scale: Anatolia (the Ottoman march thinned to a frontier, Konya and Sivas strengthened — see Shattered Rum), the cities of the Golden Horde on the Volga (Sarai al-Jadid, Bolghar, Astrakhan and their neighbours, enlarged), and Yemen (see the Zaydi Imamate).

The cities carry much of the difference. Location totals, in thousands (a "location" is the city together with its district):

Location Base game Mod Tabriz 34 251 Baghdad 67 228 Yazd 9 207 Urgench 15 196 Samarkand 43 173 Isfahan 20 150 Shiraz 9 144 Bukhara 61 141 Kerman 5 132 Nishapur 15 130 Sabzevar 5 104 Qom 22 92 Soltaniyeh 9 88 Hamadan 21 88 Herat 7 75 Rey 74 20

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text:
The second change is social. The base game's Iran is nine parts peasant and tribesman with no one to keep a register. In the mod:

Share of the Persia region Base game Mod Peasants 77.5% 70.5% Tribesmen 14.1% 16.3% Burghers 1.0% 7.6% Clergy 0.1% 2.2% Nobles under 0.1% 1.2% Slaves 7.3% 2.2%

This matters more in 1.4 than it did before, because estate power now comes from pop types. A realm with real townsmen, a real clerisy and a real military nobility has real estates; the Dīwān and the Amirs draw their weight from these people.

By confession the plateau in 1337 is about two-thirds Sunni, with Shia communities at roughly one in six — concentrated on the Caspian coast (Gilan, Tabaristan, Talysh), in Khuzestan and Lesser Lur, and in pockets of Khurasan around Nishapur, Esfarayen and Sabzevar — and Zoroastrians, Christians and Jews making up the rest. Iran is not yet a Shia country, and nothing in the setup pretends it is.

docs.title: Towns and cities
docs.text:
The base game ranks 41 places between the Euphrates and the Pamirs as towns or cities, so most of Iran starts as open countryside. The mod ranks 85 more there — 77 towns and 8 cities — and raises Tabriz to a megalopolis. Kerman, Sabzevar, Kashan, Qazvin, Maragheh, Hillah, Erbil and Shamakhi become cities, and Ganja is raised from town to city; the road halts, shrine towns and district seats between them (Semnan, Damghan, Bastam, Mashhad, Karbala, Kufa, Kazerun, Lar and many more) become towns.

Each starts with a set of buildings suited to what it was:

Kind of place What you find in it Iranian town or city A full bazaar economy: cloth and fine cloth, paper and a scriptorium, pottery, glass, jewellery, dyes, tools and weapons, a marketplace. Even the smallest qaṣaba has a paper guild and a scriptorium. Khurasani town or city The same, with more paper and pottery and a caravanserai — the Khurasan road. Caravan town Extra marketplace, granary and caravanserais; walls. Pilgrimage town or city Extra scriptoria and paper: shrine towns are book towns. Kāshī town or city Kāshī Guilds and kilns — Kashan and Saveh, the tile and lustreware centres. Fortified small town A castle over a small market. Shiraz The book city: the largest scriptorium and paper sector in Iran, fine cloth and dyes, almost no metalwork. Kerman Weapons, tools and fine cloth, two caravanserais. Mosul Metalwork and jewellery, with a castle.

What the mod's own buildings in these places do is on Buildings.

docs.title: Corrections on the marches
docs.text: Four changes correct who lives in particular places, each for a stated historical reason.

docs.title: Türkmen in the Jazira
docs.text: The base game has no Türkmen at all between Mosul and Diyarbekir. The mod seeds about 162,000 of them — 155,000 tribesmen and their chiefs, Sunni — across the Jazira: the largest groups around Diyarbekir, Mosul, Sinjar and Mardin, smaller ones from Urfa and Harran to Cizre. These are the winter pastures of the clans that within two generations become the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu. They are a pastoral population inside Jalayirid, Sutayid, Artuqid and Kurdish lands, not a country of their own.

docs.title: No Hazara in 1337
docs.text: The name Hazāra — Persian for the Mongol military "thousand" — is first attested in the late fifteenth century. In 1337 the central Afghan highlands held Mongol military households living beside the older Iranic population; the people later called Hazara are the result of another century and a half of that. So every Hazara pop in the base game (151,365 people in 19 locations) is divided in three, keeping its size, class and religion: one third Mongolian, one third Persianized Mongol, one third the settled Iranic culture of the place (Khorasani or Tajik). Nobody is made Shia; these people were not Shia yet.

docs.title: Khorasani Sistan and the lower Helmand
docs.text: "Afghan" in this period means Pashtun, and the base game spreads Pashtuns across the whole south-east. The mod keeps them where the sources put them — Kandahar, Kabul, Ghazni and the Sulaymān range — and makes the settled, Persian-speaking country Khorasani: Sistan proper (Zaranj, Zabol, Farah — the Nīmrūz of the Tārīkh-i Sīstān), the lower Helmand (Bost and Garmsir, the old Ghaznavid winter capital and its canal lands) and Herat's own district (Adraskan). In all, 441,410 people in six provinces. The Mihrabanid maliks of Sistan (MIH) rule as Khorasanis.

docs.title: Mongol Neguderi, Persianized Besüd
docs.text: The Negüderi (NGD) were a raiding soldiery on the Indian march of the Chagatai ulus, not a court. They stay Mongolian (they are not among the Chaghatay tümens below); only a third of their nobles — the men who dealt with the towns of Ghazni and Kandahar — are Persianized. Their neighbours the Besüd (BSD) rule as Persianized Mongols. Both belong to Ulus Chaghatay, not to the Ilkhanid succession.

docs.title: The Persianized Mongol
docs.text:
By 1337 the great military houses of the western Ilkhanate were three generations deep in Iran: Muslim since Ghazan's conversion in 1295, Persian in their chanceries, married into the country's notable families, born in Soltaniyeh, Kayseri and Diyarbekir rather than on the Orkhon. Ḥasan-i Buzurg's grandson would be Sulṭān Aḥmad Jalāyir, poet, calligrapher and patron of Ḥāfiẓ. Giving them the same culture as the Mongols of Mongolia was simply wrong.

The mod therefore adds a culture, Persianized Mongol:

  • its language is Persian;
  • it belongs to both the Mongolian and the Iranian culture groups, and not to the steppe group;
  • it thinks well of Mongolian, Oirat, Farsi, Adhari, Khorasani and Tajik culture; Mongolians and Oirats regard it as kindred.

The practical effect is that a Persianized Mongol court finds it cheap to accept its Persian-speaking subjects — as it should — while still being counted as Mongol by its own soldiery.

Rule as Persianized Mongol Stay Mongolian Chobanids (CHB), Jalayirids (JAL), Hüleguids (HLG), Besüd (BSD) Gurgan (GRG) under Ṭoghā Temür, the Sutayids (SUT), the Negüderi (NGD), the Jurmanids (JUR) and Ughanids (UGH) of Fārs, and the Dughlat (DGH) of Kashgar

The line runs through conversion. Persianization came through Islam, and the houses that had not come in — the two Tengri-following garrison hordes of eastern Fārs, two valleys from Shiraz — are still culturally on the steppe. Ṭoghā Temür's camp faces Khurasan and the Türkmen plain, and stays Mongol too.

Ten characters carry the new culture at the start: of the Chobanid house and court, Ḥasan-i Kūchak, his father Tīmūrtāsh and grandfather Chūpān, Malik Ashraf, Dimashq Khwāja and Sūrgān, with the two Chinggisids the Chobanids keep, Sātī Beg and Sulaymān Khān; on the Jalayirid side Ḥasan-i Buzurg and the child Muḥammad Khān.

As a population the Persianized Mongols are very small — about 60,000 people. Roughly 9,000 are nobles — the Muslim Mongol aristocracy of the western cities and the Persian-using fringe of the eastern march; most of the rest are the former "Hazara" third in the Afghan highlands. In both great regencies the ruling culture is well under one percent of the realm. That is the point: see A Thin Stratum below.

docs.title: Chaghatay
docs.text:
The tümens of Transoxiana and the Oxus country were a third case. By the 1330s the Barlas, Jalayir, Suldus, Arlat, Apardi, Yasa'uri and Qara'unas were Mongol by descent and by tribal name only. They spoke Turkic, were Muslim, and wintered beside the towns they taxed. They called themselves Chaghatay. The nomads of the eastern half, who had kept closer to the old ways, called them qara'unas, "mongrels", and were called jete, "robbers", in return. They were Turkicized, not Persianized: their Iranization is the Timurid story, not a fact of 1337.

The mod gives them a culture of their own, Chaghatay:

  • its language is the Turkic of Transoxiana (the base game's Karluk);
  • it belongs to the Mongolian, Turkic and steppe culture groups, so every rule in the game or the mod that asks for "a Mongol" or "a steppe people" still finds it;
  • it thinks well of Mongolian, Persianized Mongol, Kyrgyz and Uzbek culture and regards Khorezmian, the same tongue, as kindred.
Chaghatay at the start Not Chaghatay The khan's seat, Chagatai (CHG); the eight western houses Apardi (APD), Arlat (ART), Barlas (BRL), Jalayirs (JLY), Khuttal (KTT), Qara'unas (QUN), Suldus (SLD), Yasa'uri (YSU); the four carved domains Fergana (FGN), Chach (CAC), Issyk-Kul (ISQ), Dzungaria (DZG) The Dughlat (DGH) and Negüderi (NGD) stay Mongolian; the Besüd (BSD) Persianized Mongol; Karategin (KRG), a mountain principality with no nomads, is Tajik

In the lands those thirteen realms hold at the start:

  • every Mongolian pop becomes Chaghatay;
  • Oirat tribesmen, nobles and soldiers become Chaghatay (in the khan's own share of the Ili and Dzungaria, every Oirat pop does: the Oirats reached Dzungaria only in the fifteenth century);
  • Khorezmian nobles and soldiers become Chaghatay, and three in four Khorezmian tribesmen; the rest stay as the older Turkic nomads outside the tümens.

Tajik townsmen and peasants are untouched, and nobody's religion or class changes. The ruling culture comes out at no more than about a fifth of a western realm: a real minority over a Tajik majority, which is why the western houses start by tolerating Tajiks. In the Dughlat lands the same shares of Khorezmian nomads become Mongolian instead. The scripted characters of these realms who were Mongolian or Khorezmian, Temür and his father among them, become Chaghatay on the first day.

A share granted from a Chaghatay khan's patrimony is Chaghatay; the Legacy of Genghis reform is open to Chaghatay hordes; and after a Bulqaq these are the people whose tribesmen, soldiers and nobles the neighbours divide up (see the Breaking of the Chaghatay).

docs.title: Protected communities
docs.text:
Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians under Muslim rule were dhimmī — protected communities with their own courts, clergy and tax status, living in the towns as merchants, physicians, craftsmen and cultivators. The base game enters most of them as slave pops, in places at absurd scale. The mod corrects this where it has reworked the population:

Community Base game Mod Jews of Iran (Kalīmī) about 9,000, most of them slaves about 61,000 burghers, peasants, clergy and notables; none are slaves Jews of Yemen (Teimani) about 287,000, all slaves about 35,000 burghers, peasants and clergy; none are slaves

The starting culture lists (below) also guarantee these communities recognition: the Jews of Hamadan, Fārs, Kerman, Qom, Yemen and Egypt are tolerated by their rulers however small their share of the realm, and six Kurdish emirates of the Armenian highlands tolerate the Armenian majorities they rule.

This pass is not finished. The Syriac and Armenian Christians of Iraq, the Jazira and Azerbaijan still carry much of the base game's slave typing, and are due the same correction.

docs.title: Culture relations
docs.text:
The base game gives the region almost no cultural attitudes. The mod adds a web of them, on one principle: the quarrels of this world were confessional and dynastic, not ethnic, and the real fault line ran between the settled country and the horde.

Who Thinks of whom Attitude Farsi, Adhari, Khorasani, Tajik one another Kindred Farsi, Adhari, Khorasani Iraqi, Kurdish, Lur, Gilak, Mazanderani, Talysh, Achomi, Semnani, Dehwar Positive Farsi, Adhari Mongolian, Oirat Negative Farsi, Adhari Persianized Mongol Positive Khorasani, Tajik Mongolian, Oirat Enemy Khorasani Persianized Mongol Negative Tajik Persianized Mongol Neutral Iraqi the four Persian-speaking cultures, Kurdish, Persianized Mongol Positive Iraqi, Kurdish, Lur, the Caspian and Baloch peoples, Afghans Mongolian Negative Kurdish, Lur, Talysh, Gilak, Mazanderani, Baloch, Afghan, Achomi, Semnani, Dehwar the four Persian-speaking cultures Positive Gilak and Mazanderani each other Kindred Azeri the four Persian-speaking cultures, Persianized Mongol Positive (not returned) Armenian, Georgian Mongolian Negative

Three things to notice.

Khurasan remembers. Merv and Nishapur were annihilated in 1220–21, and a century later Khurasan and Transoxiana are still under Mongol hordes. Their hatred is the only "enemy" attitude in the web, and it is one-sided — the victim remembers, the conqueror never noticed. The Sarbadar rising is this anger in the form of a state.

Iraq is Persianate ground. Iraqi culture belongs to both the Arabic and the Iranian culture groups. ʿIrāq-i ʿArab and ʿIrāq-i ʿAjam are one name split in two; Baghdad inherited its chancery houses from Ctesiphon thirty kilometres away, and the Iraqi scribal class shares the dīwān tradition with urban Iran. In play, an Iranian court accepts Iraqis cheaply and an Iraqi one accepts Iranians cheaply, and Iraqi townsmen staff the Dīwān alongside Persian ones.

Outsiders see one people. Any culture that holds an opinion of one of the four Persian-speaking cultures holds the same opinion of all four. "Tāzīk" is the outsider's word for the settled, Persian-speaking world as a whole.

Attitudes matter because the cost of accepting or tolerating a culture depends on what that culture thinks of yours: kindred peoples are far cheaper to accept, hostile ones far dearer. A Mongolian-culture horde ruling Khurasanis pays heavily for every people it recognises; a Farsi dynasty ruling Adharis pays almost nothing.

docs.title: Starting accepted and tolerated cultures
docs.text:
The starting lists are new in 1.4 and have not yet been verified in play; what follows is how they are designed to come out.

In the base game each country's accepted and tolerated cultures are a hand-written list, often inherited from a different map. In the mod, on the first day of the campaign, each of the 83 realms the mod touches — every member of the Erānzamīn organisation, the Kurdish emirates, Yemen, the Chagatai khan and his carved domains, Egypt and Delhi — has its lists set by one rule:

  • only cultures holding 2% or more of the realm's people are considered (the protected communities above are the exception);
  • each is priced at what it would really cost that realm to accept or tolerate it;
  • the realm takes the combination that recognises the most people — an accepted person counting fully, a tolerated one at 40% — while using no more than 85% of its culture capacity. The remainder is yours to spend.

Some results, as planned:

Realm Ruling culture Accepts Tolerates Chobanids Persianized Mongol Adhari, Mongolian, Azeri — Jalayirids Persianized Mongol Iraqi, Kurdish Lur Gurgan Mongolian — Adhari, Semnani Injuids Farsi Lur Kalīmī Muzaffarids Farsi Kalīmī — Kartids Khorasani Mongolian, Tajik Persianized Mongol Sutayids Mongolian — Armenian, Oirat Eretnids Turkish Turkoman Armenian Mihrabanids Khorasani Tajik, Baloch — Ormus Farsi Omani, Achomi Bahrani Hazaraspids Lur Farsi — Sarbadars Khorasani — — Yemen Yemeni Hadhrami Teimani Egypt Lower Egyptian Coptic, Levantine, Upper Egyptian, Syriac, Alawite Mizrahi

The table repays reading. Ṭoghā Temür, a Mongol khan ruling a million and a half mostly Iranian subjects who resent the horde, can afford to tolerate two peoples and accept none. The Chobanid regent, three generations Persianized, accepts the Adharis who are half his realm. A Chinggisid Regency also cuts the upkeep of accepted and tolerated cultures by about two-thirds, which is what lets the two regents carry lists that long; lose the regency and the bill comes due.

Capacity itself comes from rank, advances and government. The Persianate Bureaucracy reform gives +2 culture capacity; an Iranic Tribal Polity has +1.

The Jalayirid list leaves the Syriac Christians of the Jazira (about 6% of the realm) unrecognised: there is room for them only by dropping the Kurds. That is a choice the player can make on day one.

docs.title: Cultural weight
docs.text:
In the base game every location's cultural influence and tradition is credited to the culture of whoever owns it. A Mongol-ruled empire therefore becomes, on paper, an overwhelmingly Mongol civilisation, and over time its Iranian and Iraqi subjects assimilate to their rulers. The opposite happened: the Ilkhanid elite became Persian or Turkic within decades. Three standing modifiers correct this.

Modifier Who has it Effect A Thin Stratum any realm whose ruling culture is in the Mongolian group — Persianized Mongol included −85% cultural influence, −95% cultural tradition The Persianate Continuum any realm ruled by Farsi, Adhari, Khorasani or Tajik culture +0.5 cultural influence, +0.5 cultural tradition The Arabic Continuum any realm ruled by Iraqi culture +0.5 cultural influence, +0.5 cultural tradition

(A matching Sinic Continuum applies to realms of the Chinese culture group.)

A fourth layer works location by location, wherever the majority is Farsi, Adhari, Khorasani or Tajik:

Location Owner of the Iranian culture group Any other owner Rural Persianate Countryside: +0.10 influence, +0.10 tradition Persianate Countryside, Foreign-Held: −0.10, −0.05 Town Persianate Town: +0.25, +0.25 Persianate Town, Foreign-Held: −0.25, −0.10 City Heart of the Persianate: +0.50, +0.50 The Conqueror's Bargain: −0.50, −0.25 Megalopolis Jewel of the Persianate: +0.75, +0.75 Jewel of the Persianate, Foreign-Held: −0.75, −0.40

"Of the Iranian group" is deliberately broad: a Kurdish, Lur or Persianized Mongol dynasty holding Isfahan counts as the Persianate world ruling itself. A conqueror from outside it is drained by every Persian city he holds — the more of the civilisation he sits on, the faster his court is absorbed by it. The location-level layer is the least tested part of this page; if the modifiers do not appear on your locations, only the three realm-level ones are in force.

docs.title: Court language
docs.text:
Every Persianate Sultanate of Iran starts with Persian as its court language — the Chobanid and Jalayirid courts, the provincial dynasties and the Baloch chiefs alike — and so do Rasulid Yemen, Delhi and the Kurdish emirates. Ṭoghā Temür's horde keeps a Turkic court. Among the ṭarīqa orders, the Qadiriyya and Rifaiyya use the Arabic of Iraq, the Yasaviyya Kipchak Turkic, and the rest Persian. In Shattered Rum, restoring a chancery in Anatolia switches the court to Persian as part of the act.

Court language feeds the same acceptance arithmetic as attitudes do: peoples who share the court's language are cheaper to recognise.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Open the culture tab before you unpause. Your lists were set for you with about 15% of capacity to spare. Check who was left out and whether you would rather have them.
  • Regents should count what the regency is paying for. The Chobanid and Jalayirid lists are affordable because of the Chinggisid Regency's discount. Plan for the day you drop the khan.
  • If you play a Mongolian-culture horde in Iran, you are on a clock. A Thin Stratum means your culture will not spread, Khurasanis and Tajiks hate you, and every people costs you more to recognise. The settled houses do not have this problem.
  • Cities are worth more than land. Population, townsmen and the cultural weight of the Persianate core are all concentrated in the ranked towns and cities. Tabriz alone holds a quarter of a million people.
  • Do not expect Pashtun levies in Sistan or Hazara anywhere. If you are used to the base game's south-east, look again.

See also: Starting the game, The Türk–Tāzīk axis, The Dīwān estate, Hordes, Ulus Chaghatay, The Amirs' Regency, Kurdish emirates, Countries and tags.

docs.title: The Dīwān estate
docs.text:
The men of the pen: they keep the registers, and the registers keep the realm.

The Dīwān is the scribal and fiscal class of a Persianate state. Together with the Amirs it takes the place the nobility holds in a European realm. In game it appears on the estate panel as The Diwan Estate.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: A dīwān is first a register, then the office that keeps it, then the people who staff the office: the chancery scribes (kuttāb), the accountants (mustawfīs), the viziers and the service families who trained their sons for a post from childhood. Their working language is administrative Persian, but the class is not an ethnic one: the urban notables of Iraq, schooled in the same Abbasid bureaucratic tradition, belong to it as fully as those of Shiraz or Herat. Their wealth is ledger-visible (cash, urban property, rent rights) and militarily defenceless, which makes them both the engine of the treasury and the first target of a ruler short of money. Rashīd al-Dīn, vizier, physician and historian, enormously rich and executed at about seventy after a generation of indispensability, is the type.

docs.title: Who belongs to it
docs.text:
Since 1.4 an estate's power comes from the pops that belong to it, and the mod decides pop by pop who is a man of the pen.

A noble pop joins the Dīwān when all of the following hold:

Condition Detail The state has a chancery The owner carries the Niẓām al-Mulk Chancery flag. It comes with Persianate Bureaucracy (the founding reform of every Persianate Sultanate), the Timurid Empire, The Niyāba ʿĀmma Charter, Mamluk Government, The Delhi Dispensation and the Rasulid Chancery. Culture Iranian or Arabic culture group; or a Muslim pop of the Indian culture group; or a Muslim Turkic pop in a country holding the Sultanate of Rum reform. Literacy Above 20. Urban setting The pop lives in a city, in a province capital, or in a location where burghers are more than 5% of the population.

Noble pops that fail the test are sorted onward: Muslim ones become Amirs; the rest fall back to the base Nobility, which a Persianate Sultanate keeps at −90% power and bars from the cabinet, the army command and the court. A rural Persian landholder is therefore an amir in game terms, and a literate Baghdadi notable is a dīwān man.

A burgher pop can also enter the Dīwān, on much stricter terms: Persian-speaking culture, literacy above 60, living in a city, in a chancery state whose economy sits beyond 75 on the capital-economy side of the capital-versus-traditional value.

The literacy and urban tests are waived during 1337 itself, so that the estate exists from the first day of a campaign.

Clergy never join the Dīwān. The jurists and the bureaucrats are separate estates on purpose.

docs.title: Where its power comes from
docs.text:
Source Effect Pops Each noble pop in the estate carries the standard noble weight (25 per pop); qualifying burgher pops carry the burgher weight (4). Base values of any chancery state +70% Dīwān power, +30% Amirs power, +40% Dīwān target satisfaction Sedentary Power Base (any chancery state) Up to +250% Dīwān power, scaled by the share of your population that is peasants, burghers and labourers Persianate Bureaucracy reform +25% Dīwān power, +5% target satisfaction Persian, the Tongue of the Diwan +5% target satisfaction while Persian is the court language Dīwān of the Realms (capital building) +50% Dīwān power, +10% political influence gain (see Buildings) Privileges Every Dīwān privilege adds power; see Estate privileges

The counterweight is the Amirs' Tribal Power Base, which scales with tribesmen. A settled, urban realm leans toward the pen by its demography alone; a realm full of tribal pops leans toward the sword whatever you grant.

docs.title: Tax and the estate's own modifiers
docs.text:
The Dīwān is assessed at 200 per pop, twice a base-game noble (100) and eight times an amir (25). It is the most taxable elite you have. It also runs a bank, has dynasties, and does not produce mercenary captains.

The estate's effects scale with its satisfaction and with how far its power stands above or below the engine's thresholds; the figures below are the listed strengths.

Satisfied Dīwān Powerful Dīwān Weak Dīwān Cabinet efficiency +15% +25% −20% Tax efficiency +10% +15% −10% Control +7.5% max control +15% urban, +7.5% rural −5% urban, −10% rural Policy change cost −10% +10% Research speed +15% Monthly prosperity +0.0025 Stability cost efficiency −20% Bank interest +5% −5% Cost to revoke privileges +75% Dīwān's own max tax −40% +25% Others' max tax Burghers +10%, clergy +15%, peasants +5% Burghers, clergy and peasants −10% each

The last two rows are the estate's character in miniature. A powerful chancery squeezes everyone else harder and shelters itself; a weak one is squeezed and cannot squeeze.

docs.title: The pen and the sword
docs.text:
The Persianate Bureaucracy reform fixes a division of labour:

  • Dīwān characters may sit in the cabinet. Amirs, burghers, clergy and base nobles may not.
  • Amirs may lead armies. Dīwān characters, burghers and base nobles may not.

Both lines can be crossed, by the Tāzīk Command of Arms and Umarāʾ at the Dīwān privileges, at a price paid to the estate whose preserve is invaded. Dīwān privileges almost all push the Turk vs Tazik value toward Tazik.

At game start every Persianate Sultanate receives two dīwān characters of Farsi culture with strong administrative ability, whatever the country's own culture, and the chancery is designed to produce a replacement each year while fewer than four are alive.

docs.title: The vizierate
docs.text:
The chancery expects to run the cabinet, not merely to sit in it. Four standing states are tracked:

Cabinet Modifier Effect No dīwān member at all The Chancery Locked Out −20% Dīwān target satisfaction, −25% cabinet efficiency, −15% tax efficiency Dīwān members, but an outsider heads the cabinet No Vizier of the Pen −5% target satisfaction, −10% cabinet efficiency, −5% tax efficiency A dīwān man heads the cabinet A Vizier of the Pen +5% target satisfaction, +5% cabinet efficiency, +5% tax efficiency, +15% crown power Two or more outsiders sit beside the dīwān Crowded Vizierate −5% target satisfaction, −5% cabinet efficiency

Once a year, if the Dīwān is locked out or two or more non-dīwān members sit in the cabinet, the chancery may deliver its ultimatum, The Registers Are Closed. It cannot recur for five years.

Choice Result "The sultan's kin sit where the sultan pleases. Open the registers or lose your hands." −20 legitimacy, −25% Dīwān satisfaction, and The Dīwān Spurned for ten years: −10% tax efficiency, −10% Dīwān target satisfaction, −10% cabinet efficiency. The AI never takes this. "Clear the table. Seat the pen." Outsiders are dismissed until the Dīwān holds a strict majority of the occupied seats; dīwān characters fill the vacancies (new ones are created if none are free) and a dīwān man becomes head of the cabinet if none presides. +10% Dīwān satisfaction, −10% crown satisfaction.

The practical lesson: seat a dīwān character as head of the cabinet and keep at most one outsider beside the chancery men.

docs.title: Muṣādara: the king's hand
docs.text: The Dīwān is not taxed openly the way its wealth would suggest; its privileges steadily lower its own tax cap. The historical answer was muṣādara, the confiscation of an official's fortune at the ruler's will, pronounced in the court of grievances. Niẓām al-Mulk condemned it as the practice that stops anyone improving what he holds. The mod gives it to you as a real tool with real costs.

docs.title: The Muṣādara Right
docs.text:
Everything here depends on the Dīwān privilege Muṣādara Right, which grants the modifier The Right of the Monarch to Confiscate. Every Persianate starting template begins with it.

Muṣādara Right Estates Dīwān power +50%, Amirs power −25%; target satisfaction: Dīwān +5%, peasants +5%, clergy −2.5%, burghers −7.5%, Amirs −10% Fisc +5% max tax on every estate; estate enrichment −20%; bank interest +5%; loan capacity −25% Realm −0.001 monthly development; centralization +0.1, absolutism +0.1, Tazik +0.05 per month Excludes Soyurghal Grants (Amirs) and the Mulk Protection Charter

As the files stand the privilege cannot be revoked once held: its revocation condition is never met by anything in the mod. The Mulk Protection Charter and Soyurghal Grants are therefore out of reach for a state that starts with the right.

docs.title: Pronouncing a confiscation
docs.text:
Muṣādara is an action of the Maẓālim court.

Requires Persianate Sultanate; the Muṣādara Right; a dīwān member in the cabinet; the court in session; debate support of at least half what a parliament request needs Cost That same amount of debate support Yield Half the Dīwān estate's treasury, reduced by the waqf shelter (below), paid into yours Dīwān −40% satisfaction, and a dīwān member of your cabinet is executed Aftermath Recent Muṣādara for five years: −5% target satisfaction for Dīwān, Amirs, burghers and clergy, −5% tax efficiency, −0.002 monthly development Cooldown Once every five years

The in-game text speaks of choosing an estate and of the vizier's death as a risk. At present the target is always the Dīwān, and the execution always happens when a dīwān man sits in the cabinet.

docs.title: The waqf shelter
docs.text:
Arbitrary seizure teaches people to hide wealth where the writ cannot reach: the pious endowment. Each confiscation prompts new endowments: an Aʿyān Waqf is founded in your capital, each of your cities has a 10% chance of another, each city a 2.5% chance of an Urban Waqf, and every location a 1% chance of a Clerical Waqf.

Once a year, in any state holding the Muṣādara Right, the endowments are reassessed. The share of your tax base sitting under Aʿyān Waqf (weighted by local Dīwān power and building level, the Grand Aʿyān Waqf counting double) becomes:

  • a standing drag that grows with that share: lower Dīwān max tax, lower tax efficiency and loan capacity, faster estate enrichment and a stronger clergy;
  • the shelter: the same share, capped at 90%, is subtracted from everything muṣādara and the Dīwān's court cases can seize.

The more you confiscate, the more is endowed, and the less the next confiscation yields. The court's Decree: Reclaim the Illegal Waqf is the way back; the waqf charter privileges close that road. See Buildings for the endowments themselves.

docs.title: The Treasury Runs Dry
docs.text:
A state with the Muṣādara Right that takes or renews a loan while drowning (more than ten loans and negative income, or loan capacity below a year of income) is offered the desperate version, at most once a year.

Choice Result "Declare maṣlaḥa — what we have taken was for the good of the realm." All loans cancelled. −15% satisfaction for Dīwān, Amirs, burghers and clergy; Recent Muṣādara for five years; +10 legitimacy; −10 stability. "The Circle of Justice needs greasing." All loans cancelled and a fifth of the treasuries of the Dīwān, Amirs, burghers and clergy seized. −30% satisfaction for each; The Great Confiscation for five years (−10% target satisfaction for all four, −10% tax efficiency, −0.004 monthly development); +15 legitimacy; −20 stability. "Nay! For confiscation is the evil that destroys the realm." Nothing happens.

docs.title: Estate events
docs.text:
While the Dīwān holds at least 25% of estate power, three events can come up on the Persianate flavour pulse:

Event Choices The Supremacy of the Pen Grant Merit Examinations and gain 15% Dīwān satisfaction, or refuse and lose 20% A Harmonious Bureaucracy +10% Dīwān satisfaction Local Audit In a location the Dīwān dominates: let the audit run for +10% control there, or avoid friction for −5% Dīwān satisfaction

docs.title: Playing with the Dīwān
docs.text:
• Put a dīwān man at the head of the cabinet from the first month. The difference between A Vizier of the Pen and The Chancery Locked Out is 40 points of cabinet efficiency and 20 of tax efficiency.
  • A strong, content Dīwān pays for itself: tax efficiency, cabinet efficiency, control. Its price is that it shelters its own wealth, so the tax you gain comes from burghers, clergy and peasants.
  • Treat muṣādara as an emergency reserve. Each use shrinks the next one and leaves endowments behind that cost you every month.
  • A Dīwān-leaning realm has few amirs content to fight for it. Watch the Amirs before a war, not during it.

See also: Amirs estate, Estate privileges, The Maẓālim court, Turk vs Tazik, Persianate Sultanate, Buildings.

docs.title: The Erānzamīn organisation
docs.text:
Interregnum — no Īlkhān since 1335.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The organisation's panel (the header, the Overview cards, the Notables tab and the role groups on the Members tab) was rebuilt for 1.4 and has not been checked through a full campaign. The rules below are what the mod sets up; the exact look of the panel, and whether every card fills in correctly every month, is still in testing.

After Abū Saʿīd no Ilkhan commanded general recognition, but nobody concluded from this that the realm had ceased to exist. The successor houses went on striking coin on the Ilkhanid standard, staffing the same dīwān, and fighting one another for the same four or five cities, on three distinct bases of claim. The khan-maker was an amir who held a Chinggisid in custody and ruled in his name, as Ḥasan-i Kūchak the Chobanid ruled through Sati Beg and then Sulaymān, and Ḥasan-i Buzurg the Jalayirid through Muḥammad and Jahān Temür: the yarlıq still issued in the khan's name, and the amir held the seal. The Chinggisid claimant was a prince of the blood pressing his own right, as Ṭoghā Temür pressed his from Khurasan. The sovereign shah had stopped borrowing a Chinggisid name and ruled in his own. Everyone else was a governor, a client, or waiting.

The organisation is the game's roll of that contest. It is a flat federation — it has no leader, no parliament and no votes — and it does two jobs: it marks who is inside the quarrel, and its panel keeps the ledger of who is winning it. The quarrel itself, with its rules and its victory, is the Succession of Erānzamīn.

docs.title: Who is in it
docs.text:
The organisation exists from the first day with 73 members: essentially every realm of the former Ilkhanate, from the Eretnids of Anatolia to the Kartids of Herat, from Georgia to Ormus. In broad groups:

Group Members at the start The great amirs' houses Chobanids (CHB), Jalayirids (JAL) with their Eretnid and Sutayid vassals and the Sutayids' own under-vassals Khurasan and the east Gurgan (GRG) under Ṭoghā Temür, the Hüleguids (HLG), the Kartids (KRT), the Sarbadars (SRB) and their smaller neighbours The plateau and the Persian Gulf coast Injuids (INJ), Muzaffarids (MZF), Ormus and Makran with their vassals, and the lesser lords between them The Christian north-west Georgia and Armenia with their vassals

Of the 73, 44 are independent and 29 are already the vassals of another member — the Sutayid house under the Jalayirids, Georgia's and Armenia's dependants, Makran's and Ormus's, and a handful of others.

Membership is wider than contention. Christian members are in the organisation, carry its passive and fight in its wars, but they are not contenders for a Muslim throne. Conversely, the ṭarīqa orders — the Safavid order at Ardabil included — are not members at all; see Tariqa orders. A full list of tags is on Countries and tags.

docs.title: Joining and leaving
docs.text:
Rule Detail Who may join later an independent country of at least duchy rank whose capital is in the region. Owning a border province does not qualify — this keeps Cairo and other neighbours out Who may be invited the same: a country seated in the region Who is barred the amirs of Ulus Chaghatay, who answer a living khan of their own Leaving not possible. A member cannot abandon the roll, and is never expelled. A member that kneels to another power stays a member and is filed as a sworn client The end the organisation dissolves the moment the succession situation ends, by victory or by running out of time

Members may freely declare war on one another; the organisation gives no military access and calls nobody into anyone's defence.

docs.title: What membership does
docs.text:
Every member carries the same passive for as long as the organisation exists.

Effect Value War score efficiency +33% Antagonism received −50% Diplomatic annexation efficiency +25% Land morale +10% Pops' threshold for joining rebels +0.10 (harder to raise)

Membership is also the key to two other things: only members can hold the Succession of Erānzamīn casus belli against each other, and only members can adopt the Chinggisid Regency or the Ilkhanate Governorate.

docs.title: The four roles
docs.text:
Each member is filed, automatically and month by month, by the basis of its claim. The roles carry no modifiers of their own — they are a filing system, shown as groups on the Members tab and as colours on the diplomatic map. The mechanics live in the reforms and disasters behind them.

Role Who is filed here Map colour Khan-Maker an independent member that rules through a Chinggisid: it holds the Chinggisid Regency or The Gurkani Regime, or simply has a living kept khan at its court dark red Chinggisid Claimant an independent member whose ruler is himself of the Borjigin line gold Sovereign Shah an independent member that rules in its own name: Farr-i Īzadī, Iranian Kingship, Ghāzī Sultanate, Sword of The Sharia, Amīr Sultanate, Timurid Synthesis, The Crowned Murshid or Sultanate of Rum blue Sworn Client a member that is the subject of another member — a sworn governorate, an ulus share, or a plain vassal tan (no role) everyone else: independent governors waiting to see who wins, Christian members, and powers that have not yet named the basis of their claim member tint

Two rules settle the edge cases:

  • Precedence. The three independent roles exclude one another in the order khan-maker, then Chinggisid, then shah. Holding a khan outranks being one: Ḥasan-i Buzurg's Jahān Temür was a Chinggisid, but the claim was the Jalayirid's. A regent who also happens to be of the blood is still a khan-maker.
  • Independence. Only an independent member can hold one of the three head roles. A vassal is filed under its overlord, whatever reform it holds. A member that becomes the subject of an outsider is nobody's client within Erānzamīn and stays a plain member.

docs.title: Moving between roles
docs.text:
Nobody appoints anyone. You change role by changing what you are.

From To How no role Khan-Maker answer the opening question with the regency (see the situation) no role Sovereign Shah take the farr or the ghazā at the opening, or adopt one of the sovereign reforms later Khan-Maker Sovereign Shah leave the regency — by the Quiet Crown, or by the fiction expiring into the Amīr Sultanate — and take a crown in your own name (see The Borrowed Mandate) Khan-Maker Khan-Maker, for good institutionalise the fiction as The Gurkani Regime any independent role Sworn Client become the subject of another member: a governorate that declares or accepts fealty, a realm vassalised in war Sworn Client independent again break free — a sworn governorate drops the khan from the khuṭba (see the Ilkhanate Governorate), an overlord releases or loses the subject anything Chinggisid Claimant only by a Borjigin coming to the throne of a realm that holds no khan of its own

In 1337 the picture is: the Chobanids and Jalayirids are khan-makers from the first day; Gurgan under Ṭoghā Temür is the standing Chinggisid claimant; 29 members are sworn clients; and nearly everyone else is unfiled until the opening event is answered.

docs.title: The panel
docs.text: Open it from the organisations list like any other. It has no buttons of its own beyond the standard ones: it is a ledger, not a control room. The verbs of the contest are on the situation panel (Press Claim, Rally, Restore, the integration actions, Declare Fealty) and, for a regent, on the Borrowed Mandate's disaster panel. The ledger is drawn up on the first day and redrawn at the turn of every month.

docs.title: The header
docs.text: Reads Meaning Interregnum — no Īlkhān since 1335 the standing title; there is no leader to show Leading: and a name the leading contender (see below) Notables how many bloc heads there are — khan-makers, Chinggisid claimants and sovereign shahs who answer to no overlord Sovereign Members how many members are not the subject of another power Consolidation of the Leader — n/24 the leader's months at the territorial gate

docs.title: Overview tab
docs.text:
• The Leading Contender. The independent member closest to the throne, with a Consolidation bar out of 24. "Leading" is measured first by unbroken months spent above the territorial gate — more than 240 locations, its own and its subjects', with its capital in the region — and only then by realm size. Twenty-four unbroken months opens the Matter of Tork or the Matter of Tazik for that realm. Fall below the gate for a single month and the count returns to zero.
  • The Five Seats. Tabriz, the Ilkhanid capital of record; Baghdad, the old caliphal seat; Soltaniyeh, Öljeitü's city; Isfahan; and Shiraz, the city of the poets. Each row shows the flag of whoever holds the city and, if the holder is someone's subject, the overlord's flag after the word for. The throne needs all five in the claimant's own hands: a seat held by a vassal is shown under its overlord's flag but does not count for him until it is his own.
  • Khans in Custody. Every kept khan currently alive, by name, under the flag of the house that holds him. If nobody holds one it reads No Chinggisid is held in custody. A subject can hold a khan too; the row shows the holder's own flag.

docs.title: Notables tab
docs.text:
One card for each bloc head, largest realm first. Each card shows:

On the card Meaning Name and ruler the head and the man himself Basis Holds a khan, Of the blood of Chinggis, or Rules in his own name Share of the realm the locations held by this head and his subjects (and their subjects), as a share of everything held by all the organisation's independent members and their subjects Bloc: n how many countries follow him

Below the cards:

  • Bloc Rolls lists every follower beside the name of the head it follows. A bloc is the head's subjects of every kind — ulus shares, sworn governorates and vassals, whether or not they are members — and their own subjects, followed by allied members who are independent and head no bloc of their own. An ally of two heads is filed under the larger. Allies are listed in the bloc but do not count toward the head's share of the realm: they are independent and counted in their own right.
  • Unaligned lists members in no head's bloc: governors waiting to see who wins, and powers that have not yet named the basis of their claim.

docs.title: Members tab
docs.text: The standard member list, grouped under Khan-Makers, Chinggisid Claimants, Sovereign Shahs and Sworn Clients, with unfiled members in the plain group.

docs.title: On the situation panel
docs.text: The succession situation's own panel borrows the same ledger for its header: it sets the Leading Contender against Your Realm, or reads You Lead the Succession when no other independent member outranks you in months of consolidation and bloc size, or No Clear Leader before the ledger has one.

docs.title: Sworn clients and sworn governorates
docs.text:
"Sworn client" is the organisation's word for any member under another member. Three quite different bonds are filed there:

Bond What it is Where it is explained Sworn governorate an Ilkhanate Governorate that has read a steward's khan in its khuṭba: autonomous, hard to annex, free to make its own wars The Ilkhanate Governorate Ulus share a prince's share of a khan's patrimony, owing men rather than money Hordes Vassal the ordinary bond — everything seeded in 1337 is of this kind —

For the ledger they are alike: the client's land and its voice count for its overlord's bloc, and a seat it holds is shown for him. For the throne they are not enough — locations held by subjects count toward the 400, but the Five Seats must be owned directly.

An overlord at peace who wants to rearrange a bloc's map can use Cede an Area on any subject: every location he holds in one area — one that borders the subject or lies in its home area, and never his own capital's — passes to the subject in a single act. No cores are granted with it.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Check the Five Seats before you plan a war. The Overview tells you at a glance which house holds each seat and whether a vassal is sitting on one you will need in your own hands.
  • Watch the Consolidation bar, not the map. The leader's 24-month clock is the best warning that someone is about to open their consolidation Matter and turn from warlord into claimant.
  • A big bloc is not a big share. Allies inflate the bloc count but not the share of the realm. Subjects do both.
  • The Khan-Makers and Chinggisid Claimants are the regent's enemy list. For a realm under the Chinggisid Regency, every other regent and every Borjigin-ruled member is a rival custody dragging its legitimacy down (see The Borrowed Mandate).
  • You cannot resign. A member that tires of the contest can defer — become a governorate, swear to someone stronger — but it stays on the roll until the question is settled.

See also: The Succession of Erānzamīn, The Borrowed Mandate, The Ilkhanate Governorate, The Matter of Tork, Government reforms, Countries and tags, Known issues.

docs.title: The Succession of Erānzamīn
docs.text:
Only one claimant can sit on Hulagu's seat — the legitimacy of the Khans does not divide.

Erānzamīn — the land of Iran — is what the Ilkhanid chancery called its own realm. Abū Saʿīd died without a son in 1335; Arpa Ke'ün lasted five months; every khan after him was some amir's khan. The army, the treasury, the registers and the provinces all survived, but the throne was, by everyone's open admission, vacant. For two decades the great houses answered the question in whose name is the Friday khuṭba read? in different ways: some enthroned a Chinggisid of convenience and ruled behind him, some took investiture as the caliph's sword, some claimed the farr of Iranian kingship outright, and many simply governed their corner and waited. The situation is that question, asked of every realm in the old Ilkhanate at once.

This page covers the situation itself. The roll of who stands where is kept by the Erānzamīn organisation; the regent's road has its own page, The Borrowed Mandate; the road that claims nothing is the Ilkhanate Governorate.

docs.title: How it starts
docs.text:
The Succession of Erānzamīn begins on the first day of the 1337 start. Three things happen at once:

  • Every location owned by a member of the Erānzamīn organisation receives Post-Ilkhanid Chaos for 40 years.
  • Every contender is flagged, receives Contender for the Throne, and is shown the opening event Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty.
  • The ṭarīqa orders seated in the region receive the same event with an answer of their own.

The situation is visible to anyone who owns land in the region, borders someone who does, or has a capital in the Middle East or Central Asia.

docs.title: The region
docs.text: "Erānzamīn" in every rule below means: the regions of Persia, Khorasan and the Caucasus, plus the areas of Iraq-i Arab (Baghdad), Jazira (Mosul) and Cappadocia.

docs.title: Who is a contender
docs.text:
A country is a contender when all of these hold:

  • it is independent (subjects do not contend);
  • its capital lies in the region — owning a border province is not enough;
  • it is Muslim. The Ilkhan's throne has been a Muslim throne since Ghazan's conversion in 1295. Georgia, the Armenian and Georgian minors and other Christian realms of the region remain members of the organisation and fight in the same wars, but they do not contend: no opening event, no contender modifier, no contender actions;
  • it is not a ṭarīqa order. The shrine-polities — the Safavid order at Ardabil (ABL) among them — deny the throne question altogether. They are not contenders and not members; see Tariqa orders;
  • it does not belong to Ulus Chaghatay. The amirs of Transoxiana answer a living Chagatayid khan; the Ilkhan's empty throne is not theirs to contend for.

There is no size floor. The roster is inclusive on purpose: a one-province Muslim lord with his seat in the region is a contender, because the simulation does not get to know who mattered later. A country that comes to meet the conditions after the start (a released subject, a conqueror who moves his capital in) is picked up at the next month's check and gains the contender's actions and the sword rule below.

docs.title: The contender package
docs.text: The contenders are not separate sovereign states with ordinary diplomatic relations. They are rival claimants to one realm, and the rules are bent accordingly.

docs.title: The sword rules the succession
docs.text:
While the situation runs, any location in Erānzamīn that a contender's army takes — by winning a siege, or by occupying an unfortified location — is annexed on the spot, provided its owner is at war with the contender. There is no waiting for the peace table. If the location taken is a province capital, the whole province changes hands with it. Land taken this way arrives as conquered and still has to be integrated (see below).

A realm that has proven its claim keeps its borders. Land owned by a state holding any of these reforms is immune and must be taken in a peace treaty like anywhere else in the world:

Immune defender Iranian Kingship Sword of The Sharia (the Dār al-Jihād reform) The Gurkani Regime The Crowned Murshid Sultanate of Rum Timurid Empire

The same rule shields you: finish your own legitimacy disaster and reach one of those reforms, and your conquests can only be taken from you the slow way. Until then, every lost siege is a lost city.

This replaces the automatic-conquest flag of earlier versions. Peace treaties still exist and still work; they are simply no longer the only way land moves.

docs.title: Contender for the Throne
docs.text:
Every contender carries this country modifier for as long as the situation lasts.

Effect Value War score efficiency +33% Antagonism received −50% Diplomatic annexation efficiency +25% Land morale +10% Pops' threshold for joining rebels +0.10 (harder to raise) AI behaviour far more aggressive, less careful, 12 fewer months between wars

Members of the organisation carry a near-identical passive of their own (see the organisation page); a contender who is also a member has both.

docs.title: Post-Ilkhanid Chaos
docs.text:
A location modifier on every location the organisation's members held at the start. It lasts 40 years, fades over that time, and is removed outright when the situation ends.

Effect Value Fort defence −66% Supply limit +50% Levy size +10% Monthly prosperity −0.002 Monthly development −0.001 Pop food consumption −10%

The Mongols forbade the rebuilding of city walls for three generations, and it shows. Sieges are short, armies can be fed almost anywhere, and levies are large. Together with the sword rule this makes the field battle the verdict and the cities its ratification: borders move every campaigning season.

docs.title: The opening choice — Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty
docs.text:
Every contender must answer the event; there is no "decide later". Which answers you are offered depends on who you are.

Answer Who sees it Immediate effects Find us a Borjigin to enthrone — Chinggisid Regency any independent contender not already a regent adopts the Chinggisid Regency reform; +10 legitimacy; Amirs +10%, Dīwān −5% satisfaction; a Persianized Mongol prince of the Borjigin line (aged 18–30) appears at court as your kept khan; every other regent in the organisation takes you for a Rival for the Regency and receives a succession casus belli on you We rule as the Caliph's sword — Ghāzī Sultanate Muslim contenders adopts Ghāzī Sultanate; +5 legitimacy; Clergy +10%, Dīwān −5% The farr of Iran does not descend through Mongol seed — Farr-i Īzadī any contender adopts Farr-i Īzadī; −10 stability, −10 legitimacy; Dīwān +15%, Burghers +10%, Amirs −15%, Tribes −25%, Clergy −5%; every regent in the organisation takes offence (Ignored the hallowed bloodline) and receives a succession casus belli on you; the Proof of Fortune follows We are governors, not kings — Ilkhanate Governorate any contender who has not just dropped a khan from the khuṭba adopts Ilkhanate Governorate; +5 legitimacy; Dīwān +5%

Some realms have only one door:

Realm Their answer Effects Chobanids (CHB) Sati Beg is kept as their khan +5 legitimacy; they already hold the Chinggisid Regency; Consolidating Opportunistic Acquisition for 20 years (Tribes levy size −50%, Amirs levy size −25%, fading) Jalayirids (JAL) Muḥammad Khan is kept as their khan +5 legitimacy; they already hold the Chinggisid Regency Gurgan (GRG), Hüleguids (HLG) I am the Khan by right of blood +15 legitimacy. A Borjigin needs no fiction Sarbadars and any Commonwealth of Martyrs the gallows' answer: coin in the Hidden Imam's name +10 devotion; both wings of the dyarchy approve Ṭarīqa orders We claim no throne +5 legitimacy

The AI weighs the options by strength and composition: the regency is not for the weak (the AI never takes it below a middling army), realms with many Turkic or Mongol subjects lean to the regency and away from the farr, a strong Dīwān pulls toward the farr, non-Muslim or heterodox neighbours pull toward the ghazā, and the weakest realms overwhelmingly defer.

What each answer means in the long run is on its own page: the regency in The Borrowed Mandate, the farr in Farr — the Proof of Fortune, the ghazā in The Burden of the Sword, deferral in the Ilkhanate Governorate, and the reforms themselves in Government reforms.

docs.title: Unsettled Legitimacy
docs.text:
A Persianate Sultanate that holds none of the recognised answers — neither a regency, a claim, a governorate, nor one of the later vindicated forms — carries Unsettled Legitimacy until it takes one. A realm ruled by a Borjigin is exempt.

Effect Value Monthly legitimacy −0.6 Amirs target satisfaction −20% Dīwān target satisfaction −20% Clergy target satisfaction −15% Burghers target satisfaction −15%

You meet it whenever you leave one answer without arriving at another — most often after dropping the regency. The Amīr Sultanate, taken on its own, does not lift it (see Government reforms).

docs.title: The kept khan dies — The Khan is Dead
docs.text:
The regent's khan is a real character at court. He cannot be interacted with, and he is mortal. When he dies, a realm still under the Chinggisid Regency must choose:

Choice Effects Enough. The mask comes off. the Chinggisid Regency is removed; −100 legitimacy; −25 stability; Amirs −30%, Tribes −30%, Dīwān +5% Enthrone his son. a new Borjigin prince is produced; The Charade Continues deepens by one step; Amirs +5%, Dīwān −5%

The Charade Continues is one modifier whose size grows with each enthronement:

Enthronement Monthly legitimacy Amirs target satisfaction Dīwān target satisfaction first −0.15 −5% −10% second −0.30 −10% −20% third −0.45 −15% −30%

After the third there is no fourth: no further enthronement is credible, and the only option left when that khan dies is to take the mask off at full price. The regency's own +0.5 monthly legitimacy is being eaten a slice at a time, by design. The orderly ways out — and what the forced exit turns you into — are on The Borrowed Mandate.

docs.title: The strategic verbs
docs.text: These appear as actions on the situation panel for every contender while the situation runs. Gold costs scale with the size of your economy; the figure given is the multiplier.

docs.title: Press Claim to Erānzamīn
docs.text: Pick a neighbour who is a member of the organisation, whom you could declare war on, and with whom you have neither truce nor alliance. You receive the Succession of Erānzamīn casus belli against them. It costs nothing and can be used every 6 months. No spy network is needed: the succession crisis is the casus belli, and pressing a claim is a public act.

docs.title: Rally Turkic Tribes
docs.text:
Call the Türkmen lineages in to the muster.

Requires prestige above 40; the realm has not leaned Tāzīk (Türk–Tāzīk axis below 0) Costs 20 prestige; gold ×6 Cooldown 10 years Brings Turkoman tribesmen of your religion, with a noble layer one-tenth their size, to one of your rural locations: 5,000 at county rank, 10,000 at duchy, 20,000 at kingdom, 30,000 at empire Leaves behind Türkmen Tribal Settlement on that location for 20 years (nobles' maximum literacy −10%) and a mild prosperity loss; the same location will not receive another wave for 10 years Politics Amirs +10%; Dīwān, Burghers and Peasants −25% each; −10 stability; 5 points toward Türk

docs.title: Restore Persian Bureaucracy
docs.text:
Recall the Iranian secretarial class to court. This is the deliberate road into the Persianate institution for a warlord who starts on the Türk side.

Requires prestige above 30; at least duchy rank; not already a Tāzīk realm (axis 50 or more) of kingdom rank or higher — such a realm already has what this grants Costs gold ×12; 20 legitimacy; 15 prestige; 10 stability Cooldown 15 years Grants the permanent right to seat the Dīwān of the Realms in your capital, even if the realm later drifts back toward the Türk pole Also Diwan Extension for 25 years, stacking with earlier uses (tax efficiency +7.5%, maximum control +5%, Dīwān target satisfaction +5%, Dīwān power +10%); Dīwān +15%, Amirs −15%; 10 points toward Tāzīk

docs.title: Integrating what you took
docs.text:
Sword-rule conquests arrive as conquered land. Three actions settle a province in the region in which you hold conquered locations; each leaves a ten-year mark on the land and each is a statement about what kind of realm you are.

Action Requires Costs Cooldown Result for your locations in the province Politics Consolidate the Diwan axis above +25; a Dīwān of the Realms in your capital; a Local Dīwān somewhere in the province gold ×3 1 year raised to core; Consolidated Diwan: maximum control +10%, raw material output +10%, unrest −0.2 Dīwān +2%, Amirs −1%, 1.5 toward Tāzīk Grant the Yurt axis below −15 5 legitimacy, 5 political influence 3 months raised to integrated only; Granted as Yurt: local manpower +30%, maximum control −7.5%, unrest −0.25 Amirs +2%, Dīwān −1%, 1.5 toward Türk Mixed Settlement — gold ×3, 5 legitimacy, 5 political influence 18 months raised to core; Mixed Settlement: local manpower +10%, unrest −0.25 none

The chancery route is slow and needs offices on the ground (see Buildings); the yurt route is fast and cheap but leaves the land half-absorbed in an amir's hands. See Türk vs Tāzīk for the axis itself.

docs.title: The casus belli
docs.text:
Succession of Erānzamīn can be held by any member of the organisation against any other member.

War goal superiority — destroy the rival in the field Cost of conquering or subjugating 75% of normal, for both sides What the attacker may take only land inside Erānzamīn Ticking war score 0.25

You come by it through Press Claim to Erānzamīn, through Press the Custody if you are a regent, and automatically when a rival answers the opening question in a way that offends you (a regent against every new regent and every new claimant of the farr; a custodian against a governorate that walks out on him). Because the war goal is limited to the region, two contenders fighting over Iran do not end up carving up Egypt.

docs.title: Winning
docs.text:
The situation ends the month any contender meets all of the following:

  • independent;
  • more than 400 locations, counting its own and those of its subjects and their subjects;
  • direct ownership of the Five Seats: Tabriz, Baghdad, Soltaniyeh, Isfahan and Shiraz. A seat held by a vassal does not count until it is your own;
  • one of the doctrinal clauses:
    • Tāzīk triumph — the Türk–Tāzīk axis at +75 or higher and the Matter of Tork resolved;
    • Türk triumph — the axis at −75 or lower;
    • a third, provisional clause — religious unity of 80% or more together with legitimacy of 75 or more.

You cannot negotiate your way onto the throne. You take the realm, and then you finish the argument about what kind of realm it is.

The halfway mark matters too: holding more than 240 locations (own and subjects') with your capital in the region for 24 unbroken months is what opens the consolidation Matter. The organisation's panel shows who is furthest along that clock.

docs.title: What the victor receives — Fatḥ-nāma, the Proclamation of Victory
docs.text:
There is one victory, not a menu. Every victor receives:

Reward Detail Prestige and legitimacy +100 prestige, +50 legitimacy Integration dividend each still-conquered location you own in Iranshahr (the region without Cappadocia) has a 25% chance to rise to integrated United Iran (permanent) +2 cultures capacity; +0.2 monthly legitimacy; −20% prestige decay; −10% court spending efficiency The Recovery (50 years) monthly prosperity +0.0025; monthly development +0.003; food production +10%

The last part depends on where the realm actually stands on the Türk–Tāzīk axis on the day:

Axis at 0 or above — Tāzīk Axis below 0 — Türk Permanent modifier Restoration of Eran: tax efficiency +5%; monthly control +0.005; stability investment +20%; cultural tradition +50%; manpower −10% Mandate of the Great Khan: manpower +25%; land morale +10%; diplomatic reputation +2; tax efficiency −15%; pops join rebels more readily (−0.10) Estate Dīwān +25% satisfaction Amirs +25% satisfaction Cabinet action unlocked Integrate into the Dīwān Invite Turkic Settlers Formable — a Türk victory is the gate to Iran o Turan

When the situation ends — by victory or otherwise — every contender loses Contender for the Throne and the sword rule, Post-Ilkhanid Chaos is lifted from the land, and the Erānzamīn organisation dissolves.

docs.title: If nobody wins
docs.text:
