docs.title: Hordes: the yam, the darugha and the ulus
docs.text:
Where the grass runs, the khan's word runs.

A Chinggisid khanate was neither a kingdom with provinces nor a crown with fiefs. It was the decimal army — tümen, minghan, jaghun — holding allotted pasture, and authority moved through it by means a settled chancery did not have: the yam relay posts, the khan's migrating camp (the ordu), and the muster. Where the khan needed a settled place held he posted a resident officer, the darugha (the basqaq of the Rus chronicles): Qutlugh-Temür at Urgench and Tuluktumur at Solkhat were both hosts to Ibn Baṭṭūṭa in 1333–34. Where he needed a whole country held he gave it to a prince of the line as an ulus, a share of the patrimony. The two answers failed differently. Appointed begs could never be khan, so they learned to keep one — Mamai, Edigü, Qazaghan. Princes with shares could be khan themselves, and their quarrels were settled at successions. The rule above both was the törü: only the seed of Chinggis reigns, and among that seed the quriltai decides.

The base game gives a steppe horde no tools of control, a flat penalty at every khan's death and a civil war that follows from it almost automatically. The mod replaces that with the choice a khan actually faced.

docs.title: Who this applies to
docs.text:
Rule Applies to The Yam and the Ordu, Darugha's Seat, Grant a Share of the Ulus, the event The Question of the Far Country Any Steppe Horde whose ruler is of the Borjigin dynasty, or which holds the Beglerbeg's Regency reform (see The Amirs' Regency and The Beglerbeg's Regency) No flat horde-unity loss at a ruler's death; the tümen levy Every Steppe Horde The succession poll Every independent Steppe Horde, except the amirs of Ulus Chaghatay, a regent's state there, and a Ṣāḥib-qirān's realm The Beglerbeg's Regency disaster Any Steppe Horde outside Ulus Chaghatay whose throne a Chinggisid has held, when its succession seats a man not of the line (see The Beglerbeg's Regency) The Törü of the Ulus succession law Seated at game start on Jochi (GLH, the Golden Horde) and Chagatai (CHG); a horde that holds it cannot change it The changed Horde Civil War Every Steppe Horde; the rule differs by whether a Borjigin has ever held the throne Horse-Lords of the Steppes and Kurultai advances Any country of a steppe or Mongolian culture, whatever its government The steppe privileges Hereditary Tümens and Bound to the Tümen Every Steppe Horde that starts from the base game's Eurasian horde setup; any Steppe Horde may hold them The tribes in the horde's parliament Every horde with the Legacy of Genghis reform

A horde ruled by a house that is not Borjigin — the Barlas, Jalayirs and the other amir houses of Transoxiana, for instance — has none of the khan's reach: no yam, no darughas, no shares to grant.

docs.title: The Yam and the Ordu
docs.text:
A horde under a khan of the line carries the standing modifier The Yam and the Ordu:

Effect Value Proximity Efficiency +33% Number of Local Governors +8

The first makes proximity carry further from the capital across the whole realm. (The in-game description speaks of flatland only; the effect as implemented is not limited by terrain.) The second is the budget of resident appointees, which is what the darugha seats are built against.

At game start every such horde also receives the one-time explanatory event The Reach of the Yam.

docs.title: Darugha's Seat
docs.text:
The Darugha's Seat is the horde's counterpart of the base game's local governor, without that building's requirement of a road to the capital and allowed in towns as well as cities.

Where A town, city or megalopolis you own that is not your capital, not a historical capital, and has no other proximity-source building Levels 1 per location Staff Nobles Effect in the location It is a proximity source of 60 (the base governor's is stronger); the country around it is measured from the seat instead of from the capital Effect on the realm Each seat adds 0.30 to the nobles' estate power Upkeep Tools, masonry, weaponry, paper, books, furniture and fine cloth; no gold Built by The khan only; estates and automation do not build it

How many seats. Seats share one budget with governors, lieutenancies, itinerant court seats and king's manors: your number of local governors (rank, plus the 8 from the yam), plus one seat for every full 10% of power the nobles estate holds. The stronger the begs, the more of the realm is run through their appointees.

The man. Building a seat fires A Darugha Is Appointed and creates a real character in your nobles estate: a 40-year-old beg with administrative and diplomatic skill between 40 and 70 and military skill between 60 and 90. He is marked as a darugha of the khan, which counts for him in the törü (below). He outlives his post.

Losing the seats. If the ruler is no longer Borjigin and there is no Beglerbeg's Regency, every Darugha's Seat in the realm is destroyed. The appointed begs remain.

docs.title: The Question of the Far Country
docs.text:
Once a year, and no more than once in five years, a qualifying horde is asked what to do about an area it does not hold in hand: a core town or city outside the capital's area, in an area where it owns at least 60% of the locations and where no darugha sits. The best-developed such town is the seat in question.

Option Requires Result Post a darugha 10 political influence −10 political influence; a Darugha's Seat is built there at once at half cost; +5% nobles satisfaction Give it to a son of the line A grown Borjigin prince who is not the ruler The area, and a neighbouring area if one qualifies, become his ulus (see below); +5 horde unity, a small gain of political influence, +3% nobles satisfaction Buy a man with no name and no people More than 100 gold A payment in gold scaled to your income; a seat is built at once for free; −5% nobles satisfaction Let it lie dark — Nothing

The area is not offered again once it has been settled by a seat or a grant.

docs.title: Granting an ulus
docs.text:
Grant a Share of the Ulus is a character interaction, available at any time the realm is at peace.

Requirements

  • The recipient is a grown man of the line of Chinggis and not the ruler. The Barlas, whom the base game files under the Borjigin dynasty, do not count (see Ulus Chaghatay).
  • Two areas that border each other. Neither may be the capital's area; you must own at least half the locations in each; neither may contain a Darugha's Seat (pull the seat down first if you have changed your mind).

What happens

  • Everything you own in both areas passes to a new country, with the prince as its ruler and its capital at the best-developed location of the first area. It is a Steppe Horde of Mongolian culture (Chaghatay, if the granting realm is Chaghatay) and your religion, with the Legacy of Genghis reform, 250 gold, two regiments of Horse Archers, and the modifier Newly Granted Share for twenty years (+0.30 maximum control and +0.005 monthly control, fading over the period).
  • It is your subject of the type Ulus.
  • You gain +5 horde unity, +3% nobles satisfaction and a small amount of political influence. The grant costs no gold: its price is the land, and a claimant with an army.
  • Inside Ulus Chaghatay during the Amirs' Regency, a share granted to a prince sets the regency's clock back by 10.

The AI now grants shares. It does so when it holds much core land at under a quarter control, when horde unity is low, or when the nobles hold more than 40% of estate power; each share already granted makes the next less likely, and it does not grant while at war.

docs.title: The Ulus subject
docs.text:
Pays the senior khan 25% of manpower, 10% of sailors, 5% of gold income Loyalty +30 loyalty to overlord (three times a fiefdom) The ulus itself +10% levy size, −25% cabinet efficiency The senior khan, per ulus +0.05 monthly horde unity, +5% levy size, +0.02 nobles estate power War Can be called into the khan's offensive and defensive wars but does not join automatically; the khan is not called automatically into its wars; it may declare wars of its own Succession Keeps its own ruler, house and succession law. If the line dies out the share returns to the khan Building The khan cannot build roads, buildings or RGOs inside it Annexation Possible after 10 years at 160 opinion, at three-quarters speed Ending it The khan may revoke the share (Revoke a Share); the holder cannot leave

An ulus cannot be created or offered through diplomacy; it exists only where a khan carved one out.

The seam. A loyal ulus may not attack the khan. Once its loyalty falls below the game's minimum-loyalty threshold, it can — and that is the succession war the system is built to produce.

The share returns. If the holder of an ulus is himself raised as khan of the senior realm, his ulus is annexed back into it at the succession poll and the realm gains 5 horde unity.

The loyalty shock at the granting khan's death that the in-game text promises ("sworn to the khan who makes it, and to no one after him") is designed but not yet scripted; today the cost of an ulus at a succession is the weight it gives its holder in the törü and in the poll.

For the unrelated sworn governors of the Ilkhanate's successors, see Custody of the Ulus and Ilkhanate governorate.

docs.title: The Törü of the Ulus
docs.text:
The base game gives hordes succession by the oldest male. The Törü of the Ulus replaces it for Jochi and Chagatai with a scored, visible field: sons, brothers, nephews and cousins of the ruler, every noble in the realm, and the rulers of your own uluses. Women are not candidates; children are, without penalty.

Term Score Of the line of the Borjigin +150 Son of the late khan +50 Grandson of the late khan +25 Named by the late khan before his death +75 Holds a share of the patrimony (rules a subject of yours) +100 Holds a district for the khan (a darugha) +25 The weight his estate carries in the realm — only for men not of the line nobles' estate power × 100, so up to +100 Reputation in the field his military skill (0–100) Seniority of years his age Unsuited to rule −1000

Blood is worth a great deal and nothing is deducted for lacking it. A capable darugha in a realm where the nobles hold much of the power can outscore a prince; that is intended.

docs.title: What happens when a khan dies
docs.text:
The base game's −50 horde unity at every ruler's death is cancelled for all Steppe Hordes. Instead, 30 to 80 days after a new ruler is seated, the realm is polled and one of the following happens. They are tested in this order:

Outcome When Horde unity The regent's own succession A Beglerbeg's Regency is running, or the house holds the office See that page There Is No One Left to Raise No grown man of the Borjigin line anywhere in the realm — the new ruler included — or ruling one of its uluses, and no Beglerbeg's Regency −50, and the Horde Civil War can begin The Amirs Raise a Khan The seat of Ulus Chaghatay only: one of the two bars is at its line and a man of the line exists to enthrone The Amirs' Regency begins A Boy on the Felt The seat of Ulus Chaghatay only: the new khan is a child or has a regent −5, and both bars stand a third lower at the next succession The Beglerbeg Outside Ulus Chaghatay: the new ruler is not of the line, on a throne a Chinggisid has held The Beglerbeg's Regency begins The Amirs Have Been Counting The new ruler is not of the line, where the row above does not apply; or the realm has 4 or more Darugha's Seats and the nobles hold over 35% of estate power; or there is a regent and 3 or more seats −20 Too Many Sons of the Line The contest reaches 4, counting 1 for every grown Borjigin man in the realm other than the ruler and 4 for every ulus ruled by one −15 The Quriltai Is of One Mind Otherwise +5

So the bill at the funeral is for the road taken in life: many shares make a contested field, many seats make the begs' play, and a realm that used neither pays nothing.

At present the four generic events (There Is No One Left to Raise, The Amirs Have Been Counting, Too Many Sons of the Line, The Quriltai Is of One Mind) carry only their horde-unity consequence. The choices their texts point to (purge or appanage; the beglerbeg's terms) are not yet written, and two of the descriptions still show a developer's placeholder note.

docs.title: The Horde Civil War
docs.text:
The mod keeps the base Horde Civil War disaster and changes two things.

When it can start.

Horde Condition A throne a Borjigin has ever held Only when the blood has failed: no living man of the line in the realm who is an adult, the ruler or the heir, and no Beglerbeg's Regency. Horde unity no longer matters Any other horde The base rule: horde unity at 40 or less; or at 75 or less with a regent; or at 60 or less with an heir

Who can be a pretender. In the base game any adult noble of the realm may claim the throne. Here a pretender must be a patrilineal Borjigin or of a steppe or Mongolian culture. Religion is not tested.

docs.title: The begs' privileges, the kuriltai and the parliament
docs.text:
A beg's hold was on tribesmen, not on peasants: a hereditary command, and men who could not leave their unit. The base game starts a horde's nobles with two privileges written for a lord and his manor (a monopoly of mill and oven; serfs tied to the land). The mod's copy of the base horde setup swaps them for two steppe privileges of the nobles' estate, which any Steppe Horde can hold.

Privilege Effect Hereditary Tümens +50% nobles' estate power, −10% political influence gain, −5% maximum control, a monthly drift toward aristocracy, and the nobles may keep a private army Bound to the Tümen +40% nobles' estate power, −10% tribesmen food consumption, +5% levy size

Both raise the nobles' target satisfaction, and both carry a line lowering "tribesmen enfranchisement", a modifier the mod defines as a test and which may have no effect in the engine.

Two smaller rules changed with them:

  • The Kurultai building may stand wherever its owner's primary culture is of the steppe group, not only where the location's majority is. A horde seated in a Tajik city (the Yasa'uri at Samarkand and Bukhara) can build and upgrade its Kurultai, and so recruit and grow its manpower.
  • The tribes sit in a horde's parliament. The Legacy of Genghis reform now lets the tribes estate take part; before, a horde's assembly seated nobles and peasants only. The reform is also open to hordes of Chaghatay culture, not only Mongolian ones.

docs.title: The tümen levy, advances and pasture
docs.text:
• Levy. The horde levy (Steppe Horde Militia) is raised from tribesmen only and at 10% of them. The base game uses the generic peasant-infantry rate and draws on the whole population.
  • Advances. Horse-Lords of the Steppes (−33% light cavalry maintenance and reinforcement cost, levies always allowed, Horse Archers) and Kurultai (−50% levy maintenance, the Kurultai building) are open to any country of a steppe or Mongolian culture — including Persianized Mongol — and no longer only to Steppe Hordes. A Turco-Mongol house that takes a sultan's titles keeps its horsemen; see The Matter of Tork for what it loses instead.
  • Steppe Tribal Pasture. A rural building for the Steppes and Khorasan regions (cold arid or continental climate, grassland or sparse vegetation, more than 1,000 tribesmen). Up to 20 levels of 1,000 tribesmen each; a level yields horses (0.45) or livestock (0.75), lowers the location's population capacity by 2,000 and gives +0.3 local tribes estate power and +2% local levy size.
  • Tribal Pasture. The larger range of the plateau and its neighbours (Persia, Khorasan, the Fertile Crescent, Anatolia, the Caucasus and the Steppes; arid, cold arid or continental climate; grassland, sparse or seasonally irrigated land). It needs more than 5,000 tribesmen and local control below 33%. Up to 5 levels of 5,000 tribesmen each; a level yields horses (1.8) or livestock (3), lowers population capacity by 7,500 and gives +1.5 local tribes estate power and +10% local levy size.
  • At game start every Steppe Horde with its capital in the Steppes or Khorasan region receives a free Steppe Tribal Pasture in each of its rural locations there that has between 1,000 and 10,000 tribesmen, and each of its locations producing salt, iron, copper, gold or silver gains +1 maximum RGO workers and 1,000 labourers.

docs.title: Playing it
docs.text:
• Count your seats before the khan dies. Four seats with the nobles above 35% of estate power turns the next succession into the begs' play. Each seat itself raises the nobles' power, and each 10% of that power opens another seat.
  • Grant shares with the törü open. A prince with an ulus gains +100 in the succession and counts four times in the contest. One share is safe; a second share to a second prince is a contested succession.
  • Keep a grown man of the line alive. For Jochi and Chagatai the civil war now has a single cause. Uluses held by Borjigin princes count as living blood for the poll.
  • A darugha cannot share ground with an ulus. The two answers are exclusive in the same area, in both directions.
  • Read the line of succession. The törü shows its candidates and their scores at all times. A beg near the top is a warning that the next accession may go to the begs.

See also: Ulus Chaghatay, The Amirs' Regency, The Ṣāḥib-qirān, The Beglerbeg's Regency, Custody of the Ulus, Ilkhanate governorate, The Matter of Tork, Military system, Buildings, Countries and tags.

docs.title: The Ilkhanate Governorate — the deferral
docs.text:
We are governors, not kings. Let the others break themselves on the throne.

Not every house of the old Ilkhanate reached for the throne. The Injuids held Fars as the fiscal governors they had been under Abū Saʿīd; the Kart maliks kept Herat as they had kept it under four Ilkhans; a dozen lesser dynasties were, quite literally, the provincial administration carrying on after the centre had gone. They read aloud whatever name the strongest neighbour sent them, kept their registers, and waited to see who would win. The mod makes that a deliberate posture: the fourth answer to the opening question of the Succession of Erānzamīn, beside the regency, the ghazā and the farr.

docs.title: Taking the road
docs.text:
At the opening event, Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty, the governorate is the answer "We are governors, not kings." It adopts the Ilkhanate Governorate reform and gives +5 legitimacy and +5% Dīwān satisfaction: the chancery approves of the caution, and nobody is provoked, because nothing has been claimed.

The AI defers according to its strength. The weakest realms take this road overwhelmingly; a realm with a real army rarely does. A realm that cannot field a host has no business claiming the ulus.

The reform is also on the reform panel for any member of the Erānzamīn organisation that holds none of the rival answers (the regency, Farr-i Īzadī, Ghāzī Sultanate, Amīr Sultanate, Sword of The Sharia) and is not a ṭarīqa order. It takes effect at once.

docs.title: The reform
docs.text:
The administrator who keeps his head down: defensible, solvent and unthreatening.

Effect Value Reading Monthly legitimacy +0.1 a recognised governor's lawful place — modest, and no more Stability cost efficiency +10% steady Fort defence +20% defensible in your corner — worth more than it looks while the region's walls stand at −66% Land morale +5% Tax efficiency +10% a well-run province Antagonism received −20% nobody marches on the humble governor Monthly prestige −0.1 a governor is not a king Province integration speed −20% no reach Diplomatic reputation −1

A governorate counts as having answered the legitimacy question: it does not suffer Unsettled Legitimacy. If it is independent, Muslim and seated in the region it is still a contender in the eyes of the situation — it keeps the contender's modifier, the sword rule and the situation's actions — but in the organisation's ledger it holds no role. Unless it is allied to a bloc head it appears under Unaligned, among the "governors waiting to see who wins".

docs.title: Swearing to a steward
docs.text:
A governorate can read a stronger man's khan in its khuṭba and become his sworn governorate. There are three ways this happens, and they all end in the same bond.

Path Who starts it How it works Declare Fealty the governorate an action on the situation panel, available to an independent governorate at peace. You choose a steward from the roll of members who hold the Chinggisid Regency, are ruled by a Borjigin, or are contending in earnest. It takes effect at once: the steward is informed (The Sermon Is Already Read) and cannot refuse. In Whose Name Do We Govern? the times while at least one regency stands, an independent governorate is pressed to choose — at most once every five years, with roughly a one-in-eleven chance each month it is due. It is offered the three strongest regencies by military strength, or to hold out: "Not yet. We were made governors by Abū Saʿīd." Swearing gives +5 legitimacy. Demand Fealty a regent a regent under the Borrowed Mandate sends robes and gifts and calls the governorate to swear. Accept, and you receive gold equal to his tax base; refuse, and you keep your corner and your quarrel.

Note the difference in who may be sworn to: the periodic event offers only regencies, while Declare Fealty also lets you kneel to a Borjigin sovereign or to any contender — a farr claimant or a ghāzī included.

docs.title: What the steward gets
docs.text: For a regent the oath is mostly titular, but the titular part is his whole case: while he rules as a Chinggisid Regency, each sworn governorate gives him +0.05 monthly legitimacy and +0.10 monthly political influence. For any overlord, the governorate's land counts toward his bloc in the organisation's ledger and toward the 400 locations the throne requires — though one of the Five Seats held by a governorate does not count as his until he owns it himself.

docs.title: The sworn governorate as a subject
docs.text:
This is not a conquered vassal. It is a deferring administrator who chose the arrangement and keeps his own house. In the game it is named Ilkhanate Governorate in the subject list, and its overlord is the Liege of the Governorates.

Term Detail How it is created only by the three paths above — it cannot be demanded in a peace treaty or offered through ordinary diplomacy Tribute pays as an ordinary vassal does Its ruler its own; the overlord's ruler does not take the seat The overlord's wars the overlord may call it to his offensive and defensive wars; it does not join automatically Its own wars it may declare war on anyone except its overlord — fellow governorates above all, and outsiders too Its defence the overlord is not drawn in automatically. When a sworn governorate is attacked by anyone else, the overlord is asked (The Governorate Calls): ride and join the war, or refuse at a cost of 5 legitimacy and the governorate's resentment Building the overlord cannot build roads, buildings or resource works in its land Annexation not before 15 years, only at an opinion of 175, and at half the usual speed Release the overlord may cancel the bond Diplomacy limited; its diplomatic capacity cost to the overlord is scaled by 0.75 Rank and succession it may change its own rank and its own heir selection

The right to fight one's fellow governorates is the heart of it. The Ilkhanid successor melee was largely a war among men who all read the same khan's name on Friday; the one bond the governorate keeps is that name, and everything else it settles by the sword.

docs.title: Dropping the khan
docs.text:
The way out is Drop the Khan from the Khutbah, an action on the situation panel for a sworn governorate that is not at war with its overlord. It is a renunciation, not a negotiation:

Effect Detail The bond ends at once; any truce with the former overlord is removed The former overlord takes offence (Ignored the hallowed bloodline of Genghis Khan) and receives a Succession of Erānzamīn casus belli against you Your reform the Ilkhanate Governorate is removed Your next answer Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty is put to you again — and for five years the governorate is not among the answers. Having dropped a khan, you must pick a side: the regency, the ghazā or the farr Legitimacy +5

An AI governorate walks out when it has grown strong enough to stand alone, or stronger than the overlord who was meant to shield it.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• For a small realm this is the safest opening in the game. +20% fort defence and −20% antagonism under a reform that provokes no one, and the option to buy a protector later with a single action.
  • Swear when you are threatened, not before. An independent governorate keeps its full freedom of action. Declare Fealty is instant and cannot be refused, so it can be held in reserve until the army is at the gates — but it requires you to be at peace, so do not wait for the declaration of war itself.
  • Choose a steward who will ride. The overlord's defence is a decision, not a guarantee. A regent already at war is much less likely to come.
  • Use the licence to fight. As a sworn governorate you can still make war on every neighbour except your overlord, with his name over your door.
  • The road has no summit of its own. The reform's ceilings on prestige, integration and reputation are not built for a realm gathering 400 locations and five great cities. Sooner or later a growing governorate drops the khan and answers the question properly; plan for the casus belli your former overlord receives the day you do.
  • For regents: governorates are legitimacy. See The Borrowed Mandate for the price of asking and the value of each oath.

See also: The Succession of Erānzamīn, The Erānzamīn organisation, The Borrowed Mandate, Government reforms, Dīwān estate.

docs.title: Kurdish emirates
docs.text: They could not be taken, and they would not expand.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
When Sharaf Khān of Bidlīs wrote the Sharafnāma in 1597 he arranged the Kurdish ruling houses the way a Persian chancery would: by rank of sovereignty, from dynasties that had once struck coin and held the khuṭba down to the hereditary lords of a single valley, each with its genealogy and its seat. The houses he describes (the Rōzhikī of Bidlīs, the ʿAzīzān of Bohtān at Jazīra, the lords of Hakkârî, Çemişgezek and the Zirqī country) were already old in 1337 and most would outlast the Ilkhans, the Timurids and the Aq Qoyunlu alike. A mîrnishîn was a hereditary principality with a court that wrote Persian and kept the etiquette of Tabriz, but its structure was confederate: the mîr ruled through tribal aghas and valley lords who kept their own followings, over a peasantry that in places such as Bidlīs and Mush was largely Armenian. It had no surveyed tax register and no salaried bureaucracy. What it had was a fortress, a lineage, and mountains that made conquest more expensive than a nominal oath of vassalage, which each successive empire therefore accepted.

The base game models these polities as generic tribes. The mod gives them their own government, the Iranic Tribal Polity, and prunes the map down to the houses that actually existed.

docs.title: Who starts with it
docs.text:
Eleven countries in 1337, all with the Kurdish Emirate reform, all members of Erānzamīn in the Sutayid camp:

Country Capital Position in 1337 Bohtan (BHT) Cizre Paramount emirate of the Jazīra; vassal of the Sutayids; overlord of Dasni Bitlis (BIT) Bitlis Paramount emirate of the Van basin; vassal of the Sutayids; overlord of Hizan, Mus and Çapakçur Hakkari (HKK) Hakkari Paramount emirate of the high Zagros; vassal of the Sutayids; holds Van, Amadiya and Zakho Hizan (HZN) Hizan Vassal of Bitlis Mus (MUS) Mus Vassal of Bitlis Çapakçur (BIN) Bingöl Vassal of Bitlis Dasni (DSN) Duhok Vassal of Bohtan Zirqan (ZRQ) Mayyafariqin Vassal of the Sutayids Egil (EGL) Sivrice Vassal of the Sutayids Çemişgezek (CEM) Çemişgezek Vassal of the Sutayids Hazro (HZR) Hazro Vassal of the Sutayids

Changes to the map around them:

  • Hakkari has absorbed two small base-game neighbours (the Şemdinli and Van highland clusters), and Dasni has absorbed Akre.
  • The base game's many small Kurdish tags in Iraqi Kurdistan, the central Zagros and the Azerbaijan fringe (Ardalan among them) do not exist at the start. Their lands begin inside the Jalayirid and Chobanid realms.
  • The Ayyubids of Ḥiṣn Kayfā (HSN) are not an Iranic Tribal Polity. They keep their base-game monarchy.

Any country of Kurdish culture that comes into being later as a base-game tribe (a rebel state, a released country) is converted to an Iranic Tribal Polity with the Kurdish Emirate reform on the day it forms.

docs.title: The government
docs.text:
Iranic Tribal Polity uses the base game's Tribal Cohesion as its government power, described in game as the mîr's standing among the aghas and valley lords who actually hold the guns. Succession is by eldest male of the house at the start; the other tribal succession laws are available.

Government effect Value Expected diplomatic spending −50% Cultures capacity +1

The extra culture capacity is there so that a mîr can accept the people he actually rules. Without it, the Kurdish emirs of Bitlis, Mus and Hizan could not recognise their own Armenian majorities.

The starting setup gives each emirate a Persian court language, a council rather than a maẓālim court, and societal values that are strongly decentralised, defensive, aristocratic and land-bound.

docs.title: The Kurdish Emirate reform
docs.text:
The defining reform. It is locked: it cannot be removed while the country remains an Iranic Tribal Polity.

Effect Value Monthly legitimacy +0.10 Land morale +10% Fort defense +25% Tribes estate levy size +25% Tribes estate power +150% Tribes estate sits in the council yes Monthly drift towards decentralization +0.10 Monthly drift towards Türk +0.05 Government reform slots +1

docs.title: Defense of the Mountains
docs.text: While an Iranic Tribal Polity is at war and is not the attacker, it gains +50% levy size. When the emirate is the aggressor the aghas stay home and the bonus is absent. This one modifier is most of the design: devastating at home, ordinary abroad.

docs.title: How it differs from a Persianate Sultanate
docs.text:
Persianate Sultanate Iranic Tribal Polity Ruling class Dīwān and Amirs, split by the chancery Nobles and a very strong Tribes estate; no chancery, so no Dīwān or Amirs estate Assembly Maẓālim court Council, with the Tribes seated Government power Legitimacy Tribal Cohesion Legitimacy question Must answer the khuṭba question or suffer Unsettled Legitimacy Not asked; the Erānzamīn legitimacy reforms are not available Türk vs Tāzīk Contested (see Türk vs Tāzīk) Drifts steadily towards the saddle Character Extraction and reach Durability

An emirate is still a member of Erānzamīn, and as a vassal it is drawn into its overlord's wars in the Erānzamīn situation whether it wants them or not.

docs.title: Levies and units
docs.text:
Under this government the base game's generic tribal levies are switched off and replaced by the mod's Iranian tribal levies, drawn from tribesmen pops of Iranian-group cultures (Kurdish among them). The same levies serve Persianate Sultanates that rule such tribes.

Levy When Share of tribesmen Unit raised Zagros Tribal Levy Ages 1–2 10% Zagros Skirmishers Tofang Tribal Levy Age 3 onwards 10% Tofang Levies Retinue of the Mir Always 2% Frontier Amir Cavalry

The steppe rule that a tribesman is a horseman does not hold in the Zagros. The mass of the levy is light infantry; the mounted element is a small elite.

Unit Type Notable traits Zagros Skirmishers Light infantry (levy only) +10% morale damage dealt, −15% morale damage taken, +10% strength damage taken, +2 initiative; +30% in hills and mountains, +15% on plateau Tofang Levies Light infantry (levy only) +10% strength and morale damage dealt, −10% morale damage taken, +2 initiative; same terrain bonuses

Fight in the hills. On open ground the skirmishers are fragile.

docs.title: Becoming something larger
docs.text:
The road out of the mountains runs through a great city. When an Iranic Tribal Polity comes to own Tabriz, Isfahan, Shiraz, Nishapur, Baghdad or Herat, it receives The Chancery Within Reach:

Option Effect "Take up the chancery — let the dīwān rise." Becomes a Persianate Sultanate; loses Kurdish Emirate; gains the Persianate Bureaucracy reform; −10 legitimacy, −10 stability "We remain the mîr of the mountains." +5 legitimacy

Taking up the chancery is a one-way door. The emirate's bonuses (the defensive levy, the fort defense, the built-in legitimacy) go with the reform, and the new sultanate inherits everything a Persianate Sultanate must deal with instead: the Dīwān and Amirs estates, the Türk–Tāzīk balance, and the khuṭba question (see Government reforms). Refusing does not close the door for good; the offer comes again with the next great city taken.

There is no other conversion. An emirate that grows without one of the six cities stays an emirate.

docs.title: Advice
docs.text:
• Play the long game. In 1337 every emirate is somebody's vassal. That is the historical position and a comfortable one: the Sutayids and the Jalayirids above them fight the succession wars while you keep +0.10 legitimacy a month.
  • Let them come to you. +50% levies, +25% fort defense and hill-fighting infantry make a defensive war in your own valleys the best fight you will get. Wars of aggression lose the levy bonus.
  • Bitlis and Bohtan start with vassals of their own. They are the natural cores for anyone trying to gather the emirates.
  • Baghdad and Tabriz are the nearest great cities, and both are prizes the great contenders for Erānzamīn fight over. Reaching one usually means winning independence first and then outlasting a succession war.
  • Decide before you take the city. Once you accept the chancery you are playing a different, much more demanding government, starting at −10 stability.

See also: Persianate Sultanate, Erānzamīn situation, Military system, Türk vs Tāzīk, Demography and cultures, Shattered Rum, Countries and tags.

docs.title: The Matter of Tork — The Place of the Sword
docs.text:
What is the Türk's place now?

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The Matter was rebuilt after the June wiki: paths now stack, the disaster closes only when you press The Answer Is Given, and the frontier march is earned through the Great Raid. The Great Raid migration, Release the March and the closing proclamation have not been verified end to end in a full campaign.

The post-Ilkhanid armies were Turco-Mongol tribal hosts, and their idea of rank ran through nearness to the house of Chinggis. A ruler who consolidates Iran without that blood — whether he rests his crown on the farr, on the ghazā, or on a shaykh's blessing — has settled his own legitimacy and, in doing so, has made the hosts' whole ordering of the world irrelevant. They do not vanish. They stand in the realm, armed, holding the pastures and most of the cavalry. Every dynasty from the Seljuks to the Safavids had to say what became of them: absorbed into the Persian-speaking service gentry, planted on a frontier, bound to the throne as disciples, driven out, or broken.

The Matter of Tork is that question as a disaster. It does not audit a claim, as the Farr Under Examination and the Burden of the Sword do. It applies a light standing friction and waits for an answer, and it is the only door to the mechanics that settle the Türk question.

docs.title: When it fires
docs.text:
All of the following must hold for a country:

  • it is a contender in the Erānzamīn situation, independent, with its capital in Erānzamīn;
  • it owns, directly or through subjects, more than 240 locations, and has held that size for 24 consecutive months (falling below resets the count);
  • at least 750,000 Turco-Mongol tribesmen (Turkic, Tatar or Mongolian cultures) live in the realm. The census is taken once a year. A realm whose tribesmen are Kurds, Lurs and Baluch never faces the Matter;
  • the ruler is not of the Borjigin dynasty, and the realm is not a Chinggisid Regency, an Amīr Sultanate or a Türkmen Confederation. A khan, or a regent ruling in a khan's name, gives the hosts no grievance; in the Türk-coded regimes the hosts are the constituency;
  • the Amirs or the Tribes estate has a target satisfaction below 65%;
  • the Matter has not already been faced. It happens once per country.

Once the gate is open the disaster is rolled monthly. In practice this is a mid-campaign event, arriving as the consolidation of Iran completes.

docs.title: The standing friction
docs.text:
While the Matter runs:

Effect Value Amirs estate target satisfaction −10% Tribes estate target satisfaction −10% Monthly Amirs rebel growth +0.01 Monthly Tribes rebel growth +0.015 Monthly legitimacy −0.10

Beginning the Dissolve or releasing a march applies An Answer Given, which cancels three quarters of this (+7.5% to both estates, −0.0075 and −0.01 rebel growth, +0.075 monthly legitimacy) until the disaster ends.

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
The panel shows three bars: Months without an answer (out of 240), Iranization — the long work, and Expulsion — the hosts moved on (out of 120).

  • At 240 months without the proclamation, the hosts answer for you (see Catastrophe). Only pressing The Answer Is Given, an eradication, or a defection war stops this clock. A finished path does not.
  • The clock is set back 12 months each time the hosts see the state respond: when the amīrs are seated at the dīwān, at each of the other three Dissolve steps, and for every Registered Pasture built.

docs.title: How it is answered
docs.text:
The Matter has three layers.

  1. An approach, chosen at the Council on the Hosts. An approach is a direction of preparation: it applies one ambient modifier and switches on its own panel actions.
  2. One or more paths, the lasting answers. Paths stack: you may dissolve the settled hosts, release a march and swear the rest as disciples in the same reign, and each completed path keeps its own rewards. Eradication alone excludes every other path.
  3. The proclamation, The Answer Is Given, which closes the Matter with whatever you have completed.

docs.title: The Council on the Hosts
docs.text:
The disaster opens with the council, which offers four approaches or an adjournment. Change Approach reconvenes it, with a two-year cooldown. Switching swaps only the ambient modifier; privileges granted, corps tiers bought, buildings and axis movement all stay, and the clock does not reset.

One trap: the council can no longer be reconvened once any path has been begun (the Dissolve claimed, a march released, the bond sworn, Expulsion ordered). Approach actions only work while their approach is active, so finish the approach-bound preparation for every path you intend to take before you begin the first.

Prices below are in scaled gold, which grows with the size of your economy.

docs.title: "We must reduce our reliance on these barbarians" — Reducing the Reliance
docs.text:
Ambient: +2.5% discipline, −2.5% Amirs satisfaction. Prepares Expulsion and Eradication, though the corps is useful under any answer. Choosing it once makes three privileges permanently grantable: Dīwān al-ʿArḍ (the chancery runs the corps: Dīwān power +20%, Amirs satisfaction −10%) or Amir-Held Commands (painless, but Amirs power +15%) — one or the other — and Fostering Households for the peasants. Either administration privilege lets you build Ghulam Barracks (towns and cities, up to three levels, staffed by slaves, lets regiments be recruited there).

Action Price Requires Effect Purchase Ghulam Levies (2-year cooldown) 6 An administrator (either privilege above, or the Ghulām Corps reform), Fostering Households, and barracks levels: 1 for the first tier, 3 for the second, 6 for the third. Tiers two and three also need the Slave Caravans Raises the corps one tier and grows slave pops at the barracks Declare Royal Inju (2-year cooldown) 6 An owned location with a Tribal Pasture not yet declared The whole province becomes crown demesne: every pasture in it is destroyed and each location gets Royal Inju (−25% local levy size, +5% local maximum control, permanent). Tribes satisfaction −5%. Half the time nothing more; 35% the location gets Pastures in Ferment for five years; 15% an amīr protests at court Institutionalize the Slave Caravans (once) 12 Caravanserai levels totalling 3, and a castle or fortress of yours adjacent to an unfortified location of a non-Muslim country The Slave Caravans: +2.5% Burghers satisfaction, +2.5% tax efficiency; unlocks corps tiers two and three

The corps tiers are permanent and survive the disaster:

Tier Manpower Discipline Other Palace Ghulam Corps +5% +1% — Ghulam Regiments +10% +2% — The Army Within the Army +15% +3% Amirs estate power −5%

The first purchase stages The First Muster, which leaves the corps Drilled to the Drum (+2% discipline, +5% morale) or with Teething Troubles (−1% discipline, −5% army maintenance efficiency) for five years. The bad result is much likelier under Amir-Held Commands.

The plot. While this approach is active and either the Amirs or the Tribes sit below 30% satisfaction, a hidden counter runs. At 24 months you are warned (The Amirs Smell the Plot); at 48 the hosts defect early (The Plot Realized) with the same civil war as the 240-month catastrophe. The counter resets the month both estates recover.

docs.title: "Iran is the Beacon of Civilization" — The Beacon of Civilization
docs.text:
Ambient: +15% pop assimilation speed, +0.05 monthly toward Tāzīk. Prepares the Dissolve. Choosing it once makes three privileges permanently grantable: Iqtaʿ Commutation and Chancery Commissions for Amir Sons (Amirs) and Salaried Pastoral Levies (Tribes). Each pleases its estate in the long run, costs satisfaction on the day it is granted, and pushes the axis toward Tāzīk.

Action Price Effect Sponsor Qanat Settlement (5-year cooldown) 6 A pastoral location gets Qanat Settlement for 20 years: +25% local assimilation speed, −0.05 unrest, a little prosperity Endow the Madrasa of the Registers (10-year cooldown) 6 Ten years of +10% assimilation speed, +5% Dīwān satisfaction and +0.05 monthly toward Tāzīk, at −5% cabinet efficiency Commission the Shāhnāma Recension (once) 12 +10 prestige, +5 legitimacy, 5 points toward Tāzīk

Three events follow at 18, 40 and 70 months under this approach: an amīr's son passes the chancery examination, the qanat reaches a winter pasture, and the margins resist. Each offers a choice between axis movement and Tribes satisfaction.

docs.title: "We must forge a new Identity" — Courting the Vilāyat
docs.text:
Ambient: +0.20 monthly toward Mysticism, −5% Clergy satisfaction, −0.05 monthly religious influence. Prepares the murīd bond. Choosing it once makes the Clergy privilege Lodge Endowments permanently grantable (+0.10 monthly toward Mysticism, Clergy power +15%, −5% tax efficiency).

Action Price Effect Endow a Khanqah (3-year cooldown) 6 A Sufi lodge is built free of charge in a location you choose; 5 points toward Mysticism; Clergy −2.5% Sponsor the Dhikr Festivals (4-year cooldown) 6 3 points toward Mysticism; Tribes +2.5%, Clergy −2.5% Invite the Shaykhs of the Order (once) free A shaykh joins the court; 7.5 points toward Mysticism; Clergy −5%

The courtship runs on its own counter of months spent under this approach:

  • 12 months — A Shaykh Preaches in the Camps. Tribes +5%. The hosts take to the devotion before the cities do, which is why the bond will hold them.
  • 36 months — The Jurists' Ultimatum. Cave, and the approach is abandoned and the courtship counter starts again from nothing (Clergy +10%); defy, and take The Jurists' Fury for ten years (Clergy −5%, clergy rebel growth).
  • 60 months — Red Headgear. Ten years of +5% morale. This event is what unlocks the bond.

The Claim of the Hidden Imam is offered once, while this approach is active, with the shaykh at court, Mysticism at −25 or beyond, and the realm not yet Shia. Accepting converts the country, the ruler, the heir and the dynasty to Shia Islam, converts a quarter of the non-Shia pops in every location with a Sufi lodge, and costs 10 stability, 20 legitimacy and 20% Clergy satisfaction. The bond does not require it: a Sunni court at Mysticism −50 may swear the hosts just the same.

docs.title: "Why tame what we can unleash upon our enemies?" — The Hosts Unleashed
docs.text:
Ambient: Tribes levy size +15%, +5% morale, +5% Tribes satisfaction. Prepares the frontier march.

Action Price Effect Proclaim the Great Raid (15-year cooldown) free Name a region as the theater. Ten years of The Great Raid (+5% morale, Tribes levy size +10%, a little prestige), Tribes +5%, and the Great Raid casus belli against anyone who owns land there Grant the Yurt (1-year cooldown) 12 Needs a holding in the theater. The largest Turco-Mongol tribal pops of the homeland send about 70% of their people to your most populous holding over ten months, and Turco-Mongol nobles ride with them. The destination gets a permanent Yurt Charter (+0.25 unrest) Release the March free See Point Them Outward below

The theater may be almost anywhere in the Old World except Iran itself (Persia and Khorasan, which includes Transoxiana), Anatolia, Arabia, Iraq and Syria, Egypt, the Maghreb, Somalia and the Sahel. The Caucasus, Hindustan and the steppe are open.

Proclaiming the raid marks every location in the region as a Theater of the Great Raid: tribesmen there do not settle, assimilate or convert while the banner stands, and local unrest rises by 0.25, for natives and newcomers alike. From the month you own a location in the theater, the hosts start to move by themselves: each month the largest Turco-Mongol pop of Erānzamīn not yet committed is paired with your most populous holding and sends about 40% of itself there over ten years, with at most two such streams per holding. The Great Raid war is a superiority war in which taking and subjugating land costs you three quarters of the usual price.

docs.title: The five paths
docs.text: Path Panel button Opens when Takes Dissolve Dissolve Them Into Us The Amirs hold Umarāʾ at the Dīwān; no civil war 10 years and four steps March Release the March The Hosts Unleashed is active, a theater is won, at peace Instant Murīd bond Bind Them to the Guide Red Headgear has fired, Mysticism at −50, four Sufi lodges standing; no civil war Instant Expulsion Remove Them From the Realm Two provinces declared Royal Inju; at peace 10 years Eradication End Them as a Class Five provinces declared Royal Inju; at peace; stability not negative; no other path begun A civil war, then 50 years

docs.title: Dissolve Them Into Us
docs.text:
The historical default: Türk becomes Tāzīk over a generation. Claiming it applies An Answer Given and The Long Work while the program runs: −25% cabinet efficiency, +25% assimilation speed, −10% levy size, −5% Amirs satisfaction, +0.10 monthly toward Tāzīk. The program is four institutional acts:

  1. Grant the Amirs Umarāʾ at the Dīwān — Niẓām al-Mulk's nightmare as the price of his solution. The grant pushes the Türk–Tāzīk axis 20 points toward Türk.
  2. Grant the Dīwān Mavājib Cash Pay.
  3. Build a Registered Pasture in every rural location with more than 20,000 tribesmen. It is built on an existing Tribal Pasture, and each one costs 5% Tribes satisfaction.
  4. Grant Salaried Pastoral Levies (Tribes) or Tāzīk Command of Arms (Dīwān).

While the Matter runs, every one of these steps can only be taken with the Amirs, the Dīwān and the Tribes all at 50% satisfaction or better. Steps 2 to 4 each move the axis 5 points toward Tāzīk.

Completion needs all four steps, 120 months since the claim, the axis at +25 or more toward Tāzīk, and the three estates at 50% again at that moment. It grants:

  • Türk Into Tazik (permanent): +10% tax efficiency, +5% maximum control, +10% stability investment, −5% levy size, +0.05 monthly toward Tāzīk;
  • Hosts of the State (permanent): Tribes levy size −75%, Amirs levy size −25%, Tribes estate power −25%, +10% manpower. The free tribal levy ends with the tribal compact;
  • what replaces it: the Cantonment of the Hosts building (two levels, in rural settlements and towns with more than 5,000 tribesmen; raises local manpower and rural control) and recruitable Divani Cavalry, light horse that deals 10% more and takes 10% less morale damage;
  • the Īlāt Compact government reform: Tribes satisfaction +7.5%, +5% tax efficiency, +5% tribesmen growth, +3% rural control, Tribes levy size −15%;
  • in roughly four pastoral locations in ten, the tribesmen settle as peasants of your culture.

docs.title: Point Them Outward — Release the March
docs.text:
The Seljuk play: the hosts planted on a frontier and pointed away from you. The march is earned by conquest in the Great Raid theater. To release it you must be at peace and hold:

  • at least a fifth of the theater's locations, and no fewer than 25;
  • 500,000 tribesmen living in your holdings there;
  • a seat: a city of yours in the theater whose area has at most one location in foreign hands.

Everything you own in the theater leaves with the seat as a new tributary — not a march, so that it can wage its own wars. It is a Persianate sultanate under the Amīr Sultanate reform, ruled by a beg of the largest Turco-Mongol people in it, of your religion if you are Muslim and Sunni otherwise, with an aggressive disposition.

Releasing it seals the compact. A realm on the ghāzī road (Ghāzī Sultanate or Sword of The Sharia) gets The Marcher Compact: +10% manpower, +5% morale, −5% antagonism received, +0.05 monthly legitimacy. Any other realm gets Hired Marches: +5% manpower, −5% tax efficiency. The ghāzī can give the hosts a mission on the frontier; a king of the farr can only pay them to stay there.

docs.title: Bind Them to the Guide — the murīd bond
docs.text:
The bond of disciple and guide replaces the bond of the khan: the cavalry is kept whole and re-sworn to the ruler as murshid. It needs five years of courtship (the Red Headgear event), Mysticism at −50 and four Sufi lodges.

The Murid Bond (permanent): +10% Amirs and Tribes satisfaction, +10% morale, +15% levy size, +1 tolerance of heretics, +0.10 monthly toward Mysticism, −5% Clergy satisfaction.

The price depends on what your legitimacy already rests on. Farr is itself a claim about the person of the king, so adding the guide's authority to it is a fusion of like with like: −10 legitimacy and −5% Clergy satisfaction. The ghāzī's claim rests on law and deed, and its jurists exist to deny that any living man carries such authority; he pays −40 legitimacy, −20% Clergy satisfaction and twenty years of The Cry of Zandaqa (−10% Clergy satisfaction, clergy rebel growth, −0.10 monthly legitimacy). He keeps his ghāzī reform, but in every case the bond closes the Muhtasib-King law for good and opens Ẓill Allāh — The Shadow of God whatever the realm's rite.

The bond also satisfies the legitimacy requirement for forming Persia. A year later The Oath of the Oymaqs asks whether to press the camps that held back.

docs.title: Remove Them From the Realm — Expulsion
docs.text:
Ten years of The Hosts Moved On: −15% levy size, −5% tax efficiency, −0.05 monthly legitimacy and heavy Tribes rebel growth. No An Answer Given here; the hosts know what is coming. At 3, 7 and 10 years a tranche of tribesmen is removed from every pastoral location (7,500 from each tribal pop, doubled at the second tranche), with Pastures in Ferment behind the first two.

At completion one of your pastoral locations is ceded to The Exiled Hosts, a new independent country that rides with +15% morale and +25% manpower for 25 years. You receive:

  • A Realm Made One (permanent): +10% maximum control, +3% stability investment, +1 tolerance of the true faith;
  • The Missing Arm (25 years): −20% manpower, −5% morale;
  • the refounding of the Amirs estate (below).

docs.title: End Them as a Class — Eradication
docs.text:
The confirmation event lets you recoil; the button returns after a year. Confirm, and both military estates drop to nothing, The Ending of a Class applies (−25% levy size, −0.20 monthly legitimacy, −50% target satisfaction for Amirs and Tribes), and the hosts defect at once as The Türkmen Confederation in a civil war, fighting under Total Mobilization of the Hosts (Tribes levy size +150%, +20% morale) for ten years.

  • Win, and the purge completes: more tribesmen are removed, and two modifiers apply together. The Post-Tribal State is permanent: +5% discipline, +10% maximum control, +15% tax efficiency, Amirs estate power −30%, +0.10 monthly toward centralization. The Fifty-Year Gap cancels the first three for fifty years and adds −30% manpower, −25% levy size and −10% morale. When the gap expires, the payoff stands alone.
  • Lose or settle, and you take The Bleeding Flank and −20 legitimacy.

Either way the Matter is closed in blood, without the proclamation.

docs.title: The Answer Is Given
docs.text:
Pressing The Answer Is Given (not during a civil war) closes the Matter. Each completed path adds to the settlement:

Completed path Added at the proclamation Dissolve +10 legitimacy, +5 stability March +10 legitimacy, +5 prestige Murīd bond +10 legitimacy, +5% Tribes satisfaction Expulsion +5 stability

Pressing it with nothing completed is legal and ruinous — The Answer Is Nothing: −50 legitimacy, −25 stability, −15% Amirs and −20% Tribes satisfaction, and The Bleeding Flank.

One caution for players aiming at Persia: as currently scripted, the formable's requirement that "the Place of the Sword is settled" recognises a Matter closed in blood (a won eradication or a won defection war) or one never posed, but does not yet count a Matter closed by the proclamation. See known issues.

docs.title: The Dehqān Revival
docs.text:
Once the hosts are dissolved, expelled or destroyed, the Qizilbāsh Aristocracy reform is closed to the realm for good, and Umarāʾ at the Dīwān, Iqtaʿ Commutation and Amir-Held Commands can no longer be granted.

Expulsion goes further and refounds the Amirs estate: Tribal Hosts (Yurt), Tribal Autonomy Rights, Umarāʾ at the Dīwān and Iqtaʿ Commutation are revoked, and Amir-Held Commands is replaced by Dīwān al-ʿArḍ. After Expulsion or Eradication — but not after the Dissolve, which fills the gentry's place with the commuted amīrs — a new charter becomes available for the Amirs estate:

Privilege Effect The Dehqan Revival Amirs levy size +15%, heavy cavalry power +10%, Amirs power +30% and satisfaction +5%, −5% tax efficiency, +0.05 monthly toward Tāzīk; privileges cost 50% more to revoke Service Tenure Registers +5% rural control, +2.5% tax efficiency, Amirs power −10%, Dīwān power +10%, Amirs satisfaction −2.5% The Shāhnāma Endowment +0.05 monthly prestige and legitimacy, +10% cultural tradition, Amirs satisfaction +5%

This is the road Iran did not take: the Persian landed gentry, the dehqāns who kept the Shāhnāma alive, rearmed as registered cavalry on service tenure instead of buying slave-soldiers or leaning on a new confederation.

docs.title: Catastrophe
docs.text:
Three roads lead to the same civil war against The Türkmen Confederation: 240 months without the proclamation (They Stopped Waiting), the plot under Reducing the Reliance, and Eradication. In each, the tribesmen and Turco-Mongol nobles of your pastoral locations change allegiance, those locations go over to the rebels, and the confederation fights under Total Mobilization.

For the first two:

  • War lost or left standing — The Flank Bleeds. The Bleeding Flank (permanent): −15% manpower, −5% morale, −0.05 monthly prestige.
  • War won — An Answer Written in Blood. Broken Hosts (permanent): −10% manpower, +2% maximum control, +5% stability investment. Weaker than any chosen path.

A realm carrying The Bleeding Flank cannot form Persia.

docs.title: The Matter of Tazik
docs.text: The mirror question — a Türk-leaning court facing the revolt of the cities, the sayyids and the lodges — is not active in 1.4. Its events, its breakaway ("The Urban Realm") and its outcomes are still in the files, but the disaster itself is switched off pending a redesign, so nothing fires. In practice this means Amīr Sultanates, Türkmen Confederations, Chinggisid regents and Borjigin rulers currently face no consolidation disaster of this kind at all.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Decide early which paths you want and prepare them in order. The council closes when the first path begins. A realm that wants both a march and the bond should finish the five-year courtship first, switch to The Hosts Unleashed, and only then release the march.
  • Watch the 50% line. The Dissolve stalls whenever the Amirs, Dīwān or Tribes dip below half satisfaction, and the standing friction is already pulling two of them down. Grant the Umarāʾ privilege first; it buys a year and a large Amirs bonus.
  • The axis requirement is modest but real. Seating the amīrs costs 20 points toward Türk; the three later steps return 15, and the Beacon tools and the Long Work supply the drift.
  • Never press the proclamation empty-handed, and do not let the clock run out with a path half-finished: buy time with Registered Pastures.
  • Under Reducing the Reliance, keep the military estates above 30%. Four years below it is a civil war against a half-built corps.
  • Eradication is for realms that already have the corps. The third tier's +15% manpower is the only thing in the Matter that offsets the Fifty-Year Gap.

See also: Türk vs Tāzīk, the Erānzamīn situation, the Amirs estate, estate privileges, government reforms, the Farr Under Examination, the Burden of the Sword, known issues.

docs.title: The Maẓālim court
docs.text:
"Here, the Shadow of God sits in judgment over his servants."

A Persianate Sultanate does not have a parliament. In the parliament slot it has the Majlis-e Mazalim: the court of grievances, where the ruler hears complaints against his own officials, commanders, judges and merchants.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: The maẓālim (literally "injustices") was the sovereign's own jurisdiction, sitting above and beside the qāḍī's court to hear what ordinary procedure could not reach: the abuses of the powerful. It is an Islamic institution of long standing, described by al-Māwardī as one of the offices of government, and the Siyāsatnāma makes holding it in person a duty no king may neglect. It is not a consultative assembly. Nobody votes the ruler his taxes there; he earns his standing by being the one authority that can call every other to account, and the "Circle of Justice" that ties the army to the treasury, the treasury to the cultivator and the cultivator to justice closes in this room.

docs.title: The court as a parliament
docs.text:
The court uses the base game's parliament machinery, with its own rules.

Who holds it Countries with the Persianate Sultanate government. Both starting forms begin with it. Who is seated Clergy, Dīwān, Amirs, peasants and Tribes. The court's rules do not seat the burghers (see the note under their cases). Who is barred The base Nobility cannot participate. Weight of the elites Agendas of the Amirs and the clergy carry +25% impact; those of the Dīwān +10%.

The base game's Western parliament events never fire for the Majlis-e Mazalim.

docs.title: How a session runs
docs.text:
A session is a debate on one matter, a decree of the crown or a petition of an estate. As far as the files show, the matter is drawn from those currently available, by weight; the crown's decrees and the chancery's petitions carry weights of 25–40, the petitions of the other estates 10, so most sessions turn on the crown's or the Dīwān's business.

Three things then matter.

While the debate is open, the matter's listed modifier applies to the whole country (for example +0.5 monthly legitimacy during a Royal Progress). It ends when the debate ends, whatever the result.

The cases. In a base parliament each estate brings an agenda, a demand you may meet to win its support. Here each estate comes before the court with a case, an accusation of which it is itself the subject: embezzlement in the chancery, forced billeting by the amirs, bribery on the qāḍī's bench. Taking up a case settles that estate's agenda and counts its weight toward the debate, as in any parliament, but what you are doing is passing judgment:

  • the accused estate loses satisfaction (10–25%);
  • every other estate gains satisfaction equal to one fifth of its own share of estate power, sometimes with a little more for the injured party;
  • in many cases a share of the accused estate's treasury is confiscated to yours;
  • a lasting benefit (or a short disruption) follows, as listed in the tables below.

Cases can be bribed through in the usual way.

The outcome. If the matter passes, its listed effects apply. If it fails, you take the base game's standard penalty for a failed debate: −7 stability and −10 legitimacy.

Two further things happen only in session: the Muṣādara action, and the support a great act of justice can lend (see The Silent Realm below).

docs.title: Muṣādara in the court
docs.text: With the Muṣādara Right, a dīwān member in the cabinet and the court in session, you may pronounce Muṣādara: half the Dīwān's treasury (less its waqf shelter) for half a request's worth of debate support, 40% of the estate's satisfaction and a dīwān minister's life, once every five years. The full account, with the endowments it provokes, is on the Dīwān estate page.

docs.title: The Silent Realm
docs.text:
One story is told in this court above all others, and the mod tells it: Bahrām Gūr, the minister Rāst-Ravishn and the shepherd who hanged his dog, from the Siyāsatnāma.

It can begin when you hold the Majlis-e Mazalim, your head of cabinet is someone other than the ruler, the Dīwān holds more than 40% of estate power, and the realm is failing: manpower under a quarter, or income negative, or a treasury below three months of income. It can happen once in twenty years.

Step What happens The Silent Realm The vizier explains that the land is poor and the people fled. Fifteen days later: The Shepherd and the Dog The ruler rides out and learns why the shepherd hanged his trusted dog; he is designed to be marked Ruler on Progress (−10 administrative and −10 military ability) for half a year. Thirty days later: The Gates of Hell The prisons are opened. Either summon the court ("This ends today. Summon the people!") or give way ("The web is too thick... I cannot cut it."): −20 prestige, −10 legitimacy, −10 stability, +20% Dīwān satisfaction, and Shadow of Corruption for ten years (pop rebel threshold −0.1, −10% tax efficiency, −15% stability investment, −0.1 monthly legitimacy) The Seven Day Execution Seven days after the summons, you choose how deep to cut. The vizier dies in every case. Verdict Result "Absolute Justice: Purge them ALL." Dīwān −20% and Amirs −20% satisfaction; you pay 12 months of income; a quarter of maximum manpower and 20 army tradition lost; +15 stability, +20 legitimacy; a large block of debate support; one location gains The Shepherd's Reward permanently (+10% development growth, +0.003 monthly prosperity); Reign of the Just Shah for 20 years, fading (pop rebel threshold +0.1, +0.15 monthly legitimacy, +15% stability investment, +10% target satisfaction for Dīwān and Amirs) "Blame the Bureaucrats: Protect the Warriors." Dīwān −50% satisfaction; you gain 6 months of income; +5 stability, +10 legitimacy; some debate support; 10 toward Turk "Blame the Enforcers: Protect the Administrators." Amirs −50% satisfaction; a quarter of maximum manpower and 20 army tradition lost; you gain 6 months of income; +5 stability, +10 legitimacy; some debate support; 10 toward Tazik

docs.title: Using the court
docs.text:
• Call it when you want the debate modifier as much as the result. A Royal Progress or a Nowrūz is worth +0.5 legitimacy a month for as long as it is before the court.
  • Cases are how you move satisfaction between estates. One judgment against a single estate lifts all the others in proportion to their power, so prosecute the estate you can afford to anger and the strong ones are the most pleased.
  • The treasury cases are real money: a grave judgment against a rich chancery or camp brings 30–40% of its hoard. Against the Dīwān, check the waqf shelter first.
  • A failed debate costs 7 stability and 10 legitimacy. Do not open a matter you cannot carry.
  • Keep the waqf charters and Reclaim the Illegal Waqf in mind as a pair: granting any charter gives up the decree.

See also: Dīwān estate, Amirs estate, Estate privileges, Persianate Sultanate, Government reforms, The Farr Under Examination, The Commonwealth of Martyrs.

docs.title: The military system
docs.text:
The sultan pays, the amir serves, and the peasant is left to his plough.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The Amirs' private regiments and the Summon the Amirs' Tümens action use the 1.4 estate-army system and have not been tested in a full campaign. Unit damage values were rebalanced for 1.4.7 and may change again.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: The post-Ilkhanid state does not arm its taxpayers. The cultivator pays the land tax and the townsman pays the market dues, and in the political theory of the age that revenue is what keeps an army in the field to protect them: the Circle of Justice. The fighting is done by people whose calling it is. There are the amīrs, mounted and armoured, who hold iqṭāʿ assignments in place of a salary and answer the muster with their retinues. There are the tribes, Türkmen and Mongol on the plains and Kurd, Lur and Baluch in the mountains, who are summoned, never conscripted. Later there are the ghulāms, purchased and salaried, loyal to the household that owns them. The mod builds the levy around those three and takes the mass peasant army away.

docs.title: Who is raised from what
docs.text:
Every levy in the game draws a share of one kind of pop. In a country with the Persianate chancery the table reads like this:

Pops Unit raised Type Share of the pop Conditions Nobles of the Amirs estate Amir Cavalry, then Frontier Amir Cavalry, then Reformed Amir Cavalry Heavy cavalry 30% One unit per age (Traditions, Renaissance, Discovery) Turkic, Mongol and Tatar tribesmen Nomadic Skirmishers, then Turkoman Light Cavalry Light cavalry 10% Traditions, then Renaissance The same tribesmen Qizilbash Cavalry Heavy cavalry 10% Age of Discovery Iranian tribesmen (Kurds, Lurs, Baluch and others) Zagros Skirmishers, then Tofang Levies Light infantry 10% Tofang Levies from the Age of Discovery Iranian tribesmen Frontier Amir Cavalry (the "Retinue of the Mir") Heavy cavalry 2% All ages Soldiers in a location with a Tamma Garrison Ilkhanate Garrison Cavalry Heavy cavalry 75% Age of Traditions only Clergy in a location with a Mutaṭawwiʿa Lodge Ghazi Volunteers Light cavalry 20% Sword of The Sharia reform Burghers in a location with a Zūrkhāna Shahr Militia Heavy infantry 10% ʿAyyār Militia Recognition privilege Peasants; nobles and burghers of the Dīwān estate Base-game levies −90% levy size

For comparison, the base game raises 10% of noble pops as knights and 2% of peasants as foot. A Persianate state raises three times the cavalry from its military nobles, five times the base rate from its tribes, and almost nothing from its villages.

Points that follow from the table:

  • Which nobles count. A noble pop belongs to the Amirs estate if it is Muslim and does not qualify for the Dīwān. Literate Iranian and Arab nobles in cities, province capitals and bazaar towns belong to the Dīwān estate and are not levied (Iraqi Arabs are as much part of the scribal class as urban Iranians). Non-Muslim nobles fall to the ordinary nobles estate unless the Amirs hold The Open Muster Rolls.
  • Arab tribesmen have no levy in a Persianate state outside Yemen. Only Turkic, Mongol, Tatar and Iranian tribesmen ride for the chancery.
  • The base game's generic tribal levies are switched off for the Persianate Sultanate, the Commonwealth of Martyrs and the Iranic Tribal Polity, and base knights are switched off for any country with an Amirs estate.
  • The same Iranian tribal levies serve the Kurdish emirates and the Commonwealth of Martyrs.

docs.title: Light and heavy cavalry
docs.text: Since 1.4 the game treats light and heavy cavalry as separate arms with their own modifiers. In this mod the amirs are heavy cavalry and the tribes are light cavalry until the Age of Discovery, when the Qizilbash become heavy. The Right to Retinue privilege gives +20% combat power to both.

docs.title: What changes the size of the levy
docs.text:
Levy size is set per estate. These are the main levers.

Source Amirs levy Tribes levy Other Persianate Bureaucracy (the baseline reform) +30% +10% Peasants −90%, Dīwān −90% Iqtāʿ Grant privilege +50% Hereditary Tuyul privilege +15% +10% Right to Retinue privilege +30% Tribal Hosts (Yurt) privilege +20% +10% Tribal Autonomy Rights privilege +10% Quriltai Convocation privilege +15% +10% The Dehqan Revival privilege +15% Chinggisid Regency reform +15% Amīr Sultanate reform +20% Türkmen Confederation reform +20% +20% Law: Amir Recruitment +50% −10% tax efficiency, drift toward Türk Law: Tribal Host +15% Drift toward Türk Law: Ghulam Corps (needs the Ghulām Corps reform) −20% to all levies, +5% discipline Law: Curtail the Umara −20% −10% Law: Rights of the Umara +10% Law: Amir Autonomy +20% +10% −20% tax efficiency Each Iqṭāʿ Grant building +20% levy size in its location Each Tribal Pasture level +10% levy size in its location Post-Ilkhanid Chaos (see below) +10% levy size in the location

Both standard starting setups begin with the Iqtāʿ Grant privilege, so the opening army of a typical successor state is its amir cavalry at +80% or more, plus whatever tribesmen it rules. The buildings themselves are described on the buildings page.

docs.title: The units
docs.text: All of these are levies. They take their size and base combat power from the standard unit of their age and type; the table lists what the mod changes. "Losses taken" is strength damage and "morale taken" is morale damage; a negative number is good for the unit.

docs.title: Amirs and garrisons
docs.text:
Unit Age Losses taken Morale taken Initiative Terrain Amir Cavalry Traditions −15% −30% 2 Hills +10%, sparse +10%, grasslands +5%, wetlands −10%, mountains −25% Frontier Amir Cavalry Renaissance −7.5% −30% 2 Hills +10%, sparse +10%, grasslands +5%, mountains −5% Reformed Amir Cavalry Discovery +10% −30% 2 Hills +10%, sparse +10%, grasslands +5% Ilkhanate Garrison Cavalry Traditions +15% −30% 2 Hills +10%, sparse +10%, grasslands +5%, wetlands −10%

The base game's mailed knights take 25% fewer losses and 25% less morale damage. Amir Cavalry is a little less armoured, steadier, at home in dry hills and bad in mountains.

docs.title: The tribes
docs.text:
Unit Age Damage dealt Losses taken Morale Initiative Other Terrain Nomadic Skirmishers Traditions −2.5% +15% morale taken 3 −15% supply weight Sparse +25%, flatland +10%, hills −10%, mountains −20%, Qanat Farmlands −10% Turkoman Light Cavalry Renaissance +7.5% +10% 3 −15% supply weight Sparse +15%, flatland +10%, hills −10%, mountains −20% Qizilbash Cavalry Discovery +5% +25% morale dealt, −15% morale taken 2 Sparse +15%, flatland +10%, hills −10%, mountains −20% Zagros Skirmishers Traditions, Renaissance +10% +10% morale dealt, −15% morale taken 2 Hills +30%, mountains +30%, plateau +15% Tofang Levies Discovery onward +10% +10% morale dealt, −10% morale taken 2 Hills +30%, mountains +30%, plateau +15%

The steppe horse is fast and fragile and wins on open, dry ground. The mountain foot is the opposite: little use on the plain, very hard to shift in the Zagros.

docs.text:

Steppe hordes raise 10% of their tribesmen (the base game raises 2% of everyone) as the base game's horde cavalry; see Hordes.

docs.title: The Amirs' own regiments
docs.text: With the Right to Retinue privilege the Amirs estate may keep private regiments, paid for from the estate's own gold. They are the Amirs' until you call them. Summon the Amirs' Tümens puts the estate's unraised regiments under your command at the price of some legitimacy, 10% Amirs satisfaction and a heavy cost in political influence; if the Dīwān estate is more powerful than the Amirs the influence cost is light. The action has a three-year cooldown. See the Amirs estate.

docs.title: Ghulāms
docs.text:
There is no slave corps to buy in 1337. The ghulām system opens through the Matter of Tork, when a realm chooses to reduce its reliance on the tribes, or late through the Age of Discovery Ghulām Corps reform. It needs three things:

  1. An administrator: the Dīwān's Dīwān al-ʿArḍ privilege, the Amirs' Amir-Held Commands privilege (the two exclude each other), or the Ghulām Corps reform. Any of them permits Ghulam Barracks.
  2. A fostering layer: the peasants' Fostering Households privilege.
  3. Barracks: one level in the realm for the first purchase, three for the second, six for the third. The second and third also need a slave route.

Purchase Ghulam Levies then costs about six months of income, has a two-year cooldown and raises the corps one tier, creating a burst of demand for slaves in your market.

Corps tier Manpower Discipline Palace Ghulam Corps +5% +1% Ghulam Regiments +10% +2% The Army Within the Army +15% +3%

The barracks themselves add manpower and a place to recruit regulars. The corps is a standing army paid in coin, which is why it suits a rich Tāzīk-leaning treasury and why the Amirs resent it: the Dīwān al-ʿArḍ costs 10% of their satisfaction equilibrium and feeds their unrest.

docs.title: Forts and sieges
docs.text:
The Mongol conquest pulled down city walls across Iran and forbade their rebuilding, and the Ilkhanate's collapse left nobody to pay for garrisons. In play this is one modifier, Post-Ilkhanid Chaos, placed at the start on every location owned by a member of the Erānzamīn organisation:

Post-Ilkhanid Chaos Fort defence −66% Supply limit +50% Levy size +10% Prosperity and development Slowly falling

It lasts forty years and fades as it goes. While it is strong, sieges in the region are short and large armies can be fed, so wars are settled by field battles and the towns follow the winner. As it fades, and as realms pick up fort defence of their own (the Ilkhanate Governorate reform gives +20%, the Amirs' Frontier Governorship privilege +15% and a fifth more garrison), walls begin to matter again.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Count your Amir nobles and your tribesmen, not your population. A populous farming province with no amirs raises almost nothing.
  • Keep the Iqtāʿ Grant privilege unless you have something to replace the cavalry with. Revoking it removes its +50% to the amir levy and, unless Hereditary Tuyul is held, the right to register grants.
  • Fight tribal cavalry on sparse and flat ground and avoid taking it into hills or mountains. Take mountain foot the other way.
  • Amir Cavalry is only strong for its age. Each age replaces it with a new unit, and the Age of Discovery version is the weakest relative to its peers; plan for ghulāms or Qizilbash by then.
  • In the first decades, win the battle and march on the capital. Do not plan a campaign around long sieges until the chaos has faded.

See also: Buildings, goods and materials, Amirs estate, Estate privileges, Government reforms, Türk vs Tāzīk, The Matter of Tork, The Erānzamīn succession.

docs.title: Periphery sultanates
docs.text: Every amputation of Delhi is performed with Delhi's own instruments.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
The Persianate order did not stop at the borders of the Ilkhanate. In 1337 its two greatest working examples stand outside Iran altogether. In Cairo a military household of Turkic and Circassian mamlūks rules through an Arabic chancery (the dīwān al-inshāʾ, the army office, the cadastral survey of 1315 that redistributed every iqṭāʿ in Egypt) and holds its warrant from an Abbasid caliph who lives in the city. In Delhi the Tughluq sultans keep a Persian-speaking court and the most far-reaching revenue registers of the age, over a countryside that is overwhelmingly Hindu and governed in practice through its own rājas and taʿalluqdārs. Both are states of the same family as the Iranian sultanates: a cavalry elite paid by revocable assignment, a scribal class that keeps the books, a khuṭba and a coinage. Neither has Iran's problem in 1337. Their legitimacy question is already answered, by the caliph in one case and by a century and a half of the Delhi dispensation in the other.

The mod therefore brings Egypt, Delhi and the Indian sultanates onto the Persianate Sultanate government, each with its own starting reform in place of the Iranian Persianate Bureaucracy. The Anatolian marches are the third periphery and have their own page: Shattered Rum.

docs.title: What they share
docs.text:
Each periphery reform counts as a working chancery. That is what creates the two Persianate estates: Muslim nobles become Amirs, and literate urban notables of Iranian, Arab or Indian Muslim culture become the Dīwān. Each reform also:

  • exempts its holder from Unsettled Legitimacy, the penalty Iranian realms carry until they answer the khuṭba question;
  • closes off the Ghāzī Sultanate, the Amīr Sultanate and the Seljuk claim. These realms have their own answer already;
  • reserves the cabinet for the Dīwān and military command for the Amirs, as in Iran;
  • cannot be combined with Persianate Bureaucracy.

Egypt and Delhi both sit with a Majlis-e Mazalim as their assembly from the first day, and both start with chancery offices already built.

Country Starting reform Rank Starting chancery buildings Egypt (MAM) Mamluk Government Kingdom Dīwān of the Realms at Cairo; Regional Dīwān at Damascus; Local Dīwāns at Aleppo and Alexandria; nine Iqṭāʿ Grants Delhi (DLH) The Delhi Dispensation, with Taluqdar Nobility Kingdom Dīwān of the Realms at Delhi; Regional Dīwāns at Daulatabad and Multan; eight Iqṭāʿ Grants Ma'bar (MAB), Rajouri (RJR), Samma (SMA), Sindh (SND), Honnavara (HNV) The Delhi Dispensation as in the base game none added

docs.title: Egypt: Mamluk Government
docs.text:
The base game's Mamluk reform, kept with its own mechanics (promoting mamlūks, Mamluk barracks, the Mamluk rank, army and promotion laws, Mamluk succession) and rebuilt as a chancery state. The principle of the military change is that the fallāḥīn fund the army; they do not fight in it.

Effect Value Can promote Mamluks / build Mamluk barracks yes Monthly army tradition +0.1 Land morale +10% Peasants levy size −100% Burghers levy size −50% Amirs levy size +75% Nobles levy size +50% Dīwān levy size −90% Tribes levy size +10% Tax efficiency +5% Maximum estate tax +10% Cabinet efficiency +5% Court spending efficiency −10% Dīwān estate power / satisfaction +15% / +5% Maximum control +15% urban, +10% rural Peasant enfranchisement full Government size / cultures capacity +1 / +2

The rural control bonus is the Nile: the most governable countryside in the mod. Egypt has no peasant host at all, so its army is the Amirs' cavalry, the mamlūk regiments and whatever it pays for.
