Egypt also starts as overlord of the Dulkadirids on the edge of Shattered Rum, and the Abbasid caliph in Cairo is the authority a victorious Anatolian ghāzī must petition for the title of Sultan of Rum.

docs.title: Delhi: The Delhi Dispensation
docs.text:
The base game already gives the Indian sultanates a shared reform; the mod calls it The Delhi Dispensation and replaces its content with the Tughluq chassis.

Effect Value Can build Mamluk barracks (the bandagān) yes Tax efficiency +10% Maximum estate tax +15% Cabinet efficiency +10% Monthly drift towards centralization +0.15 Dīwān estate power / satisfaction +25% / +5% Nobles estate power −60% Amirs levy size +40% Peasants levy size −50% Dīwān levy size −90% Tribes levy size +10% Maximum urban control +15% Government size / cultures capacity +1 / +2

Three things set it apart from the Iranian model:

  • Harder extraction. Higher tax efficiency and a higher tax ceiling than any Iranian reform gives at the start.
  • A garrison-city state. The control bonus is urban only. Delhi's writ runs through fortified towns; the countryside is thinner.
  • A real Nobles estate. The Amirs are a closed Muslim service order, so Hindu lords stay in the Nobles estate as hereditary right-holders. Their power is cut less deeply than in Iran (−60% against −90%), and the peasant levy is halved, not abolished, because the Indian foot soldier is a real tradition.

The Open Muster Rolls privilege of the Amirs is the historical way to open that closed order: while it stands, non-Muslim noble pops qualify as Amirs. See Estate privileges.

The reform belongs to Muslim countries with a capital in South Asia that do not hold Persianate Bureaucracy. It is locked: it is held from the start or granted by the events below, and cannot be dropped by choice.

docs.title: The five lesser sultanates
docs.text: Ma'bar, Rajouri, Samma, Sindh and Honnavara hold this reform in the base game but on mismatched governments. At game start the mod moves all five onto the Persianate Sultanate government with favourite-son succession and a Persian court language.

docs.title: The Governor's Khutba
docs.text:
The base game's Fall of Delhi releases breakaway states, and without correction many of them appear as Hindu polities on a default government. Two days after it forms, any of those breakaways (the Bahmanis, Malwa, Gujarat, Jaunpur and the unnamed provincial sultanates) is put on the Delhi chassis:

  • Persianate Sultanate government, The Delhi Dispensation, favourite-son succession, Persian court language;
  • primary culture becomes Dehlavi, with the local majority kept as an accepted culture;
  • Sunni state religion if it was not already Muslim;
  • a transplanted service class: Dehlavi Sunni noble pops of 1,000 in the capital, 500 in every other city and 250 in every town.

Countries that rise in India without being one of those scripted breakaways are left alone. A Hindu rebellion stays Hindu.

docs.title: The Faith of the Realm
docs.text:
If a country holding The Delhi Dispensation ever leaves Islam, it must choose at once:

Option Effect "The dispensation is ended. Let the realm be what its people are." Loses The Delhi Dispensation (and with it the chancery, the Dīwān and the Amirs); −100 stability, −100 legitimacy "The amīrs remember Khusraw Khan. Kill the apostate; find a believer." The ruler and all his children are executed; a Dehlavi Sunni amīr takes the throne; the old religion is restored

Changes within Islam do not trigger it.

docs.title: The Rasulid Chancery
docs.text: Yemen (YEM) starts with a third reform of the same family, Rasulid Chancery: the Egyptian block with a kept peasant levy (−50%, not −100%), a much stronger Tribes estate (+75% power, +25% levy size), a higher urban control ceiling (+20%) and a rural penalty (−5%).

docs.title: Advice
docs.text:
• Egypt is rich, well administered and thinly armed. With no peasant levy, protect the Amirs' satisfaction and keep the treasury able to hire.
  • Delhi starts with the best fisc in the mod and the largest unreconciled countryside. Regional Dīwāns at Daulatabad and Multan are your reach; build more before the distant provinces test you.
  • In India, the reform travels with the state. Every scripted breakaway from Delhi receives The Delhi Dispensation, so Persianate India does not depend on Delhi surviving.

See also: Persianate Sultanate, Government reforms, The Dīwān estate, The Amirs estate, Estate privileges, Buildings, Shattered Rum.

docs.title: The Persianate Sultanate
docs.text:
The sultan rules through a dual settlement: the pen keeps the registers, the sword keeps the field.

The Persianate Sultanate is the government type of almost every state the mod touches: the successor amirates of the Ilkhanate, the Persian dynasties of Fārs, Herat and the Caspian shore, and — in their own regional dress — the Mamluks, Delhi and Rasulid Yemen. It is not a monarchy with different art. It has its own estates, its own cabinet rules, its own levy system, its own societal value and its own reform tree.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: By 1337 the lands from Anatolia to Bengal shared a recognisable way of running a state. A Turco-Mongol or Turkic military class held commands and revenue assignments (iqṭāʿ); a Persian-writing secretarial class — Iranian, and in Iraq equally Arab — staffed the dīwān, kept the tax registers and wrote the diplomas; jurists and Sufi shaykhs supplied the courts and the pulpits; and the ruler's right to rule was argued, not inherited. The theory of this state was written by Muslim statesmen and scholars — Niẓām al-Mulk, Ghazālī, Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī — for whom the just king, the farr that marks him and the circle of justice were ordinary Islamic political thought. The mod calls the working machinery of that state the chancery, and nearly everything on this page hangs from it.

docs.title: Who has it
docs.text:
At the 1337 start:

Group Countries Opening reform Türk-dominant successor amirates Jalayirids (JAL), Chobanids (CHB), Eretna (ERE) and the other Turco-Mongol amirates — about twenty in all Persianate Bureaucracy; JAL and CHB also start as a Chinggisid Regency Tāzīk-dominant dynasties Muzaffarids (MZF), Injuids (INJ), Karts (KRT), Shirvan (SRV), Hormuz (ORM), the Caspian houses and others Persianate Bureaucracy The periphery Mamluks (MAM), Delhi (DLH) and the Muslim Indian minors, Rasulid Yemen (YEM) Mamluk Government, The Delhi Dispensation, Rasulid Chancery Sufi orders The landless tariqa orders Tariqa Order (a special case — no chancery)

The full roster is on the countries and tags page. Not everyone on the plateau is a sultanate: the Sarbadārs are a Commonwealth of Martyrs, the Kurdish principalities are Kurdish emirates, and the Chaghatayids and their neighbours are hordes.

Later in the game a country becomes a Persianate Sultanate when:

  • a new country appears with a tribal government but a sedentary Iranian-world culture (Persian, Khurasani, Azari, Tajik, the Caspian peoples, Iraqi Arab, Armenian, Georgian and their neighbours) — it is converted on the spot and given Persianate Bureaucracy;
  • a Kurdish emirate takes one of the great seats — Tabriz, Isfahan, Shiraz, Nishapur, Baghdad or Herat — and accepts the offer to take over its chancery;
  • a Sufi order rises in arms, a Commonwealth of Martyrs gives way to a sultan, or a Zaydi imam makes his house hereditary (see those pages);
  • an Anatolian march is founded during the Rise of the Ottomans, or a breakaway sultanate splits from Delhi;
  • The Ṣāḥib-qirān's realm settles down as the Timurid Empire.

Any new country whose capital lies in the Erānzamīn region also joins the Erānzamīn organisation automatically.

docs.title: The chancery
docs.text:
Five reforms carry the chancery — Persianate Bureaucracy, Mamluk Government, The Delhi Dispensation, Rasulid Chancery and Timurid Empire — and a realm holds exactly one. The details differ (see government reforms); the Iranian form is the reference:

Area Persianate Bureaucracy Administration +10% cabinet efficiency, +10% tax efficiency, +10% maximum estate tax, +0.10 monthly toward centralization Control +15% maximum urban control, +5% maximum rural control Dīwān +25% power, +5% satisfaction; seated in the cabinet; almost never rebel Other estates Amirs, nobles, burghers and clergy kept out of the cabinet; nobles −90% power Command Only the Amirs lead armies Levies Peasants −90%, Dīwān −90%, Amirs +30%, tribes +10% Other +2 cultural capacity; tributary subjects allowed

Persianate states are built around their cities: urban control is high and resilient, rural control is thin. And the settled population does not fight. Your soldiers come from the Amirs' households, the tribes and whatever you pay for — see the military system.

docs.title: Two service estates
docs.text:
The base game's nobility is replaced by the Dīwān and the Amirs. Under 1.4 an estate's weight comes from its pops, and the mod adds two scaling terms on top:

Modifier Effect Base values Dīwān +70% power, Amirs +30% power; both start from a 40% satisfaction equilibrium Sedentary Power Base Dīwān power rises with the share of peasants, burghers and labourers in your population (+250% at a fully sedentary realm) Tribal Power Base Amirs power rises steeply with the share of tribesmen (+250% for every tenth of the population that is tribal) Persian court language Dīwān +5% satisfaction At war Amirs +2.5% satisfaction

A realm with many tribesmen has strong Amirs whatever its laws say. The Türk vs Tāzīk slider then tilts the balance by up to ±50% either way.

docs.title: The two prohibitions
docs.text:
Two lines are drawn by the chancery itself, and both are still in force:

Prohibition How to lift it What lifting it costs The Dīwān may not lead armies. The Dīwān privilege Tāzīk Command of Arms Dīwān +10% satisfaction, +75% power; +10% cabinet efficiency; +0.05 centralization, +0.10 Tāzīk a month. Amirs −10% satisfaction, −15% power. The Amirs may not sit in the cabinet. The Amirs privilege Umarāʾ at the Dīwān, or the Amīr Sultanate reform Privilege: Amirs +10% satisfaction, +75% power; −10% cabinet efficiency; −10% political influence gain; +0.05 decentralization, +0.10 Türk a month. Dīwān −10% satisfaction, −15% power.

The objection on each side is professional, and each side has its texts: the Siyāsatnāma complains at length about military men ruining the registers, and the amirs' retort that a tāzīk has no business at the head of a host was proverbial. While the Matter of Tork is running and unanswered, neither privilege can be granted unless the Amirs, the Dīwān and the tribes are all at 50% satisfaction or better.

docs.title: The vizierate
docs.text:
The Dīwān expect one of their own to head the cabinet. Exactly one of the first three applies; the fourth stacks.

Situation Modifier Effect No Dīwān member in the cabinet The Chancery Locked Out Dīwān −20% satisfaction, −25% cabinet efficiency, −15% tax efficiency Dīwān present, an outsider heads the cabinet No Vizier of the Pen Dīwān −5% satisfaction, −10% cabinet efficiency, −5% tax efficiency A Dīwān member heads the cabinet A Vizier of the Pen Dīwān +5% satisfaction, +5% cabinet efficiency, +5% tax efficiency, +15% crown power Two or more non-Dīwān members in the cabinet Crowded Vizierate Dīwān −5% satisfaction, −5% cabinet efficiency

In practice: fill the cabinet with Dīwān characters, make one of them head, and keep at most one seat for a relative or favourite. The base-game habit of packing the cabinet with royal kin is punished here.

docs.title: Legitimacy is an answer, not an inheritance
docs.text: The Sultanate runs on legitimacy, and a Persianate Sultanate that has not said in whose name it rules suffers Unsettled Legitimacy: −0.6 legitimacy a month, Amirs and Dīwān −20% satisfaction, clergy and burghers −15%. The answers — Chinggisid Regency, Ilkhanate Governorate, Farr-i Īzadī, Ghāzī Sultanate and what they grow into — are the first tier of the reform tree, and the choice is put to you in the opening event of the Erānzamīn situation. The periphery chanceries, the Timurid Empire, the Rûm reforms and a ruler of Chinggis Khan's own house are exempt.

docs.title: Succession, court and justice
docs.text:
• Succession defaults to Favored Son Succession: the son the late ruler preferred and the amirs will accept. The other base-game Muslim and steppe succession laws remain selectable.
  • The parliament is the Majlis-e Mazalim — the ruler sitting in judgment on his own officials rather than bargaining with estates. See the Mazālim court.
  • Courtiers belong to the Dīwān by default, so the pool you draw ministers from is the pool the vizierate wants.

docs.title: Laws the mod adds
docs.text:
The two Persian law groups unlock with the same Age of Renaissance advances as the base bureaucracy and nobles' rights laws, but every starting sultanate already has a policy in each.

Law Policy Effects Enact Persian Bureaucracy Diwan Administration +5% cabinet efficiency, +3% max control; Dīwān +5% satisfaction, +20% power; Amirs −5% satisfaction; −10% army maintenance efficiency; +0.05 Tāzīk 2 years Iqta Assignments +5% tax efficiency; −10% max rural, −3.3% max urban control; Amirs +50% power, +5% satisfaction; +7.5% heavy and light cavalry power; +0.05 decentralization 2 years Rights of the Persian Nobility Curtail the Umara Amirs −5% satisfaction, −10% power, −20% levy; tribes −10% levy; +5% max control; a large tax-efficiency bonus (listed as +50%); +0.05 Tāzīk 5 years Rights of the Umara Amirs +10% satisfaction, +10% power, +10% levy; +0.05 Türk 5 years Amir Autonomy Amirs +30% power, +5% satisfaction, +20% levy; tribes +10% levy; −20% tax efficiency, −5% max control; +0.10 decentralization, +0.10 Türk 5 years Recruitment (added options) Amir Recruitment Amirs +50% levy; −10% tax efficiency; +0.10 Türk 2 years Tribal Host Tribes +15% levy; +0.10 Türk 2 years Ghulam Corps Needs the Ghulām Corps reform. +5% discipline; −20% army maintenance efficiency, −20% levy size; Amirs −25% power, −10% satisfaction; +0.10 toward quality 5 years

All Muslim countries, sultanate or not, also gain the religious law Hisba — Enforcement of Public Morals:

Policy Open to Effects in brief Lax Enforcement — The Open Bazaar All Burghers pleased, clergy displeased; +2.5% tax efficiency, +5% cabinet efficiency, a little prosperity; −10% levy size, −10% land morale Customary Enforcement — The Qāḍī's Discretion All All estates +2.5% satisfaction; beer and liquor imports banned Strict Enforcement — The Stick in the Bazaar All Clergy pleased, burghers −5%; +10% levy size, +25% land morale; −2.5% tax efficiency; wine, beer and liquor imports banned The Muhtasib-King Ghāzī Sultanate or Sword of The Sharia (closed to a realm that took the murid bond in the Matter of Tork) Clergy +10%, burghers −10%; +25% levy size, +25% land morale, +25% conversion speed; −5% tax efficiency, a little less prosperity Ẓill Allāh — The Shadow of God A Shia realm deep on the mystical side, or one that took the murid bond +0.1 legitimacy a month; +25% land morale, +10% levy size; burghers +5%, clergy −5%; +1 tolerance of heretics; +2.5% tax efficiency

docs.title: Finishing a conquest
docs.text:
Conquered land in Erānzamīn is not simply left to integrate. Contenders in the Erānzamīn situation choose how each province is absorbed — Consolidate the Diwan, Grant the Yurt or Mixed Settlement — and each choice pleases one estate and moves the Türk–Tāzīk slider. The requirements and effects are tabulated on the Türk vs Tāzīk page.

The winner of the situation receives one permanent cabinet action, decided by the sign of the slider at the moment of victory:

Cabinet action Awarded to Needs Effect Integrate into the Dīwān A Tāzīk victor (slider 0 or above) A province in Iran, Khurāsān, the Caucasus, Iraq or the Jazīra with a Local Dīwān and land still only conquered Integration in that province runs at +600% until it is done Invite Turkic Settlers A Türk victor (slider below 0) A province in the same lands with land still only conquered A wave of tribesmen migrates in over ten years from the most populous Turkic province outside your borders; integration runs at +300%

Both hold a cabinet seat while they run and end by themselves when the province is integrated.

docs.title: Formable realms
docs.text: Realm Who Requirements Persia A country of the Iranian culture group Own Tabriz, Isfahan and Shiraz and three quarters of the Persia region. Not a Chinggisid Regency. The question of right settled: the Farr vindicated or endured, the Ghāzī wager won or held, or the murid bond sworn. The place of the sword settled: the Matter of Tork resolved without the hosts founding a rival — or never raised, in a realm with fewer than 750,000 tribesmen. Becomes an empire. Iran o Toran A Chinggisid Regency, Gurkani Regime, Amīr Sultanate, Timurid Synthesis or Timurid Empire Win the Erānzamīn situation as a Türk realm. Hold three quarters of the Persia and Caucasus regions together with Cappadocia, Arab Iraq, the Jazīra and western Khurāsān. Takes up the Ilkhanate's own tag (ILK) and becomes an empire. Rûm A Muslim country of the Turkic culture group Hold 85% of Anatolia, come out of the Rise of the Ottomans as the winner without being the Ottomans, and hold a completed claim: the vindicated Seljuk inheritance or the Caliph's investiture. See Shattered Rûm.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
• Answer the legitimacy question in the first month. Unsettled Legitimacy is the single worst modifier a new sultanate can carry, and every answer except a self-made Amīr Sultanate removes it at once.
  • Staff the cabinet from the Dīwān. The swing between The Chancery Locked Out and A Vizier of the Pen is 30% cabinet efficiency and 20% tax efficiency.
  • Do not expect peasant levies. Budget for the Amirs' and tribes' goodwill, or for paid soldiers.
  • Lift a prohibition only when you mean to change sides. Each of the two privileges hands one estate +75% power and pushes the slider 0.10 a month — they are commitments, not conveniences.

See also: Government reforms, Türk vs Tāzīk, Dīwān estate, Amirs estate, Estate privileges, Mazālim court, Military system, Erānzamīn situation, Starting the game.

docs.title: The Ṣāḥib-qirān
docs.text:
The khan reigns. I conquer. Let no one confuse the two.

New — largely untested in play

The ending, the released state and the fortune have been run with debug tools and corrected after several short tests. No campaign has yet reached this point by play. See Known issues.

At Balkh in April 1370 Temür of the Barlas took the citadel, had his rival Ḥusayn killed, married Ḥusayn's Chinggisid wife Saray Mulk, set Soyurghatmish on the felt and received the oath of the amirs of the ulus one by one. He never took the title of khan. He ruled for thirty-five years as amīr and güregen, son-in-law of the line, and his panegyrists called him Ṣāḥib-qirān, Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction, as they had called great conquerors before him.

What held the amirs to him was not descent and not an office. It was his dawlat: the fortune a man is seen to have while he keeps winning and keeps giving. He campaigned almost every year and emptied his treasury on his followers after each campaign. The fortune was his and not his house's, and at his death in 1405 his sons and grandsons fought for four years over a realm none of them had made.

The base game schedules Timur: between 1360 and 1400 an event places the historical man at the head of the Timurid tag around Samarkand. The mod switches that off. The conqueror is whoever ends the Amirs' Regency as Ṣāḥib-qirān. It may be Temür Barlas. It may be a Qara'unas, a Jalayir, or a darugha with no house at all. If the regency never happens, or ends with the khan triumphant or in the Bulqaq, there is no Timur.

docs.title: What changed from the base game
docs.text:
• The base spawn event cannot fire, nor can the two base events that favoured the historical man beforehand (his childhood chain and the "Lame" nickname).
  • Temür Barlas still exists as a character at the start, in the Barlas dynasty and without the base game's extended life expectancy. He can die young like any other amir's son.
  • The base formable Timurids (any Uzbek-culture country holding 80% of the Persia region) is closed. The Timurid tag is not a nation to be formed.
  • The Rise of Timur situation is the mod's own copy with different outcomes, and is shown under the conqueror's name.
  • The automatic conquest the base game gives the man for life belongs to his fortune here, and is lost when it falls.

docs.title: Becoming Ṣāḥib-qirān
docs.text:
In the regency's fourth stage, all of the following at once:

  • the regent holds a living khan;
  • his ruler has a wife of the line of Chinggis (Marry into the Line, or any Borjigin wife);
  • the legitimacy gap has stood at 60 or more for five years running.

The event Ṣāḥib-qirān then reaches him.

docs.title: The founding
docs.text:
The amirs are sorted first, by what each thinks of the man:

The house Becomes Independent, opinion of him 0 or better, bordering him, with its capital in the same area as his Annexed outright, with its men, treasury and people. Temür's own Barlas and the houses around Kesh and Samarkand were his household, not his following Independent, opinion of him 0 or better, anywhere else A Sworn Amir Everyone else Free. He holds The Ṣāḥib-qirān's Reckoning on each for twenty years: taking the amir's seat makes him submit, subjugation is cheap and land is dear

Ulus Chaghatay is dissolved. The khan stays in his tent: a Ṣāḥib-qirān still rules behind one.

A new state rides out. If the Timurid tag does not already exist, it is released from all his land with him as ruler, seated at his capital, and his old realm is folded into it. A player is moved to the new state.

The new state Name Timurids only if the man is Temür Barlas. Otherwise it is named for his house: the Qara'unas, Barlas, Jalayir, Suldus, Arlat, Apardi, Yasa'uri, Khuttalani, Negüderi, Besüd or Dughlat Gurkanate. A man from one of the land-named domains, or with no house, founds The Ṣāḥib-qirān's Realm Government Steppe Horde with Legacy of Genghis and the reform Güregen of the Ulus: +0.15 monthly horde unity, +5% land morale, −0.05 monthly prestige, −10% political influence gain, −2% maximum control Culture and religion His old realm's Rank Raised to kingdom if lower At once 1,000 gold, twelve regiments of horse archers and a Kurultai at his seat, all his land made core, +50 horde unity, +25 prestige, 50 political influence (the new state starts with no accepted or tolerated cultures) Lord of the Conjunction, ten years +10% land morale, +0.10 monthly horde unity, +0.10 monthly prestige

The situation Rise of [his name] begins for him. His realm is never a member of the Erānzamīn organisation or a contender in its succession, and the horde succession poll is not run for it.

docs.title: Fortune
docs.text:
The regency's legitimacy gap is not thrown away. It becomes the Fortune of the Ṣāḥib-qirān, 0 to 100, shown on the situation's panel. Because the ending requires the gap at 60, he starts in the high band.

It drains each month At peace 0.6 At war 0.3 After more than three years at peace 1.2 It is filled by A great battle won +4 A siege won +2 A war won +10 Divide the Plunder +10 A declared conquest ambition made good +15 A war lost −15

docs.title: The bands
docs.text:
Fortune Modifier Effect 60 or more Fortune of the Ṣāḥib-qirān +20 subject loyalty, +0.10 monthly horde unity, +5% land morale, −30% antagonism received, +100% loot, less rebel support and −10% separatism in what he takes. What his armies occupy in a war becomes his at once, as conquered land 30 to 59 — The amirs wait to see what the next campaign brings Under 30 A Failing Fortune −15 subject loyalty, −0.15 monthly horde unity. His sworn amirs no longer ride unasked Empty for two years running The Amirs Ride Away Every sworn amir breaks free. −25 prestige, −25 horde unity. His fortune is reset to 15

Whatever the band, he carries His Name Goes Before Him: −60% antagonism received, −20% political influence gain. Temür took Delhi, Damascus and Baghdad and no league ever formed against him; each court dealt with him singly.

docs.title: Succession
docs.text: The fortune is the man's. At every later accession (The Sons and the Amirs) the new ruler starts at 25, in the low band, whatever was left. Once the Conjunction has held (below) heirs start at 50 instead.

docs.title: Sworn amirs
docs.text:
A Sworn Amir is a follower, not a governor.

Diplomatic capacity None Loyalty He has none of his own. What holds him is the overlord's fortune: +20 in the high band, −15 in the low Pays Manpower, not gold War Rides unasked in every war, offensive and defensive, while the fortune is not low. In the low band he must be called and may refuse Levies +10% levy size for him; +5% levy size and +0.05 monthly horde unity for the overlord Annexation Not before 30 years, and only at very high opinion Leaving He cannot cancel the tie himself and can turn on his overlord only when his loyalty has failed. The overlord can release him (Release a Sworn Amir)

The status exists only by the founding. It cannot be offered or asked for through diplomacy.

docs.title: The situation's actions
docs.text:
Action What the mod changes Declare Conquest Ambition He names a region. His subjects' borders count as his own, so a region his sworn amirs touch can be named. Nothing obliges him to name Persia first: the AI chooses by the region's wealth against its rulers' strength, counting a realm exhausted by war at half its muster Plan Invasion The neighbours of his subjects are offered as targets as well as his own. When it declares the war, his sworn amirs are put into it as attackers, unless his fortune is low Divide the Plunder New. A year's income, once a year: fortune +10, nobles +5% satisfaction, and The Plunder Divided (+10 subject loyalty) for three years The reform action that settles the horde It becomes a Persianate Sultanate with the Timurid Empire reform, Persian as court language, empire rank and designation-then-contest succession (see Government reforms)

The base event Our Legacy, which asks the conqueror where his authority comes from, is not fired: he already rules as güregen behind a khan.

Divide the Plunder needs the situation to be running. A Ṣāḥib-qirān whose realm was not released as the Timurid tag (because that tag already existed) has the fortune but not the button.

docs.title: How the situation ends
docs.text:
Outcome Condition Result The Conjunction Holds Two declared conquest ambitions made good — he and his subjects hold six in ten locations of each region — while he still owns the seat his rule began from and his fortune is not low +50 prestige. The fortune continues, and from now on each heir starts at 50 The Amirs Ride Away The fortune has lain empty for two years and the sworn amirs have gone The campaign bonus lapses and outstanding claims of conquest expire The Sons Divide The founder is dead and an heir's fortune has stayed under 30 for five years running; or the realm has neither ruler nor heir The same The realm is subjugated As in the base game —

The ambitions may be any regions: Iran, Hindustan, the Qipchaq steppe, China.

docs.title: The army is lost
docs.text: Once in a game. If the Ṣāḥib-qirān loses a war to an outsider while his fortune is already under 30, the sworn amirs ride away at once (−25 prestige, −25 horde unity), and he and they are treated as the orphans of a broken ulus: every outside neighbour holds Break the Tümens on each for 25 years, the victor holds it whether he borders them or not, and the Breaking of the Chaghatay opens as after a Bulqaq.

docs.title: Playing it
docs.text:
As the Ṣāḥib-qirān. You are not running an empire yet; you are keeping a following. Stay at war: fortune drains at half speed in a war and at double speed after three years of peace. Keep it at 60 and occupied land becomes yours without a peace treaty, your amirs ride without being asked, and other courts barely register your conquests. Let it fall under 30 and the amirs must be asked, and a lost war can end everything. Divide the plunder every year you can afford it. Name a conquest ambition your amirs' borders reach, take six tenths of the region, then name another: two made good, with your first seat still yours, makes the house last. Your heir starts at 25 unless you have done that.

Against him. While his fortune is high you cannot buy time by letting him occupy land. He is weakest at peace and under an heir. Beat him in a war when his fortune is low and his following dissolves.

The AI does not march west by rule. It names the richest region whose rulers it can beat, sends embassies and gifts to neighbours clearly stronger than itself, and falls on a great realm that has just been bled.

See also: The Amirs' Regency, Ulus Chaghatay, Ulus and regency numbers, Persianate sultanate, Government reforms, Hordes, Known issues.

docs.title: Shattered Rum
docs.text: In Konya the khuṭba is read over an empty throne.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
The Seljuk sultanate of Rūm did not fall in a day. After the Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 its sultans ruled as clients, confirmed by the Ilkhan's diploma and supervised by his governors; the last of the line died in 1308, and from then on Anatolia was an Ilkhanid province in which Türkmen begs held their marches (uc) by patent from Tabriz. When Abū Saʿīd died in 1335 the patents stopped meaning anything. What remained was a land of some two dozen beyliks, each as sovereign as its sword, and one open question that strength alone had never answered here: by what warrant does a beg become a sultan? Two answers were available in the fourteenth century. The frontier houses pressed the ghazā against the Roman coast and sought confirmation from the Abbasid caliph in Cairo, as Bāyezīd I did in 1394. The houses of the interior looked to Konya, the old dār al-mulk, where the Karamanids had already tried once in 1277 to raise the Seljuk inheritance and been thrown out within the year.

Shattered Rum is the mod's rebuild of the base game's Rise of the Ottomans situation around that question. The base race between beyliks is kept; what changes is that winning the race is no longer enough.

docs.title: What the mod changes at a glance
docs.text:
• The situation is renamed Shattered Rum and its opening events are rewritten. The Ottomans are no longer the presumed winner: whichever beylik is strongest is simply "the strongest of the marches".
  • Every beylik is switched to the Persianate Sultanate government when the situation starts, and is offered a three-way constitutional choice.
  • The situation's victory ending now requires a legitimacy answer: a vindicated ghazā doctrine or a vindicated Seljuk claim. A beylik that conquers Anatolia with neither gets the failure ending.
  • A new reform, Claimant of the Seljuk Inheritance, opens a new disaster, The Seljuk Inheritance, with a four-step state-building programme and its own crown, the Sultanate of Rum.
  • Rum as a formable country now needs one of two "doors" in addition to the base requirements.
  • All beyliks start at Duchy rank (the base game gives that rank to the Ottomans alone), and beylik squabbles draw far less outside hostility.

docs.title: Who takes part
docs.text:
The participants are the countries holding the Anatolian Beylik reform. In 1337 these are the Türkmen marches of the base game:

Ottomans (TUR), Karamanids (KAR), Germiyanids (GRM), Aydınids (AYD), Saruhanids (SRU), Karasids (KRD), Menteşeids (MEN), Candarids (CND), Hamidids (HMD), Teke (TEK), Alaiye (ALY), Dulkadirids (DUL), Sahib Ataids (SHP), İnançids (INA), Tavas (TVS), Ahis (AHI), Kubadids (KBD), Tacettinids (TDJ), Haciemirids (HCI), Bafra (BFR), Artuqids (ATQ) and Dilmaçids (DIL).

Not all of them start free. Germiyan holds the Karasids, Saruhanids and Aydınids as vassals (and Aydın holds the İnançids, Menteşe holds Tavas); the Dulkadirids answer to Egypt, the Dilmaçids to the Sutayids, and four northern marches pay tribute to the Eretnids. Only independent beyliks are ranked in the race.

A beylik founded or freed later (a released uç bey, a new Turkish or Türkmen march) takes the Anatolian Beylik reform, joins the roll, and receives the Persianate Sultanate government and Duchy rank on the spot.

The Eretnids (ERE) are the exception. The mod starts them as a full Persianate Sultanate with a working chancery (the Ilkhanid provincial administration of Rūm, still running at Sivas), as a vassal of the Jalayirids and a member of Erānzamīn. They hold Sivas and four tributary marches (Kubadids, Tacettinids, Haciemirids, Bafra). The Seljuk claim is open to them through the reform screen, and its third step is cheaper for a realm that already keeps a chancery.

docs.title: The Anatolian Beylik reform
docs.text:
Effect Value Unjustified war on same religion penalty −25% Non-culture levy size +25% Antagonism received −30% Government size / reform slots +1 / +1 Tributary subjects allowed

The reform cannot be removed before 1340 or while Shattered Rum is active. While a march holds it, the Erānzamīn-style Unsettled Legitimacy penalty does not apply: a beg has no khuṭba problem until he claims more than a march.

docs.title: How it starts
docs.text:
The situation can begin from April 1337 and before 1350. On the day it starts:

  1. Every beylik becomes a Persianate Sultanate with favourite-son succession. Without a chancery this is mostly dress: the Dīwān and Amirs estates only fill once the realm has the Persianate Bureaucracy reform (see the Dīwān estate). A march cannot simply adopt that reform; it has to be built or bought through one of the two roads below.
  2. The strongest independent beylik (by military strength plus tax base) is named, and receives the base game's Legacy of Osman reform whoever it is. (In the base game a non-Ottoman leader silently failed to get it.)
  3. Five days later every beylik receives The Marches Without a Master, the choice of road.

docs.title: The Marches Without a Master
docs.text:
Option Effect Leads to "The frontier is our patent. Press the ghaza." Adopt the Ghāzī Sultanate reform; +10% Clergy satisfaction; +5 legitimacy The Ghāzī Burden of the Sword "The inheritance of the House of Seljuk waits at Konya. We claim it." (capital must be in Anatolia) Adopt Claimant of the Seljuk Inheritance The Seljuk Inheritance disaster "Our fathers were begs. Their tents are enough." +5 stability Nothing, at a price (below)

The AI leans towards the ghazā when it borders a non-Muslim country, towards the Seljuk claim when it owns Konya, and towards the tents when it is small.

Deferring is a real choice but not a free one. A beylik with none of the four answers (Ghāzī Sultanate, Sword of The Sharia, Claimant of the Seljuk Inheritance, Sultanate of Rum) carries March Without a Mandate: −0.5 legitimacy per month. Both reforms are designed to remain available from the reform screen afterwards.

docs.title: The race
docs.text: The situation tracks the three strongest independent beyliks and re-ranks them every month. The base game's machinery around the leader is untouched: the offer of Leader of the Turks to a non-Ottoman front-runner, the vassalisation and integration events, decaying castles, Bey Fortresses and Seljuk Mints, The Balkan Wars once the leader passes 120 locations, and the empire-tier event for a leader who holds Constantinople.

docs.title: Actions on the situation panel
docs.text:
Action Who can use it Cost Effect Consolidate the Conquest Any beylik −5 legitimacy, −5 stability; once a year Fully integrates every location you own in one conquered Anatolian province Summon to Obedience A claimant who has proclaimed custody of Konya −5 legitimacy; once every 6 months Grants the Custody of Rum casus belli on a neighbouring beylik or any neighbour with its capital in Anatolia (no truce, no alliance with it) Endow a Chancery A vindicated ghāzī (see below), at peace, with no chancery yet Three years' income, −40 legitimacy, −20 stability; a Regional Dīwān must already stand Grants Persianate Bureaucracy, the privileges Land Registers, Muṣādara Right, Iqtāʿ Grant and Right to Retinue, and a Persian court language Petition the Caliph for Rum A vindicated ghāzī with a working chancery who is currently the strongest beylik One year's income +25 legitimacy, +10 prestige, and the Caliph's investiture: the Cairo door to forming Rum

"Vindicated ghāzī" means the Burden of the Sword has ended in one of its two successes, Sword of Islam or Guardian of the Thughur.

Custody of Rum is a superiority war in which the attacker can only demand locations in Anatolia, with conquest and subjugation at a reduced war-score cost. The keeper of Konya has no writ over Syria.

docs.title: Claimant of the Seljuk Inheritance
docs.text:
Open to any Muslim Persianate Sultanate with its capital in Anatolia that has not taken another answer to the legitimacy question (Ghāzī Sultanate, Chinggisid Regency, Farr-i Īzadī and the rest all exclude it). Owning Konya is not required to declare. Taking the city is the first step of the programme, and holding it already is the Karamanids' entire head start.

Effect of the reform Value Antagonism received +20% Monthly prestige +0.1 Clergy satisfaction +3% Nobles satisfaction −5% Monthly drift towards centralization +0.05

Once taken, the reform cannot be dropped. The claim ends vindicated or broken, never quietly shelved.

docs.title: The Seljuk Inheritance
docs.text:
The disaster begins within months of adopting the reform, and fires only once per country. It follows the same economy as the Farr Proof of Fortune: a claim under audit bleeds legitimacy, and only war and state-building pay it back.

On start: −40 legitimacy. Your fathers' patents ran from the Ilkhan's chancery; the claim voids your own paperwork.

While it runs:

Effect Value Monthly legitimacy −1.0 Minting income −30% Court spending efficiency −10% Nobles satisfaction −5% Diplomatic reputation −1

What feeds legitimacy:

Source Effect Being at war +0.3 legitimacy per month and +7.5% Nobles satisfaction for as long as the war lasts Winning a war +5 legitimacy and Glory of the Claimant's Arms: +0.4 per month for 12 months, extended by each further victory Winning a major battle +1 Gaining a location +1 Losing a battle −2 Losing a location −3 Losing your capital −20 Losing a war −10 and Shame of the Claimant's Arms: −1.0 per month for 6 months

Each of these arrives as a short notification event with three buttons: acknowledge, silence that kind of notice, or silence them all. The legitimacy change is applied either way.

docs.title: The Program of the Inheritance
docs.text:
Four buttons on the disaster panel, taken in order. Each costs gold and a rising amount of legitimacy up front, and pays back twice: a permanent modifier, and The Claim Advances, a relief of +0.5 legitimacy per month for five years that each further step extends.

# Step Requires Cost Permanent reward 1 Proclaim Custody of the Old Capital Own Konya 3 months' income, −10 legitimacy The Old Capital: +0.2 monthly legitimacy, +0.05 monthly prestige; +10 prestige; unlocks Summon to Obedience 2 Strike the Sikka Step 1; own Konya 6 months' income, −20 legitimacy The Sikka of Konya: +0.15 monthly legitimacy, +15% minting income; +5 prestige 3 Restore the Diwan of Rum Step 2; a Regional Dīwān and two Local Dīwāns built One year's income, −30 legitimacy, −5 stability, and a further −10 stability when the chancery is constituted The Persianate Bureaucracy reform; The Diwan of Rum: +0.15 monthly legitimacy, +5% cabinet efficiency; the privileges Land Registers, Muṣādara Right, Iqtāʿ Grant and Right to Retinue; Persian court language 4 Reopen the Trunk Road Step 3; own Konya and Sivas 8 months' income, −40 legitimacy The Trunk Road Reopened: +0.1 monthly legitimacy, +5% tax efficiency, +2% maximum rural control; +5 prestige

A realm that already has the Persianate Bureaucracy (the Eretnid case) pays only −10 legitimacy for step 3 instead of −30 and −5 stability, and receives no new privileges; the follow-up −10 stability still applies.

With all four standing, the permanent rewards return +0.6 of the −1.0 bleed, and the relief covers the rest for as long as it lasts.

Losing Konya un-builds the claim. If the city leaves your hands after step 1, the step is revoked, The Old Capital modifier is removed, and you lose 15 legitimacy and 10 prestige. The other steps stay, but you must retake the city and proclaim again (paying again) before you can be vindicated.

docs.title: How it ends
docs.text:
The disaster panel shows two counters: The Program of the Inheritance (0–4) and The Vindication Clock (months at legitimacy 60 or more, out of 36; cumulative, not consecutive).

Ending Condition Result Vindicated All four steps standing; 36 months on the clock; legitimacy 60 or more now; and either 60+ locations with your capital in Anatolia, or 3+ subjects The claimant reform is replaced by Sultanate of Rum; +25 legitimacy, +15 prestige; the Konya door to forming Rum Broken Legitimacy falls to 5 or below The claim is stripped; −25 legitimacy, −25 prestige; the country can never declare it again Abandoned The claimant reform is lost by other means The disaster ends quietly

A broken claimant keeps whatever he built: the modifiers of completed steps and, if he reached step 3, the chancery. The apparatus outlives the claim.

docs.title: Sultanate of Rum
docs.text:
The crown that sits on top of the chancery. On adoption: +15 stability and promotion to Kingdom rank if lower.

Effect Value Monthly legitimacy +0.10 Tax efficiency +10% Cabinet efficiency +15% Dīwān estate power +15% Dīwān satisfaction +5% Amirs satisfaction +1.5% Monthly drift towards centralization +0.10 Maximum urban control +5% Cultural tradition +5% Diplomatic reputation +1

Under the Sultanate of Rum, literate Muslim Turkic notables of the towns can enter the Dīwān estate. Elsewhere the chancery class is drawn from Iranian, Arab and Indian Muslim pops only; the restored sultanate trains its own.

docs.title: The ghāzī road
docs.text: The frontier answer reuses the Erānzamīn machinery unchanged: Ghāzī Sultanate, the Burden of the Sword disaster, and its successful endings. It is the natural road for the coastal and north-western marches that border Byzantium and the Latin lordships. What it does not give you is a chancery. A vindicated ghāzī who wants one must buy it with Endow a Chancery at full market rate (three years' income against the claimant's one), and only then can he send the embassy to Cairo with Petition the Caliph for Rum.

docs.title: How the situation ends
docs.text:
Shattered Rum ends when one of these is true:

  • the year 1565 has passed;
  • no beylik is left;
  • the strongest beylik is independent and owns more than 500 locations and at least 50 towns or cities;
  • after 1400, the strongest beylik owns fewer than 100 locations and is at peace.

Victory needs the leader to have passed the size test and to hold a completed legitimacy answer: Sword of Islam, Guardian of the Thughur, or the vindicated Seljuk Inheritance. The winner then receives the base game's rewards (The Rise of the Turks: the Pashas reform, the Eyalet Division policy, and the Legacy of the Ottomans or Legacy of the Turks). If the winner is not the Ottomans and the Ottomans no longer exist, the winner is also made into Rum at once.

Failure (Stagnation of the Turks) is what happens otherwise, including to a leader of any size who never answered the question. He has conquered a province, not founded a sultanate.

docs.title: Forming Rum
docs.text:
The formable keeps its base requirements: a Turkic, Muslim country that owns 85% of Anatolia and has concluded the situation as its winner. The mod adds a second gate, shown as "You hold a completed claim to Rum":

  • the Konya door: the vindicated Seljuk Inheritance, self-declared; or
  • the Cairo door: the Caliph's investiture from Petition the Caliph for Rum.

Forming Rum raises the country to Empire rank.

docs.title: The Ottomans
docs.text:
The Ottomans are one march among many. Their starting population is reduced to the frontier norm and made markedly more pastoral, while Karaman's towns (Konya and Larende above all) are strengthened; see Demography and cultures. Their AI is still pushed to annex, and the base Ottoman content remains theirs.

Because the Ottomans run a Persianate Sultanate for the whole campaign, base content gated on the monarchy government would otherwise go missing. The mod keeps the Imperial Harem reform available to them, lets the capital Sergeantry building be built by Persianate Sultanates, and ships a twin of the base event The One True Emperor (from 1537, for an Ottoman empire holding Constantinople) that fires under the new government.

docs.title: Advice
docs.text:
• Decide early. Every month on the fence costs 0.5 legitimacy. If you mean to stay a small march, accept that and find an overlord.
  • Karaman is the natural Seljuk claimant: it owns Konya on day one and can proclaim immediately. Everyone else must take the city first, and declaring before you can take it means bleeding at full rate with no step to show for it.
  • Do not start the programme at peace. The +0.3 for being at war and the +0.4 for each won war are what keep you above the Broken line while the −40 opening hit heals.
  • Build the offices before you need them. Step 3 needs a Regional Dīwān and two Local Dīwāns standing; see Buildings.
  • Step 4 needs Sivas, which the Eretnids hold. Plan that war, or that vassalage, from the start; Summon to Obedience gives you the casus belli once Konya is proclaimed.
  • Garrison Konya. Losing it costs a step, 15 legitimacy, and the price of proclaiming again.
  • On the ghāzī road, budget for the chancery. Three years' income and −20 stability is a peacetime purchase.
  • The size test for victory (500 locations, 50 towns or cities) is the base game's and is larger than Anatolia: the winner is expected to have crossed into the Balkans or Syria.

See also: The Ghāzī Burden of the Sword, Farr Proof of Fortune, Persianate Sultanate, Government reforms, The Dīwān estate, Buildings, Erānzamīn situation, Kurdish emirates, Countries and tags.

docs.title: Starting the game
docs.text:
Whose name is read on Friday?

The campaign opens on 1 April 1337, sixteen months after the death of the last Ilkhan. This page covers what the map looks like on that day, who holds what, what happens in the first month, and how to think about the opening years.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: Abū Saʿīd died in November 1335 without a son, and within two years every plausible prince of the house of Hülegü had been raised and destroyed by one amir or another. What was left was an empire with its army, treasury, chancery and provinces intact and nobody on the throne. The great amirs ruled in the name of Chinggisid princes they kept in their own households; the provincial dynasties of Fārs, Yazd, Herat and the Caspian coast governed as they always had and waited; in Khurasan the villagers of Bāshtīn killed a tax collector and found they had started a commonwealth.

docs.title: One honest anachronism
docs.text:
The calendar says April 1337. The map is the settlement of 1337–38.

The base game's April snapshot catches the successor states in mid-move. The mod places them where the dust settled: Ḥasan-i Kūchak already holds Tabriz, Ḥasan-i Buzurg has already fallen back on Baghdad, the Sarbadars already hold Sabzevar, and each of the two great amirs already keeps a Chinggisid in custody — including Sātī Beg and Sulaymān Khān, who were raised a year or two after the start date. The alternative was scripting the same railroad of events into the first eighteen months of every campaign and pretending the player's decisions had anything to do with them.

The base game's scripted opening war — the Hüleguids against the Jalayirids, with half of Iran called in on one side — is removed for the same reason. Nobody in Erānzamīn is at war on day one. The first war is yours, or your neighbour's.

docs.title: The great houses
docs.text:
Realm Seat Ruler Standing on day one Chobanids (CHB) Tabriz Ḥasan-i Kūchak 59 locations, about 2.6 million people, kingdom rank. Rules under a Chinggisid Regency. Holds the only Dīwān of the Realms in Iran, the megalopolis of Tabriz, and the Ilkhanid mint at Ganja. No subjects. Jalayirids (JAL) Baghdad Ḥasan-i Buzurg 84 locations, about 2.2 million people, kingdom rank. Rules under a Chinggisid Regency with the child Muḥammad Khān. Overlord of the Eretnids and the Sutayids, and through the Sutayids of eight emirates of the Jazira. Holds four of the six shrines of the Imāms and a Regional Dīwān in Baghdad. Gurgan (GRG) Gorgan Ṭoghā Temür 50 locations, about 1.6 million people, kingdom rank. A steppe horde, and its khan is a Chinggisid in his own right. Holds Soltaniyeh, the Ilkhans' own capital. Overlord of the Jauni Kurban of Nishapur and Mashhad. Injuids (INJ) Shiraz Ghiyāth al-Dīn Kay-Khusraw 51 locations, about 1.5 million people. Holds Shiraz and Isfahan — two of the Five Seats. Overlord of Khunj. Kartids (KRT) Herat Muʿizz al-Dīn Ḥusayn 33 locations, about 700,000 people. The one city of Khurasan that came back from the Mongol conquest, and the furthest from everyone else's wars. Muzaffarids (MZF) Yazd Mubāriz al-Dīn Muḥammad 27 locations, about 530,000 people. Small, compact, and sitting on Yazd, one of the most populous districts of the plateau. Sarbadars (SRB) Sabzevar ʿAbd al-Razzāq 6 locations, about 156,000 people. Not a sultanate at all: a Commonwealth of Martyrs, Shia, surrounded by people who want it dead. Hüleguids (HLG) Hoveyzeh Mūsā Khān A single marsh town in Khuzestan. The last prince of the old house, beaten by Ḥasan-i Buzurg in 1336 — nearly powerless, and still a Chinggisid.

Around them sit some sixty smaller realms: Kerman, the Atabegs of Greater and Lesser Lur, Shabankara, Ormus and its Persian Gulf dependencies, the lords of Gilan and Mazandaran, the Shirvanshah, the maliks of Sistan, the Baloch chiefs of Makran, Georgia and Armenia (which keep their base-game vassals). The full list, with tags, is on Countries and tags.

Beyond the old Ilkhanid frontier the mod also rebuilds the Chagatai khanate as an organisation of a khan and fifteen amirs, splits Yemen between the Rasulid sultanate and the Zaydi Imamate, moves Egypt and Delhi onto the Persianate Sultanate government, and seats seven ṭarīqa orders — the Safavid order at Ardabil among them — as landless shrine-polities.

docs.title: Who rules whom
docs.text:
There are no scripted alliances among the successor states at the start, and only a handful of overlords:

Overlord Subjects Jalayirids Eretnids (Sivas), Sutayids (Diyarbekir) Eretnids four small Anatolian tributaries, as in the base game Sutayids Bohtan, Bitlis, Hakkari, Çemişgezek, Egil, Hazro, Zirqan, the Dilmaçids Bitlis Hizan, Mus, Çapakçur Bohtan Dasni Gurgan Jauni Kurban Injuids Khunj Ormus Fal, Jāsk (and the Jarwanids across the water) Makran Bampūr, Buleda, Kolwa Lahijan Ranekouh

The base game's long lists of Jalayirid and Gurgan vassals are gone. Qom, Kashan, Hamadan, Tabaristan, the Kartids and the towns of Khurasan all start independent, and every independent Muslim realm seated in the region is a contender. The Jalayirid bloc is the only large one on the map; everything else has to be built.

docs.title: The Tabriz problem
docs.text:
There is exactly one Dīwān of the Realms in Iran at the start — the grand chancery, the top of the three-tier dīwān ladder — and it stands in Tabriz, in Chobanid hands. Baghdad has a Regional Dīwān, one tier down. Nobody else in Erānzamīn has a chancery building at all. (Two more Dīwāns of the Realms exist far away, in Cairo and Delhi; they belong to other stories.)

Whoever holds Tabriz holds the central office of the Ilkhanate's bureaucracy, the largest city between Cairo and Delhi, and one of the Five Seats. The Jalayirids and Chobanids fought over it for two decades. The mod gives you the institutional reason their war mattered: see Buildings for what the chancery tiers do.

docs.title: The Five Seats
docs.text:
Five cities decide the succession: Tabriz, Baghdad, Soltaniyeh, Isfahan and Shiraz. Nobody can win the Succession of Erānzamīn without owning all five directly. On day one they are split four ways:

Seat Holder Tabriz Chobanids Baghdad Jalayirids Soltaniyeh Gurgan Isfahan Injuids Shiraz Injuids

The Erānzamīn organisation panel shows the holders at any moment.

docs.title: What happens on day one
docs.text:
• The Succession of Erānzamīn and The Sarbadar Phenomenon both begin. Every contender is shown Hulagu's Seat Stands Empty and must say on what ground he rules: through a Chinggisid he keeps, as the Caliph's sword, by the farr of Iranian kingship, as a mere governor, or — for Ṭoghā Temür and Mūsā Khān, Chinggisids themselves — by his own blood. The options differ by who you are; they are laid out on the situation page. Read it before you click.
  • Both estates of a Persianate Sultanate exist from the first day. The Dīwān and the Amirs each start with two named men: the scribes are Persian whatever the dynasty's culture, the amirs share the ruler's.
  • The starting privileges are already granted. A Tāzīk-leaning court (the Injuids, Muzaffarids, Kartids, Shirvan, the Caspian lords and most city-states) opens at +25 on the Türk–Tāzīk axis with Land Registers, Tax Farming, Provincial Auditors, Iqtāʿ Grant and Right to Retinue. A Türk-leaning one (the Chobanids, Jalayirids, Eretnids, Sutayids, Kerman, the Lur atabegs, the Baloch chiefs) opens at −25 with Iqtāʿ Grant, Frontier Governorship, Right to Retinue and Tribal Hosts (Yurt), and only Land Registers on the Dīwān's side. Both have the Muṣādara Right and the Boneh System. See Estate privileges.
  • The countryside is built out. Every member of the Erānzamīn organisation receives, free, its qanāt networks, irrigation works, farming villages and desert clay pits where the land supports them. Some qanāts start damaged.
  • Each realm's accepted and tolerated cultures are set from who actually lives in it. See Demography and cultures.

docs.title: What you are called
docs.text:
A Persianate Sultanate seated in the region does not use the base game's titles:

Rank Realm Ruler Under a Chinggisid Regency Faction Regent County, Türk-leaning Tūmān Tūman-bāshī County, Tāzīk-leaning Ḥukūmat Ḥākim Duchy, Türk-leaning Amirate Amīr Duchy, Tāzīk-leaning Vilāyat Vālī Kingdom Sultanate Sulṭān Empire Pādshāhī Pādshāh

The Chobanid and Jalayirid rulers are therefore "Regents" of "Factions" on day one. Nobody is a Sulṭān until he stops ruling in another man's name. The Sarbadar head is a Khwāja of a Commonwealth; the Zaydi ruler an Imām.

docs.title: Opening priorities
docs.text:
There is no single right opener, but a few things are true almost everywhere.

  1. Answer the opening event deliberately. It fixes the ground of your legitimacy for the first decades, and each answer opens a different system: a kept khan leads to the borrowed mandate, the frontier answer to the burden of the sword, the Iranian answer to the proof of fortune. The two regents have no choice to make — their khans are already in the house.
  2. Know which pole you start on. The starting privileges already lean your court one way. Drifting to the middle costs you the trust of both estates; committing costs you one of them. See the Türk–Tāzīk axis.
  3. Count seats, not provinces. The Injuids start with two of five and no army to speak of; Gurgan holds the Ilkhans' own capital with a horde behind it; the two regents hold one each and the only chanceries. Whoever you play, you can see from the first day whose land you must eventually own.
  4. Mind the one bloc that exists. The Jalayirid regent can call the Eretnids, the Sutayids and eight Kurdish emirates. Nobody else starts with more than a vassal or three. If you are small and west of the Zagros, that is your weather.
  5. You are surrounded by rivals, not neighbours. Members of Erānzamīn start with a standing −50 opinion of one another, and contenders may take each other's land far more cheaply than ordinary states can. Sitting still does not keep you safe.
  6. A small realm has other roads. Declaring fealty to a regent, or holding out as a governor, are real positions in this contest, not failure states — see the Ilkhanate governorate.

See also: The Succession of Erānzamīn, The Erānzamīn organisation, Demography and cultures, Countries and tags, Persianate Sultanate, What's new in 1.4.

docs.title: Ṭarīqa Orders and the Shia Rework
docs.text:
The lodges are waiting to hear whose name to recite.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The orders load and the Two Pirs has been exercised with a debug kit, but the endgames (the khurūj and its coronation, Rise Against the Patron, Capture the Court) and the rebel-banner events have not been played through to the end in a 1.4 campaign. One in-game tooltip on the Manifestation event still describes an older version of the rising (provinces coming over, half a war chest); this page describes what the event actually does.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: By 1337 the Sufi orders were among the most durable institutions between the Nile and the Jaxartes. A ṭarīqa was a chain of teaching from master to disciple, a shrine, an endowment, and a web of lodges whose deputies (khalīfas) answered to the shaykh at the shrine rather than to any governor. Princes endowed them because a shaykh's blessing was worth having when thrones had no settled owner. This world was not divided into "Sunni" and "Shia" as later centuries would understand the words. Reverence for ʿAlī and the Prophet's house ran through Sunni orders as a matter of course; the Kubrawiyya, the Ṣafaviyya at Ardabīl and others stood in a confessional middle ground that modern historians call ʿAlid loyalism. Explicit Shiism, messianic or juristic, grew out of that ground in particular places over generations: the Ṣafavī order was a respectable Sunni house under Ṣadr al-Dīn in 1337 and a militant Shia movement under Junayd and Ḥaydar a century later. The mod therefore starts every order Sunni and makes the change of confession a long, costly and optional passage, not a starting trait.

docs.title: The Shia rework
docs.text:
The base game gives Shia Islam a list of schools and nothing else. The mod separates three things the base game ran together.

Layer What it answers Where it lives Imamate and doctrine Whose Imamate, and what follows from it Religious aspects (four slots) Establishment Which network runs your religious institutions The religious school slot Law Which madhhab the courts apply The sharia law policy, as in the base game

docs.title: Aspects
docs.text:
Shia countries have four aspect slots. Adopting or changing an aspect costs 30 stability. A Shia realm may hold no Imamate aspect at all, and most do at the start: that is the confessional ambiguity of the post-Mongol decades, and committing is meant to be a decision.

Aspect Requires Effects The Twelve Imams No other Imamate +1 tolerance of the true faith, a small clergy satisfaction bonus The Ismaili Imamate No other Imamate +5 maximum literacy, drift towards mysticism The Zaydi Imamate No other Imamate +5% land morale, drift towards jurisprudence Quietist Awaiting The Twelve Imams +10% stability cost efficiency, +5% improve relations The General Vicariate The Twelve Imams +10% clergy power, a small clergy satisfaction bonus, drift towards jurisprudence The Manifestation The Twelve Imams +10% land morale, +20% conversion speed, −10% stability cost efficiency, drift towards spiritualist Qiyām bi'l-Sayf The Zaydi Imamate; not Taqiyya +10% manpower, +5% land morale, drift towards mysticism Usuli Rationalism The Twelve Imams +5% research speed, +10% clergy power, drift towards jurisprudence Akhbari Traditionism The Twelve Imams +10% stability cost efficiency, +1 tolerance of the true faith Taqiyya Not Tabarra, not Qiyām bi'l-Sayf +10% improve relations, +1 tolerance of heretics Tabarra Not Taqiyya +25% conversion speed, +1 tolerance of the true faith, −15% improve relations

Quietist Awaiting, The General Vicariate and The Manifestation exclude one another, as do Usuli Rationalism and Akhbari Traditionism. Countries that share an aspect like each other a little more; rival positions cost opinion, and two realms that both claim The Manifestation dislike each other most of all (−20).

A landed state may claim The Manifestation or Qiyām bi'l-Sayf freely. An order may not until it has circulated a sayyid genealogy (see the Two Pirs below).

docs.title: Establishments
docs.text:
The generic labels Ja'farī, Ismā'īlī and Imāmīya are no longer offered to Shia countries as schools; the branch is now the Imamate aspect.

Establishment Open to Leaning required Effects The Hilla Hawza Shia None (always available) +10 maximum literacy, +5% research speed, drift towards jurisprudence The Shaykhiyya Shia Not on the jurisprudence side +5% land morale, +5% manpower, drift towards mysticism The Kubrawiyya Sunni or Shia Mysticism beyond 50 +5 maximum literacy, +1 tolerance of heretics, drift towards mysticism The Nurbakhshiyya Shia Mysticism beyond 50 +10% conversion speed, +5% land morale, drift towards mysticism The Nimatullahiyya Sunni or Shia Mysticism beyond 50 +5% trade income, +5% improve relations, drift towards mysticism

The Zaydiyya, The Nizari Daʿwa and The Tayyibi Daʿwa are kept from the base game and re-described as networks. The Hilla Hawza counts as a school of jurisprudence wherever the game asks for one.

Two Sunni schools were also rebalanced: Ḥanafī now gives +5% cabinet efficiency and +5% tax efficiency, Shāfi'ī +10% export efficiency and +10% clergy power, and both drift towards jurisprudence.

docs.title: Other religion-level changes
docs.text:
• Sunni and Shia realms now accumulate religious influence (+0.05 a month, to a cap of 400). The Zaydi imamate page covers where it is spent.
  • The blanket bans on importing wine, beer and liquor have been removed from the Sunni, Shia and Ibadi religions. Prohibition was a matter of market inspection and policy, not an automatic consequence of the faith.

docs.title: Who starts with what
docs.text:
Country Imamate aspect Establishment Sarbadars (SRB) The Twelve Imams, The General Vicariate The Shaykhiyya Baduspanids (BDS) The Twelve Imams unchanged Tabaristan (MZN), Tulam (TLM), Khorshidi (LCK), Hillah (HLL), Ispahbad (IHB) The Zaydi Imamate unchanged Gilgit (GLI), Hunza (HNZ), Sindh (SND) The Ismaili Imamate The Nizari Daʿwa Chobanids (CHB) none The Hilla Hawza

Each entry applies only if the country is Shia when the game starts. The Chobanids are the deliberate case of a Twelver-leaning court that has not committed.

docs.title: The orders in 1337
docs.text:
A Tariqa Order is a country without land. Its capital, the shrine-seat, is a city that belongs to someone else, and its presence on the map is the lodges it keeps in other rulers' locations. Seven exist at the start, all Sunni, all with a Persianate Sultanate's court and an elective succession among the shaykh's house.

Order Tag Shrine-seat Base Establishment Starting lodges Ardabil (the Ṣafaviyya) ABL Ardabil none chosen yet Ṣafavī Tabriz, Ahar Kubrawiyya KBW Semnan Popular The Kubrawiyya Damghan, Nishapur Kazaruniyya KZR Kazerun Urban Shāfi'ī Shiraz, Siraf Qadiriyya QAD Baghdad Urban Ḥanbalī Mosul, Samarra Khwajagan KWJ Bukhara Urban Ḥanafī Samarkand, Karmana Yasaviyya YSV Turkestan Tribal Ḥanafī Otrar, Sawran Rifaiyya RIF Wasit Popular Shāfi'ī Basra, Hillah

Each also starts with a Grand Khānaqāh at its shrine-seat. Six lean strongly towards mysticism; the Khwajagan, the sober masters of Bukhara, lean towards jurisprudence. Ardabil has not yet chosen a base, so that choice is the first decision of a Ṣafavī game.

At the opening of the Succession of Erānzamīn an order has its own answer to the empty throne: it claims nothing and gains +5 legitimacy. Orders are exempt from the unsettled-legitimacy penalty that landed sultanates suffer.

docs.title: The order's reforms
docs.text:
Tariqa Order itself allows lodges to be planted and gives +10% improve relations, +1 diplomatic reputation, +50% levy size and a drift towards mysticism. On top of it an order takes exactly one base, which decides whom it recruits and how it can end.

Base Unlocks Bonuses Endgame The Tribal Base Tribal Devotion Circle +10% land morale, +50% tribal levies Proclaim the Khuruj The Popular Base Rural Zāwiya +10% manpower Rise Against the Patron The Urban Base Endowed Waqf +1 diplomatic reputation, +5 maximum literacy Capture the Court

docs.title: Lodges and chapters
docs.text:
All of an order's buildings stand in other rulers' locations and need good relations with the host to be built. Each sends a monthly donation (futūḥ) back to the shrine-seat; the "income" column gives the relative size.

Building Where For the host Converts to Income Tariqa Lodge (3 levels) Any settlement Lower maximum control, −0.1 unrest, a little prosperity Sunni, slowly 1 Grand Khānaqāh (1 level) A capital, town or larger, with Muslim pops +0.1 monthly legitimacy for the country whose capital it is; prosperity none 3 Tribal Devotion Circle (2 levels) Rural settlements and towns none Sunni, slowly 0.5 Rural Zāwiya (2 levels) Rural settlements and towns −0.1 unrest, a little prosperity Sunni, slowly 0.5 Endowed Waqf (3 levels) Towns and cities Prosperity Sunni, slowly 2

Devotion Circles, Zāwiyas and Waqfs are chapters: the count of chapters of your own base is what the Two Pirs measures. After the recitation changes, the buildings change with it:

Building Replaces For the host Converts to Ghulāt Khānaqāh Tariqa Lodge Lower maximum control, +0.1 unrest Shia, at twice the lodge's rate Qizilbash Lodge Tribal Devotion Circle +0.2 unrest Shia Dervish Takiya Rural Zāwiya +0.1 unrest Shia Futuwwa Brotherhood Endowed Waqf +0.1 unrest Shia

The three militant buildings employ ten times the people of the chapters they replace. Once an order has declared, it can no longer build ordinary Tariqa Lodges, only Ghulāt ones.

A host who destroys a Rural Zāwiya or a Dervish Takiya is remembered for ten years; that memory is what licenses Rise Against the Patron.

docs.title: Patronize An Order
docs.text:
Any Muslim ruler who is not an order, and who has an order's Tariqa Lodge somewhere in the realm, can endow it. The action sits in the panel of the Sarbadar Phenomenon and so is only offered while that situation is active (see the Commonwealth of Martyrs).

Price Six months of the patron's income Cooldown 5 years If the order accepts The order receives the endowment. The patron gains +10 legitimacy and +5 stability, and a Grand Khānaqāh is founded in the patron's capital (+0.1 monthly legitimacy while it stands). If the order refuses The gold is returned, the patron loses 15 legitimacy, and the order gains 5.

An AI order accepts almost always. Refusal becomes likely only when the order's opinion of the patron is below −50, or when a radical order is courted by a non-Shia throne. For an order, patronage is the main source of large sums; for a ruler, it is some of the cheapest legitimacy available in the years after 1335.

docs.title: The Two Pirs
docs.text:
A disaster for orders: the succession at the shrine is contested between the quietist establishment and a militant claimant.

It can begin for a Sunni order that has at least five chapters of its base, has not been through it before, and has not upheld the quietist within the last 20 years. The chance is 2.5% a month. While the disaster is active the order suffers −1.0 monthly legitimacy and −1 diplomatic reputation.

It opens with a three-way choice.

Choice Result Let the recitation change. The order, its shaykh, heir and house become Shia with no Imamate claimed yet. Permanent Militant Zeal (+10% land morale, +15% conversion speed, −25% improve relations). Every Tariqa Lodge in the shrine-seat's area becomes a Ghulāt Khānaqāh; the rest stay veiled. The passage begins and the legitimacy drain continues until it is completed. The claimant can burn somewhere else. The disaster ends. +10 legitimacy; The Exile's Wound for 20 years (−10% manpower, −0.1 monthly legitimacy). The question cannot return for 20 years. Petition for land. The disaster ends for good. The order takes ownership of its shrine-seat, becomes an ordinary landed country, loses the Tariqa Order reform and gains +20 legitimacy.

docs.title: The passage
docs.text:
The disaster panel shows three bars and the actions that fill them.

Bar Midpoint Completion The Chapter Census (chapters of your base, anywhere) 10 20 The Shrine-Seat Province Recites (Shia share of the province) 50% The Wider Area Recites (Shia share of the surrounding area) 15% Action Requires Price Cooldown Effect Send Forth the Khalifas A location you do not own, with Muslim pops and no chapter 3 months' income 12 months A new chapter of your base, at once Plant the Seed A location with non-Shia Muslims 1.5 months' income 6 months 2% of every non-Shia Muslim pop there becomes Shia Proclaim the Mystery Legitimacy 20 or more; a veiled Tariqa Lodge 15 legitimacy 24 months That lodge becomes a Ghulāt Khānaqāh Spread the Sayyid Genealogy Legitimacy 60 or more; five lodges (veiled or unveiled) 6 months' income once Permanent House of the Prophet (+0.1 monthly legitimacy); the order may now claim The Manifestation or Qiyām bi'l-Sayf Claim the Age 10 chapters; half the shrine-seat province Shia free once The Proofs Multiply until the passage ends (+0.5 monthly legitimacy, +25% conversion speed); Shia risings in the region now offer the order their banners

docs.title: Completion
docs.text:
The passage completes when all of these hold:

  • the Age has been claimed;
  • 20 chapters stand;
  • 15% of the shrine-seat's area is Shia;
  • legitimacy is 50 or more;
  • the order holds The Twelve Imams with The Manifestation, or The Zaydi Imamate with Qiyām bi'l-Sayf (two aspects, 30 stability each).

The Manifestation then fires. Every chapter becomes its militant twin, the last veiled lodges unveil, The Proofs Multiply ends, and the order gains permanent The Manifest Order (+25% levy size, +5% land morale). The order chooses between consolidating (+10 legitimacy, with the endgames open on its own schedule) and rising at once.

docs.title: The khurūj (tribal orders)
docs.text:
Proclaim the Khuruj needs a completed passage and at least three Qizilbash Lodges. When proclaimed:

  • the shrine-seat location becomes the order's own;
  • the order becomes an army-country under a Persianate Sultanate with The Khurūj reform (+20% land morale, +10% discipline, +50% supply limit);
  • two Turkoman Light Cavalry regiments muster at the shrine-seat for every five lodges (rounded up), with 500 manpower in reserve for each pair;
  • the treasury receives 24 months of income;
  • war is declared, with the Succession of Erānzamīn casus belli, on every country whose capital lies in the shrine-seat's area.

Rising directly from the Manifestation event does the same for an order of any base, counting all its militant chapters: tribal orders muster Turkoman Light Cavalry, the others muster Dervish Corps. On that road the shrine-seat is not handed over; the order takes the field landless.

The Khurūj is not an answer to the khuṭba question, so the risen order carries the same unsettled-legitimacy penalty as any undecided sultanate (−0.6 monthly legitimacy and lower estate satisfaction). That drain is the clock.

docs.title: The coronation
docs.text:
A risen order that takes Tabriz, Isfahan, Baghdad, Nishapur, Shiraz or Herat receives The Khuṭba of the Twelve:

  • the conquered city becomes the capital and the order becomes a settled country of kingdom rank;
  • The Khurūj is replaced by Persianate Bureaucracy and The Crowned Murshid (+0.1 monthly legitimacy, +10% land morale, +5% discipline);
  • +100 legitimacy.

The Crowned Murshid ends the legitimacy drain, but it stands only while the realm leans towards mysticism beyond 50. If the jurists pull the realm back, the reform is lost and the crown keeps only the throne.

docs.title: Rise Against the Patron (popular orders)
docs.text: Available when a host has destroyed one of the order's Zāwiyas or Takiyas within the last ten years, or when the order is at war. Choose a realm that hosts at least two of them. Every location in that realm with a Zāwiya or Takiya passes to the order, which becomes a landed Commonwealth of Martyrs, musters two Dervish Corps regiments per five lodges, and receives 12 months of income. As written, this does not require the Two Pirs to have run.

docs.title: Capture the Court (urban orders)
docs.text:
Needs a completed passage. Choose a Muslim realm that hosts at least two of the order's Endowed Waqfs or Futuwwa Brotherhoods.

Price Twelve months of the order's income Cooldown 20 years Effect The target's ruler, heir and dynasty become Shia; the realm takes the order's Imamate (Zaydi if the order is Zaydi, otherwise The Twelve Imams) and the Ṣafavī establishment. The order gains +20 legitimacy and a Grand Khānaqāh in the captured capital.

The order remains an order and can repeat the act elsewhere after the cooldown.

docs.title: Shia risings and their banners
docs.text:
When Shia religious rebels open a civil war, the mod asks who leads them.

If an order is in reach (it has claimed the Age or completed the passage, has not settled, and keeps a building in the region of the rebels' capital), it receives The Banners Seek a Pir. Accepting is a full khurūj on the spot: the order annexes the rebels and their land, musters its lodges, receives 24 months of income, and goes to war with the country the rebels rose against and with the neighbours of the shrine-seat. Declining costs nothing in numbers.

If no order is in reach, the rebels decide for themselves in In Whose Name Is the Coin Minted:

Answer Result No name but the Imām's. A new Commonwealth of Martyrs with a full 25 years of Revolutionary Zeal, The Twelve Imams and The General Vicariate, the Shaykhiyya establishment, and membership of the Sarbadār Movement. Favoured where Sarbadar Preachers have prepared the ground and where the rising is in a city. The waiting is over. A Persianate Sultanate with The Twelve Imams and The Manifestation and the Nurbakhshiyya establishment. Favoured in the countryside.

docs.title: Practical advice
docs.text:
Playing an order

  • Income is lodges. Build Tariqa Lodges widely before anything else, and take every patron's endowment.
  • The Two Pirs needs five chapters to begin at all. An order that never builds chapters stays a quiet, wealthy Sunni house indefinitely, which is a legitimate way to play the Khwajagan or the Qadiriyya.
  • If you mean to walk the passage, enter it with legitimacy high and a full treasury. Spread the Sayyid Genealogy needs 60 legitimacy and the drain starts at once, so commission it in the first months.
  • Unveil lodges sparingly. Each costs 15 legitimacy; let Plant the Seed do the work in the home province and save unveiling for the places where the 50% line is close.
  • Claim the Age as soon as it is available. It halves the drain.
  • Completion needs 60 stability for the two aspects, on top of legitimacy 50. Arrive with both.
  • Before proclaiming the khurūj, look at who has a capital in your shrine-seat's area: you will be at war with all of them at once, and you need one of six great cities to stop the bleeding.

Living next to an order

  • A Tariqa Lodge is good for the location and one Patronize away from +10 legitimacy. Host them.
  • Watch for lodges turning into Ghulāt Khānaqāhs. From then on the building raises unrest and converts your subjects, and removing a village order's Zāwiya gives it the pretext to rise against you.

See also: the Commonwealth of Martyrs, the Zaydi imamate, the Succession of Erānzamīn, Persianate Sultanate, the Ghāzī Burden of the Sword, Buildings, countries and tags, known issues.

docs.title: Türk vs Tāzīk
docs.text:
The men of the sword and the men of the pen.

Every Persianate Sultanate carries one extra societal value: Turk vs Tazik, shown in game as a slider between Turkic Military Tradition on the left and Tazik Administration on the right. It is not a culture slider — your pops stay whatever they were. It measures which of the two service elites your state defaults to: the Amirs or the Dīwān.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: Persian chancery writers of the Ilkhanid and post-Ilkhanid centuries divided the ruling class into Turk and Tāzīk: the Turco-Mongol military households who held commands, pastures and iqṭāʿ, and the Persian-writing secretaries, accountants and judges who kept the registers. The division was one of function and household more than of language — Iraqi Arab secretaries of Baghdad and Ḥilla belong to the Tāzīk side as surely as the Juvaynīs of Khurāsān, and a Persianised Mongol amir remains a man of the sword. Both sides were Muslim, both wrote and patronised Persian, and no court ran without both. What a ruler decided, month by month, was whose advice counted and whose grievances were heard first.

docs.title: The two poles
docs.text:
The slider runs from −100 (fully Türk) to +100 (fully Tāzīk). As with every societal value, the listed effects are the values at the extreme and scale down toward the centre; at 0 neither side applies.

Turkic Military Tradition (−100) Tazik Administration (+100) Amirs estate power +50% −50% Dīwān estate power −50% +50% Tribes estate power +25% — Dīwān satisfaction equilibrium — +8% Amirs levy size +25% −40% Tribes levy size +25% −40% Manpower +15% −15% Heavy and light cavalry power +15% each — Tax efficiency −10% +10% Cabinet efficiency — +10% Maximum urban control −5% +12.5% Maximum rural control −15% +5% Raw material output +10% — Cultural influence — +15% Cultural tradition — −15% Court spending efficiency — −10% Tribesmen desired population +15% rural, +5% towns −50% rural, −75% towns Nobles desired population +3% rural, +1% towns +1% rural, +3% towns Subject loyalty +15 +15 Monthly drift +0.10 toward decentralization +0.10 toward centralization

Both ends raise subject loyalty: either elite, once clearly in charge, is a party your subjects can deal with. The muddled middle gets nothing.

The Amirs also read the slider directly. Their opinion of the crown gains up to +20 at the Türk extreme and loses up to 20 at the Tāzīk extreme (one point for every five on the slider). The Dīwān have no mirror-image opinion term; their reward for a Tāzīk realm is the satisfaction and power in the table.

docs.title: Where you start
docs.text:
Starting setup Slider Who Türk-dominant sultanates −25 Jalayirids (JAL), Chobanids (CHB), Eretna (ERE) and most of the Turco-Mongol amirates Tāzīk-dominant sultanates +25 Muzaffarids (MZF), Injuids (INJ), Karts (KRT), Shirvan (SRV), the Caspian and Persian Gulf dynasties, Rasulid Yemen (YEM)

The Türk-dominant setup also starts with the Tribal Host recruitment law, Amir Autonomy and Iqta Assignments; the Tāzīk-dominant setup starts with Amir Recruitment, Curtail the Umara and Diwan Administration. Those laws are a large part of why each side keeps drifting the way it began (see below).

docs.title: Steady drift
docs.text:
Reforms, laws, privileges and a few long modifiers each add a monthly push. A push of +0.05 is 0.6 points a year; they all stack.
