Source Typical push per month Amirs privileges 0.05–0.20 toward Türk each. The heaviest are Hereditary Tuyul (0.20), Tribal Hosts (Yurt) and Universal Tarkhan (0.15), Umarāʾ at the Dīwān (0.10). Dīwān privileges 0.05 toward Tāzīk each; 0.10 for Tāzīk Command of Arms, Mavājib Cash Pay, Ṣāḥib-Dīwān Plenipotentiary and Chancery Commissions for Amir Sons. Laws Amir Recruitment, Tribal Host, Amir Autonomy: 0.10 Türk. Rights of the Umara: 0.05 Türk. Diwan Administration, Curtail the Umara: 0.05 Tāzīk. Government reforms From 0.025 to 0.15 either way — the full list is on the government reforms page. Amīr Sultanate (0.15 Türk) and Chinggisid Regency (0.10 Türk) are the strongest early pushes; Iranian Kingship, Ghulām Corps and Khāṣṣa Crown Demesne (0.10 Tāzīk each) the strongest later ones. Cabinet The base game's "change societal values" cabinet action works on this slider in both directions, at 1 point a month multiplied by cabinet efficiency. It is by far the fastest deliberate lever.

Note that the plain Iqtāʿ Grant privilege carries no drift of its own. It is the iqṭāʿ buildings it permits that move the slider (next section).

docs.title: One-off jumps
docs.text:
Action Jump Building a Local Dīwān +1 Building a Regional Dīwān +2.5 Building the Dīwān of the Realms +5 Completing a Qanāt Network +1 An Iqṭāʿ Grant building −0.025 A grant slipping into Unaudited Iqṭāʿ −0.25 A Tuyul −0.5 Consolidate the Diwan on a conquered province +1.5 Grant the Yurt on a conquered province −1.5 Restore Persian Bureaucracy +10 Rally Turkic Tribes −5 The Mazālim event The Seven Day Execution −10 if you blame the bureaucrats, +10 if you blame the enforcers Amirs' and crown issues carried at the Mazālim court up to ±5 Steps of the Matter of Tork +5 per completed step of the dissolution programme; −20 once, the month Umarāʾ at the Dīwān is first held while the Matter runs

Many of the mod's flavour events also move the slider by 5 or 10 either way depending on whose side you take.

docs.title: What reads the slider
docs.text:
Threshold What it gates Below 0 Rally Turkic Tribes is available. Petty Persianate realms in Erānzamīn use the Türk rank titles (Tūmān, Amirate) instead of the Tāzīk ones (Ḥukūmat, Vilāyat). At the Erānzamīn victory, a slider below 0 gives the Türk settlement (Mandate of the Great Khan, the Invite Turkic Settlers cabinet action and the road to Iran o Toran). 0 or above At the Erānzamīn victory, gives the Tāzīk settlement (Restoration of Eran and the Integrate into the Dīwān cabinet action). Below −15 Grant the Yurt is available. Above +25 Consolidate the Diwan is available (it also needs the Dīwān of the Realms in your capital). The in-game tooltip currently says 15; the real threshold is 25. +25 or above A Qanāt Network can be built without the Land Registers privilege. Also one of the conditions for closing the Matter of Tork by dissolution. +50 or above A kingdom can seat the Dīwān of the Realms on the slider alone (an empire, or a realm that has used Restore Persian Bureaucracy, can seat it regardless).

The three province-integration actions and the two rallying actions belong to the Erānzamīn situation and are only offered to its contenders. In brief:

Action Needs Cost Result Consolidate the Diwan Slider above +25; Dīwān of the Realms in the capital; a Local Dīwān in the conquered province Gold (3 months of income) Integrates the province at once; +10% max control, +10% raw material output and lower unrest there for 10 years; Dīwān pleased, Amirs slightly displeased; +1.5 Grant the Yurt Slider below −15 5 legitimacy, 5 political influence Integrates the province at once; +30% local manpower, −7.5% max control and lower unrest for 10 years; Amirs pleased, Dīwān slightly displeased; −1.5 Mixed Settlement — Gold, 5 legitimacy, 5 political influence Integrates the province at once; +10% local manpower and lower unrest for 10 years; no estate reaction, no slider movement Rally Turkic Tribes Slider below 0; prestige above 40 20 prestige and gold Türkmen tribesmen and their nobles arrive in one rural location (more for higher ranks); Amirs +10%, Dīwān, burghers and peasants −25% each; −10 stability; −5 Restore Persian Bureaucracy Prestige above 30; at least duchy rank; not already a Tāzīk (+50) kingdom Gold, 20 legitimacy, 15 prestige, 10 stability Diwan Extension for 25 years (+7.5% tax efficiency, +5% max control, Dīwān +5% satisfaction and +10% power; stacks); Dīwān +15%, Amirs −15%; +10; permanently allows the Dīwān of the Realms

docs.title: Playing the axis
docs.text:
• Pick a side early, or pay for the middle. Every bonus in the pole table is zero at the centre. A realm sitting at ±25 gets a quarter of one column. The slider rewards commitment, and so does subject loyalty.
  • Your starting laws are the drift. A Türk-dominant start carries about 0.45 a month toward Türk from its starting laws and privileges alone (more under a Chinggisid Regency). If you mean to turn such a realm Tāzīk, change the recruitment law and the nobility law first; otherwise you are rowing against them.
  • Going Tāzīk costs soldiers. At the Tāzīk extreme the Amirs and the tribes each raise 40% fewer levies and manpower falls 15%. Plan to replace them with paid troops — see the military system.
  • Going Türk costs the countryside. −15% maximum rural control and −10% tax efficiency at the extreme, with the Dīwān at half power. The Türk realm is rich in horsemen and poor in registers.
  • The cabinet seat is the real lever. One point a month from the cabinet outweighs any three privileges. Use it to cross a threshold (−15 for Grant the Yurt, +25 for Consolidate the Diwan, the sign of the slider before the Erānzamīn victory), then free the seat.
  • Watch the Amirs' opinion. A Tāzīk realm takes up to −20 Amir opinion from the slider itself, on top of whatever the privileges you revoked cost you.

See also: Persianate Sultanate, Government reforms, Dīwān estate, Amirs estate, Estate privileges, Erānzamīn situation, Matter of Tork, Buildings.

docs.title: Ulus Chaghatay
docs.text:
The khan's seat is the organisation's leader. It need not stay where it is.

New in 1.4 — largely untested in play

The organisation, its roster, the qubchur and the panel load and run. Pledges, risings, raids, client kings and the broken-tümen event were built in November 2026 and have had only spot tests; their balance and the AI's handling of them are unverified. See Known issues.

In 1337 the Chagatai khanate was one ulus made of many hereditary followings. The Barlas around Kesh, the Jalayir at Khujand, the Suldus at Balkh, the Qara'unas in the Afghan lands and the Dughlats at Kashgar each held a domain with its own house and its own horsemen. They were tümens of one people under one khan, and a strong khan such as Kebek or Tarmashirin could command them and move them about; a weak one ruled what his amirs let him rule. Six khans sat at Almaliq in the twelve years after 1334.

In 1346 the amir Qazaghan of the Qara'unas did not wait for a khan to die. He rose, killed Qazan Khan in battle, raised a khan of his own choosing at his own camp and governed the western ulus in that man's name. It was out of that generation of regents that Temür of the Barlas came (the account followed here is Beatrice Manz's, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane). Ordinary vassalage describes none of this, so the mod makes the khanate an international organisation whose leader is a country: the realm that holds the khan. This page covers the ulus while a khan leads it, and how an amir comes to take him. What follows is on The Amirs' Regency and The Ṣāḥib-qirān; every price and threshold is collected in Ulus and regency numbers.

docs.title: The roster in 1337
docs.text:
The base game makes eleven amir houses vassals of Chagatai. In the mod they are independent members of the organisation, four more domains are carved by whole provinces out of the khan's own territory, and two settled mountain dynasties sit in the ulus as client kings.

Member Tag Standing Notes Chagatai CHG Khan (leader) Court at Almaliq; Changshi Khan, of the Borjigin; Tengri. Keeps 57 locations: the Ili, Zhetysu, the Talas and the road north to the Emil Barlas BRL Amir of the Ulus Kesh; the house of Temür Jalayirs JLY Amir of the Ulus Khujand Yasa'uri YSU Amir of the Ulus Samarkand and Bukhara Suldus SLD Amir of the Ulus Balkh Khuttal KTT Amir of the Ulus The Vakhsh valley Arlat ART Amir of the Ulus Maymana Apardi APD Amir of the Ulus Andkhoy Qara'unas QUN Amir of the Ulus Kabul Negüderi NGD Amir of the Ulus Ghazni Besüd BSD Amir of the Ulus The central Afghan highlands Dughlat DGH Amir of the Ulus Kashgar Ulus of Fergana FGN Amir of the Ulus New. Andijan; 16 locations; Sunni Ulus of Chach CAC Amir of the Ulus New. Tashkent and the middle Syr Darya; 27 locations; Sunni Ulus of Issyk-Kul ISQ Amir of the Ulus New. Balasagun, the lake and the Chu; 17 locations; Tengri Ulus of Dzungaria DZG Amir of the Ulus New. Urumqi and the northern Tian Shan; 10 locations; Tengri Badakhshan BKH Client King of the Ulus A Persianate court; its state religion is set to Sunni at the start Karategin KRG Client King of the Ulus A Persianate court; Tajik

The four new domains are named after their land and start with randomly generated rulers, because which house held which eastern valley in 1337 is poorly attested. Each starts with a Kurultai in its capital. The khan's seat and the fifteen amirs are Steppe Hordes; the two client kings are Persianate Sultanates.

Qocho (QCH) is not a member. It remains an ordinary vassal of Chagatai.

No member of the ulus joins the Erānzamīn organisation or counts as a contender in the Erānzamīn succession, although Transoxiana and Tukharistan lie in the region that would otherwise qualify them. The same holds for any state whose capital stands on a tümen's ground while the ulus exists.

Culture. The khan's seat, the eight western houses (Apardi, Arlat, Barlas, Jalayirs, Khuttal, Qara'unas, Suldus, Yasa'uri) and the four carved domains are Chaghatay by culture, not Mongolian. The Dughlat and the Negüderi stay Mongolian and the Besüd Persianized Mongol. See Demography and cultures.

docs.title: The three standings
docs.text:
Khan. The leader of the organisation is a country, shown as "Khan". In 1337 it is Chagatai. Leadership never changes by vote. It moves only by script: when the amirs raise a khan of their own, when an amir wins a rising, and by the events of the regency.

The khan's realm Monthly prestige +0.05, and a further +0.005 for every Amir of the Ulus and every Client King Monthly horde unity +0.05

Amir of the Ulus. Every member that is not the leader and not a client king holds this status automatically, and loses it automatically on leaving or on becoming the leader.

Each amir Morale of armies +5% Monthly horde unity +0.02

Client King of the Ulus. A settled house that keeps its own court and law under the ulus. Badakhshan and Karategin hold it from the start, and it is what the ulus gives a settled house raised on a broken tümen's ground (below).

Each client king Government Persianate Sultanate with Persianate Bureaucracy and the reform Client of the Ulus: +0.05 monthly legitimacy, −0.02 monthly prestige. The khan's name answers the legitimacy question for it, so it carries no Unsettled Legitimacy Status +0.02 monthly legitimacy What it does Pays the qubchur. May pledge its whole weight to an amir What it cannot do It is not an amir. It has no kingmaker score, is not counted among the amirs, and cannot rise, claim the khan, raid, ask for pledges or be pledged to When it ends A client that is no longer in the ulus loses the reform and becomes an ordinary Persianate ruler with the ordinary question to answer

Members also see one another with the opinion bonus "Of the same ulus".

docs.title: The khan's rights
docs.text:
These are the rules of the organisation while a khan leads it.

Rule In play The ulus rides with the khan When the khan is attacked by an outsider, every member joins his defence. When he declares a war, every member is called The khan protects his amirs An amir attacked by an outsider can call the khan, and the khan is called automatically A pledged tümen rides for its house A house can call the tümens pledged to it into its own wars, offensive and defensive. Nobody can be called against the house he is pledged to Wars inside the ulus When the khan is attacked by one of his own members, only the lords pledged to the seat are bound to join him; the rest may be asked Passage Members have military access through one another's lands at all times No war inside the ulus No member may declare war on another without a casus belli, and before the regency's second stage not at all — except with one of the ulus's own claims: Rising Against the Khan, Take the Khan, Restore the Ulus, Feud of the Tümens Nobody leaves A member cannot leave the organisation until the regency's third stage Closed membership Nobody can apply, be invited or found a rival; the organisation dissolves only by a regency's ending, or if fewer than two members remain The qubchur Every amir and client king pays the khan (below)

The whole ulus is drawn as one realm on the political map, the amirs in a lighter tint of the khan's colour.

docs.title: The qubchur
docs.text:
Qubchur for the Khan is a monthly payment from every junior member to the leader.

  • The total is 5% of the junior members' combined tax-and-trade income. Each member's part is in proportion to his own tax-and-trade income, and the whole sum goes to the leader.
  • Under a regent the total is halved. The amirs sent Qazaghan gifts, not the khan's due.
  • Like other organisation payments it has a slider:
Share of the qubchur paid Effect on the payer, per month In full +0.02 prestige Between half and full A proportional part of that +0.02 Half Nothing Below half Growing penalties, reaching −0.30 prestige and −0.10 horde unity at nothing paid

The AI always pays in full. The payment's in-game description still reads "one part in a hundred"; the rate charged is 5%.

docs.title: A realm's weight
docs.text:
Most of what happens in the ulus is decided by weight. Every member is weighed on one scale each month, and all members' weights together make 100.

Part Out of Measured as the member's share of the whole ulus's total Host 40 Military strength Tax base 30 Tax base Ruler 20 The ruler's three abilities added together Prestige 10 Prestige

Land is not counted. A hundred empty pastures weigh nothing against Samarkand.

A house's effective weight, the number the panel shows and the bars read, adds and subtracts what stands behind it:

Counts for A tümen pledged to it The pledger's whole weight A subject that is itself a member of the ulus The subject's whole weight. The subject has none of its own, and any pledge of its own is void A subject outside the ulus Its host and tax base reckoned on the ulus's scale, counted whole An ally outside the ulus A quarter of what he would weigh (host and tax base only; no single friend is reckoned at more than 15 before the quarter is taken) A patron outside the ulus who is not an ally 15% of what he would weigh, with the same limit All outside allies and patrons together At most +10 Largesse given as regent +3 for two years A raid won +2 for three years Its own pledge to another house or to the khan Its whole weight leaves it

Hovering any house on the panel lists these parts one by one.

docs.title: The two bars
docs.text:
The amirs can raise a khan of their own when either of two readings is at its line:

Bar Reading Line Power of the begs The nobles' estate power in the khan's own realm At least 50% of estate power and at least twice the crown's The three greatest amirs against the khan The effective weights of the three heaviest amirs added together, divided by the khan's own 4.00
  • Both lines stand a third lower after a child khan's accession (A Boy on the Felt), and return to normal once a grown khan is seated without a regent.
  • The bar cannot be met for 15 years after a Khan Triumphant, or for 10 years after a failed rising.

The bars are tested in two places only: at a khan's death, and by Rise Against the Khan. On the 1337 map the second bar read 5.25 on the first day and 3.5 after the first month in the author's test, so the first succession can go either way.

docs.title: Kingmaker score
docs.text:
The panel ranks the khan and the three amirs best placed to take a khan under Standing in the ulus. The ranking is for reading; the bars decide whether there is a regency, and the score decides who gets it.

Term Score The house's effective weight as a share of all the amirs' weight × 400 (a quarter of the amirs' weight scores 100) The ruler's military skill × 0.5 The ruler's administrative skill × 0.2 A wife of the line of Chinggis +25 An ally or patron outside the ulus whose ruler is of Chinggis's line +10, once Renown 2 per point, to a limit of 60 Of the line himself (the khan's seat only, on the panel) +50

Renown belongs to the ruler and dies with him. He gains 3 for a great battle won and 1 for a siege won while a regency lasts, 2 for a raid won at any time, and a kinsman confirmed over a tümen starts with 5 (see the regency page).

A house that has pledged its tümen, or is another house's subject, is out of the ranking.

docs.title: The panel
docs.text:
Ulus Chaghatay has its own organisation panel, recalculated at the start of each month.

Where What it shows Header Amirs (the number of amirs), Weight of the Begs (nobles' estate power in the khan's realm) and Great Amirs to Khan (the second bar's ratio) The Khan The seat, its ruler and the heir its own succession law names today. During a regency: the held khan and his age, then the state and regent that keep him, and the regent's heir The Succession The two bars with their lines, the khan's weight by part, the three greatest amirs by weight, Standing in the ulus, and one line saying what the bars come to today: "his heir would succeed" or "the amirs would raise a khan of their own". During a regency it shows the stage, the legitimacy gap and the regent's heir against the best rival instead Pledges Every house that has pledged its tümen and to whom, and every house with a patron outside The Amirs Every amir, heaviest first, with his weight and his share of the amirs' combined weight

The actions described below are on this panel.

docs.title: Pledges
docs.text:
A pledge puts a house's whole weight behind another. It has no term: it stands until it is taken back, until the house it was given to leaves the ulus or takes the seat itself, or until a rising that house leads is broken.

Action Who What it does Pledge Our Tümen Any amir or client king not already pledged All our weight counts as the chosen house's, in the bar of the three greatest amirs and in its kingmaker score. We drop out of the kingmaker ranking. We cannot pledge to the khan's seat, to a client king, or to a house that has itself pledged. If that house takes the khan we gain 20 favours with it and 10 prestige Take Back Our Pledge A pledged house Our weight is our own again from the next monthly reckoning Ask for a Pledge An amir who has not himself pledged Ask another house to stand behind us. An AI house agrees if what it weighs comes to 0 or more; the list shows, for each house, what it will answer and why before we pay, and a refusal still costs the asking. A player's house is asked by event (An Amir Asks for Our Tümen). A house that is another house's subject cannot be asked Ask a Lord to Stand with the Seat The khan, while no regency stands Ask a house that is not among the three likeliest kingmakers and has not pledged. If it agrees its whole weight counts as the khan's against the three greatest amirs, it gains 5 prestige, and khan and lord gain +30 opinion of each other. Pledges to the khan lapse when a regency begins

What an AI house weighs when asked for a pledge

Term Value A tümen is not lent for nothing −25 Its opinion of us A sixth of it A royal marriage between the houses +25 An alliance +15 Rivalry −100 We are at least twice its weight +30 We are at least a quarter heavier +15 We are the lighter house Down to −100 by how much lighter (half its weight −50, a tenth −90) It is itself among the three likeliest kingmakers Down to −66, most for the likeliest We are among the three likeliest kingmakers +10 It has already pledged elsewhere −30, and a sixth of the difference between its opinion of us and of the house it stands behind

A house talked away from another leaves that house with −40 opinion of both ("A pledged tümen was talked away").

What a lord weighs when the khan asks

Term Value A lord's caution −15 Its opinion of the seat A sixth of it A royal marriage / an alliance / rivalry +25 / +15 / −100 The seat is at least twice its weight +25 The seat still outweighs it +10 It outweighs the seat −20 How near the amirs are to overruling the khan (the second bar against its line) Down to −30 One of the three greatest amirs is its neighbour +15 A cautious ruler / an opportunistic ruler +10 / −10

docs.title: Friends outside the ulus
docs.text:
An ally outside the ulus already counts for a quarter of his weight. Two actions add a lighter tie, the patron: he owes no riders and is owed none, counts for 15% of his weight, and is owed 20 favours if his house comes to hold the khan. A house can have one patron, and a patron can back one house.

Action Who Notes Seek a Patron Outside the Ulus An amir without a patron The candidates are the outside neighbours of any member. A player is asked by event Back an Amir of the Ulus Any country outside the ulus that borders a member Choose an amir who has no patron and is not our rival or at war with us. It takes effect at once

Backer and house gain +30 opinion of each other; the seat of the ulus takes −30 of the backer.

What an outsider weighs when asked

Term Value A stranger's caution −20 Its opinion of the house A sixth of it It is a rival of the house −100 It is a rival of the khan's seat / borders it / is its ally +30 / +10 / −100 The house's kingmaker score is at least half the best amir's, but under nine tenths +25 The house is the strongest, or nearly −10 The house is no contender −30 Temperament Opportunistic +15, expansionist +10, cautious −10, isolationist −30

A patron of Chinggis's line is worth a further +10 kingmaker score, as Tughluq Temür's confirmation was to Temür in 1360. A patron cannot be raided by the house he backs, and backing an amir gives every other chief of the ulus a cause to raid the backer.

docs.title: Rise Against the Khan
docs.text:
An amir who has done everything right need not wait for a funeral.

Who An amir among the three likeliest kingmakers, at peace, while no regency stands When One of the two bars is at its line Effect The casus belli Rising Against the Khan on the khan's seat for five years. The goal is his capital. The khan is told (An Amir Has Risen) Who fights The tümens pledged to us can be called. On the khan's side only the lords pledged to the seat are bound to join

If we win, the khan is put to death, we take a prince of the line into our keeping and the Amirs' Regency begins with us as regent, whoever tops the ranking. The legitimacy gap starts at 35 instead of 50: we killed a khan.

If we lose, the khan has broken the begs:

Who Pays The amir who rose −20 prestige, −15 horde unity, twelve months of his tax-and-trade income to the khan, and two locations other than his capital Every house pledged to him Six months of income and one location. Its pledge is void The land Goes one place at a time to the lords pledged to the khan, whoever has had least so far first; to the khan himself if there are none The khan +15 prestige, +10 horde unity Each lord pledged to the khan +10 prestige The ulus No regency can begin for 10 years The amir himself One chance in two he is executed. If he lives, his house is asked whether a kinsman should take the tümen in his place

docs.title: Lead a Raid
docs.text:
In 1337 the khan led nobody anywhere, and the tribes on the edges never stopped. The Qara'unas and the Negüderi went down every winter into Sistan, Kirman and the Indus country. A raid was for herds, silver, captives to ransom or sell, and a payment not to return; almost never for land.

Who An amir, or the regent. The khan on his seat does not raid, and client kings do not Against One of our own neighbours outside the ulus: no truce, not an ally, not our subject, not our patron Effect War is declared at once with The Tümen's Raid. The realm we ride against holds a claim to answer us for five years The war Won in the field. Land costs double in the peace, and the war score ticks fast

The faith. A free Muslim may not be enslaved and war on Muslims wants a cause.

The target At the declaration Unbelievers, to a Muslim raider A ghazā: +5% clergy satisfaction Of our own faith, both Muslim, and we have a cause Nothing Of our own faith, both Muslim, and no cause −10 prestige, −5% clergy satisfaction

A cause is that they are our rival, that they back an amir of the ulus, or that they are at war with the seat of the ulus.

If the raid Is won Gold worth twice their tax base at once (they lose half as much). +5 horde unity, +2 renown, +2 weight in the ulus for three years. Then the captives (The Spoils): ransom them to their lord for twice their tax base, which he pays, or sell them for three times their tax base — at −10 prestige and −10% clergy satisfaction if we and they are both Muslim Is lost −10 prestige, −10 horde unity

A regent's raid counts as a war won for his legitimacy gap.

docs.title: The ground of a broken tümen
docs.text:
A horde whose armies are all destroyed shatters; the engine turns it into a settled country. Inside the ulus the mod intervenes. If the broken house's old capital is still loose, one house is asked to dispose of the ground (The Ground of a Broken Tümen): the member of the ulus at war with it (the heaviest, if several), failing that the member that beat it in a war within the last three years, and only if nobody broke it at all, the seat.

Option Result The pastures are ours. Every place the broken house held that nobody else has taken becomes ours as conquered land Raise a chief of our choosing over a new tümen. The ground becomes a Steppe Horde and an Amir of the Ulus again, with a Kurultai and two regiments of horse archers. Its chief is our vassal with +50 opinion of us, and its whole weight counts as ours Set a settled house over it, under the ulus. The ground becomes a Client King of the Ulus, our vassal with +50 opinion, its whole weight counted as ours. It can never contend for the khan

docs.title: The khan's own house
docs.text:
Chagatai is a Steppe Horde under a Borjigin khan, so everything on the Hordes page applies to it: the yam, darugha seats, shares for princes, and The Törü of the Ulus as its succession law. Three things bind those rules to this page:

  • Every Darugha's Seat adds to the nobles' power in the khan's realm, which is the Power of the begs bar.
  • A share granted to a Borjigin prince weakens the khan's own weight against his amirs today, but puts a man of the line with an army into the field.
  • A darugha can be the kingmaker. If, when the amirs raise a khan, the best darugha in the old seat's realm outscores every amir, the area of his seat is released to him as a new amir house and he takes the khan.

The amirs keep their own succession. The horde succession poll is not run for them, only for the seat of the ulus. While a khan or regent leads the ulus he is asked to confirm each amir house's new chief or set a kinsman over it (see the regency page).

The Barlas are not of the line. The base game files Temür, his father and their ancestors under the Borjigin dynasty. The mod moves them, and whoever rules the Barlas at the start, to a Barlas dynasty of their own. Temür ruled behind a khan because he was not a Chinggisid, and without the change the infant Temür would be the youngest "prince of the line" in the ulus.

docs.title: Playing it
docs.text:
As the khan (Chagatai). Your danger is on the Succession card. Keep the nobles in your own realm under half of estate power (every darugha seat pushes them up) and watch the three greatest amirs against you. You cannot attack them, so you grow at the expense of outsiders or not at all. Use Ask a Lord to Stand with the Seat on the lesser houses: each one adds its whole weight to yours, joins you if a great amir rises, and takes the rebels' land if he is beaten. Have a grown heir; a child's accession lowers both bars by a third for the next succession.

As an amir who wants the khan.

  1. Get into the top three. The score is mostly your share of the amirs' weight: host first, then tax base, then your ruler's abilities, then prestige. A wife of the line is +25.
  2. Gather pledges. Each pledged tümen adds its whole weight to yours and takes a rival out of the ranking. Houses agree when you are clearly heavier, married or allied to them, and well thought of; the likeliest kingmakers will not. Marry and ally first, then ask.
  3. Find friends outside. An ally counts for a quarter of his weight, a patron for 15%, to +10 in all; a patron of Chinggis's line adds +10 to your score.
  4. Raid. A raid won pays, raises horde unity and lends you +2 weight for three years.
  5. Wait for the bar, then choose. If the khan dies with a bar at its line, the amir with the highest score is handed the khan with the gap at 50. If you rise and win, you take him whatever your rank, with the gap at 35. If you rise and lose you may lose your head.
  6. Or stand behind the winner. A house that pledged to the man who takes the khan is owed 20 favours and gains 10 prestige.

As a lesser house. You are the remedy both sides want. Pledged to the khan you gain prestige and a share of any broken rebel's land; pledged to a great amir you are owed favours on the day he wins, and you pay half his fine on the day he loses.

As a neighbour. Attacking any member while a khan leads the ulus calls the khan to its defence, and attacking the khan brings in every member. Back an Amir of the Ulus is the cheap way to trouble the khan. Once a regency reaches its third stage the regent's strongest neighbours are handed a claim on the ulus, and after a Bulqaq every neighbour of a tümen has one.

See also: The Amirs' Regency, The Ṣāḥib-qirān, Ulus and regency numbers, Hordes, The Beglerbeg's Regency, Custody of the Ulus, The Erānzamīn organisation, Demography and cultures, Countries and tags, Known issues, What's new in 1.4.

docs.title: The Zaydi Imamate and Yemen
docs.text:
He is Imam who is qualified, who calls the people to himself, and who rises.

New in 1.4 — not yet verified in play

The imamate organisation, its tenets, the zakāt payment, the Imam's actions and the rebuilt Yemen are new and have not been played through in a full campaign. Numbers below are read from the files; how the AI uses bayʿa, how much zakāt actually flows, and the road to the Imam's House are the least-tested parts.

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text: Zaydī Shiʿism holds that the imamate did not end in occultation and is not inherited. Any descendant of ʿAlī and Fāṭima — Ḥasanid or Ḥusaynid — who is learned enough to rule by his own reasoning in the law, just, and brave, and who publicly calls the community to himself (daʿwa) and rises against unjust rule (khurūj), is Imam once the scholars and the tribes give him their oath (bayʿa). The oath binds both ways: the sworn owe him the sword and their zakāt, he owes them justice. Since al-Hādī ilā al-Ḥaqq founded the imamate at Ṣa'da in 897 the office has passed among sayyid houses rather than down one line, rival imams are common, and the imam's army is the highland tribes — Ḥāshid, Bakīl, Khawlān — under their own shaykhs. In 1337 the Imam is the great jurist al-Muʾayyad bi-llāh Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza. Below him, on the coast and in the southern highlands, the Rasulid sultans run one of the wealthiest states of the age: heirs of the Ayyubid order in Yemen, masters of the Aden customs house where the Red Sea and Indian Ocean trades meet, builders of the madrasas of Zabīd and Ta'izz, and authors of treatises on agriculture and astronomy. Each held what the other could not: the sultans the plain and the ports, the imams the mountains.

docs.title: Yemen in 1337
docs.text:
The base game ships one Rasulid country owning everything from Jāzān to Ḥaḍramawt, and no imamate. The mod redraws it.

Country Government Capital Holds Yemen (YEM) — the Rasulids Persianate Sultanate with the Rasulid Chancery reform; Shāfiʿī; kingdom rank Ta'izz (moved from Zabīd) The Tihāma, the southern highlands, Aden, Ḏamār and Ma'rib, the Ḥaḍramawt coast and wadi Zaydi Imamate (ZYD) — new Theocracy with The Zaydi Imamate reform; Zaydī; duchy rank Ṣa'da Ṣa'da, Ḥūth, Šahāra, Ḵamir, Ṯulā, Kawkabān, Ṣan'ā' and the Jawf fringe Yām (YAM) Tribe; Zaydī (the base game makes them Ismaili, which is a sixteenth-century fact) Najrān Najrān and Ẓahrān
  • The Rasulid sultan is al-Mujāhid ʿAlī. Yemen keeps cores on Ṣan'ā', Ṯulā and Kawkabān — the Rasulids held them within living memory.
  • The Imam is al-Muʾayyad bi-llāh Yaḥyā of the Āl Ḥamza, 67 years old and a formidable administrator (90 / 55 / 35). The imamate holds cores on Ḏamār, Ḥajja, Radā', the Ḥarāz edge and the Ma'rib country: the reach of the imams whenever they pushed out of the north.
  • Yām is the Imam's vassal and a sworn member of his imamate.
  • The two states are not at war at the start, and no other Yemeni country was changed: Ḥaḍramawt, Dhofar and the sharifs of Jāzān are as the base game has them.

docs.title: The land and its people
docs.text:
The total population of Yemen proper is left roughly where the base game put it (about 2.75 million); what changed is who those people are. A player will notice:

  • Cities exist. Ta'izz, Zabīd, Ṣan'ā' and Aden are cities; Ṣa'da, Ḏamār, Ibb, Radā', Najrān, Ḥays, Jāzān, al-Shiḥr, Tarīm and Shibām are towns. In the base game Yemen had two towns and no city.
  • Estates exist. The base game gave Yemen no nobles, no burghers and almost no clergy. The cities now carry burghers, scholars and a small military aristocracy.
  • The confessional line is in the right place. The Tihāma, the south and Ḥaḍramawt are overwhelmingly Sunni; the northern highlands are about four-fifths Zaydī; Ṣan'ā' is roughly two-thirds Zaydī; the Ḏamār belt is split evenly.
  • Jews are not slaves. The base game typed Yemen's Jews as slave pops at a fifth or more of every highland district. They are now burghers, clergy and peasants at about 3% in the main towns and less elsewhere. The mainland Nestorian pops are gone; Socotra's Christians stay.
  • Tribesmen are where the armies come from. A share of the Tihāma and Abyan peasantry is tribal (the Rasulid auxiliaries, below), while the settled Ḥāshid and Bakīl country is mostly peasants — terrace farmers who are tribesmen in politics, not in livelihood.
  • The land is no longer uniform desert. The southern highlands (Ta'izz, Ibb) are subtropical farmland, the Tihāma wadis and the Ḥaḍramawt oases are flood-irrigated, the central plateau is cold and grain-growing. Goods follow: indigo at Zabīd, gems at Ṣan'ā', iron at Ṣa'da, sugar and cotton on the Tihāma, salt at Aden. Aden is also now one of the best natural harbours on the Indian Ocean rim.

See Demography and cultures for the mod-wide population work.

docs.title: The imamate as an organisation
docs.text: The Zaydi Imamate appears twice in the interface: as a country, and as an international organisation named after its seat — at the start, the Imamate of Ṣa'da. The organisation is the community of a living Imam. Its leader is the ruler of the leading country, who carries the title Imam.

docs.title: Membership is bayʿa
docs.text:
Who may swear Any Shia country that is not itself the Imam of an imamate. Sunnis cannot. How The religious action Swear Bayʿa to an Imam: 30 religious influence and 10 prestige, at peace. There is no free "join" button. The Imam may also invite. One oath at a time Swearing to one Imam withdraws you from any other. Twelvers and Ismailis May swear, but doing so makes them Zaydī: their commitments to a hidden Imam lapse and they take the Zaydi Imamate aspect. Leaving Only at peace. Costs 10 prestige and the Zaydi Imamate aspect, and you cannot swear to the same Imam again for five years. Automatic loss A member that stops being Shia leaves. A member that attacks the Imam is expelled.

What the oath does:

  • The sword. Members are called automatically into every offensive war the Imam declares, and every member defends every other. All members give each other military access when at war.
  • Zakāt. Members pay the Imam (next section).
  • Every member gets +1 tolerance of the true faith and +0.02 monthly religious influence, plus whatever the tenets grant.
  • The Imam additionally gets +0.10 monthly devotion, +0.05 monthly prestige and +0.05 monthly religious influence.

AI countries are reluctant. Their willingness starts at −40 and moves with their opinion of the Imam (half of it), +40 if they are his subject, +30 if they already hold the Zaydi aspect, +15 for a shared culture, −20 if they hold a hidden Imam, and a sliding penalty for military strength: a state as strong as the Imam is at −30, one twice his strength at −60. In practice the Imam's own vassals and small Zaydī neighbours swear; equals do not.

A player cannot found a new imamate in the current build — the organisation exists only where the setup places it. The rival claimant of 1337, al-Wāthiq bi-llāh al-Muṭahhar, is present as a candidate inside the imamate rather than as a second organisation.

docs.title: Zakāt to the Imam
docs.text:
Each month the sworn members together owe the Imam the canonical fortieth: 2.5% of their combined tax and trade income, shared among them in proportion to their income. The Imam himself does not pay.

The payment has a maintenance slider on the member's side, and the slider is the politics. A member who pays less than half is withholding zakāt and loses up to 0.05 prestige a month at zero; one who pays above half gains up to 0.02 a month at full. With only Yām sworn at the start the sum is small — zakāt becomes real money only if larger Shia states swear.

docs.title: How an Imam is chosen
docs.text:
The imamate's succession law is Rising of the Qualified Sayyid. It is fixed while the country holds the Zaydi Imamate reform. Candidates are the men of the clergy estate in the country (the Imam's brothers and sons included); women and foreign rulers are excluded. Each is scored:

Qualification Score Of the blood of ʿAlī and Fāṭima +100 Administrative ability + the full value Military ability + the full value Age + half the candidate's age

Blood weighs most but does not decide it: among sayyids the learned and the brave win, and being the Imam's son counts for nothing in itself. In the current build "sayyid" means the two houses scripted for 1337, the Āl Ḥamza (the Imam's) and the Āl al-Muṭahhar (his rival's). Each has three or four men at the start. By the numbers the front-runner when Imam Yaḥyā dies is not his son but al-Muṭahhar al-Wāthiq, the rival — which is roughly what the doctrine would predict.

The imamate is a theocracy: its currency is devotion, not legitimacy.

docs.title: Tenets
docs.text:
The imamate's doctrine is held by the organisation and binds every member. The Imam changes a tenet from the organisation's laws; each change takes a year and is paid in religious influence and devotion. The 1337 imamate holds the mainstream Hādawī position on all three questions (marked start).

Price tier Cost The Imam's ruling 40 religious influence, 15 devotion The Imam's ruling, against the grain 80 religious influence, 30 devotion The Imam's ruling, against the doctrine 120 religious influence, 75 devotion, 20 prestige

docs.title: Making of the Imam
docs.text: Tenet Price Effect Recognition of the Qualified (start) ruling Imam: +2.5% clergy satisfaction. Members: +0.5 tolerance of the true faith Explicit Designation against the grain Imam: +0.05 monthly legitimacy, −2.5% clergy satisfaction The Sword Alone against the grain Everyone: +5% army morale, +25% tribes estate power

docs.title: Who May Be Imam
docs.text: Tenet Price Effect Open to the Sayyids (start) ruling Imam: +2.5% clergy satisfaction The Imam's House against the doctrine Imam: +0.10 monthly legitimacy, −5% clergy satisfaction. Unlocks Proclaim the Imam's House

docs.title: The Companions
docs.text:
Tenet Price Effect Preference without Cursing (start) ruling Everyone: +1 tolerance of heretics Cursing of the Companions against the grain Everyone: +10% pop conversion speed, −2 tolerance of heretics Acceptance of the Companions against the doctrine Everyone: +2 tolerance of heretics, drift toward Jurisprudence

Two cautions. The first two tenets do not change how the heir is scored: the election runs as described above whatever the doctrine says, until the Imam's House is actually proclaimed. And the legitimacy bonuses do little for a theocracy that runs on devotion; they matter once the imamate has become a sultanate.

docs.title: The Imam's actions
docs.text:
Both are religious actions.

Action Who Price Conditions Effect Declare the Imam's Jihād The Imam of an imamate 20 devotion, 10 prestige At peace; once every 12 months Choose a neighbour who is of another religion or is a rival living Imam, with whom you have no truce or alliance. You receive The Imam's Jihād casus belli on them for ten years Swear Bayʿa to an Imam Any Shia country outside an imamate 30 religious influence, 10 prestige At peace Join the chosen imamate (see above)

The Imam's Jihād is a religious war of conquest: its war goal is to take a province, and because the sworn are called automatically, it brings the whole imamate with it. Against the Rasulids — Sunni, adjacent, and sitting on the imamate's cores — it is available from the first day.

docs.title: The road to a sultanate
docs.text:
The imamate never built a bureaucracy; when it took the lowlands, it captured one. In play this is a two-stage road, entirely optional.

Stage one — The Dīwān of the Lowlands. The event fires when the imamate takes a location that holds a Regional Dīwān or a Dīwān of the Realms, or any of Ta'izz, Zabīd, Aden or Ṣan'ā' (the last only if it has been lost and retaken).

Choice Effect Let the scribes serve the Imam. Take up the dīwān. −20 devotion, −5 stability, −10% clergy satisfaction, −5% tribes satisfaction. The Imam now holds the dīwān. If the imamate already holds the tenet The Imam's House, stage two happens at once The Imam rules by the Book and the sword. Disperse them. +10 devotion, +5% clergy satisfaction. The offer does not return for 20 years

Stage two — Proclaim the Imam's House. A religious action costing 50 devotion, 20 prestige and 5 stability. It needs a held dīwān, peace, a living son of the Imam, and the tenet The Imam's House (itself the most expensive ruling there is). Then:

  • the country becomes a Persianate Sultanate under the Rasulid Chancery and a second reform, The Imam's House (+0.05 monthly religious influence, +1 tolerance of the true faith, +5% army morale, +25% tribes estate power, +25% tribes levy size);
  • succession changes to Favored Son Succession;
  • −10 legitimacy and −10 stability on the day;
  • The Jurists' Grievance for 25 years: −10% clergy satisfaction and −0.05 monthly legitimacy.

The organisation survives: the sultan is still Imam, the sworn still march and pay. The highland levy is kept, and the Tihāma levies are added to it. This is the Qāsimid state of the seventeenth century, reached early.

docs.title: Armies
docs.text:
Yemen's two states field armies that are good on opposite ground. Neither unit set can be recruited; all four are raised as levies.

Unit Type Raised by Character Qabīlī Highlanders Light infantry The imamate (and the Imam's House): from peasants and tribesmen of mountain, hill and plateau locations Takes 25% less morale damage and deals 10% more; deals 15% more strength damage but takes 10% more; +2 initiative. +35% in mountains, +30% in hills, +15% on plateau Tribal Horse of the Jawf Light cavalry The imamate: from tribesmen, nobles and clergy where horses reach the market +2 initiative; +10% in mountains, hills, plateau and sparse country, +5% in desert. Few in number Tihama Arab Horse Light cavalry The Rasulid Chancery (and the Imam's House): from lowland tribesmen where horses reach the market +2 initiative; takes 10% more morale damage. +10% on flatland and desert; −25% in mountains, −10% in hills and on plateau Tihama Arab Foot Light infantry The Rasulid Chancery (and the Imam's House): from lowland tribesmen Takes 10% more morale damage. +10% on flatland; −20% in mountains, −10% on plateau, −5% in hills

The reforms sit on top of this:

The Zaydi Imamate Rasulid Chancery Levies +15% levy size; tribes +25%, peasants +33% Amirs +75%, nobles +50%, tribes +25%; peasants −50%, burghers −25% Fighting +20% army morale, +15% defensiveness +10% army morale; may build mamluk barracks State +0.05 monthly devotion, +0.10 monthly religious influence, +1 tolerance of the true faith, +2.5% clergy satisfaction, one extra reform slot A chancery state: +5% tax efficiency, +5% cabinet efficiency, the Dīwān in the cabinet and the Amirs in command, +20% maximum urban control, −5% maximum rural control Tribes +50% tribes estate power; tribes sit in parliament +75% tribes estate power

The mod's amir heavy cavalry also takes −25% in mountains everywhere. The Rasulid mamlūk core is small and excellent on the plain; it does not belong on a ridge.

docs.title: Playing the Rasulids
docs.text:
You are a rich Persianate chancery state at the edge of the Persianate world. The Rasulid Chancery is a complete constitutional answer in itself: Yemen does not suffer the legitimacy crisis that pushes Iranian sultanates to choose a path in the government reforms, and it stands outside the Erānzamīn situation. Your money is the coast — Aden's harbour, Zabīd, the Tihāma wadis — and your urban control is high while your rural control is capped low, which is the highlands problem stated as a number.

The imamate is not a country you can absorb cheaply. Its Qabīlī levy is far larger than its size suggests and close to unbeatable in its own mountains, your Tihāma auxiliaries and your cavalry are penalised there, and the Imam holds a ten-year casus belli on you whenever he cares to pay for it. Fight him on the plain or at the walls of the lowland cities; take Ṣan'ā' (your core) if you can, and do not expect to keep Ṣa'da. You cannot join or use the imamate organisation: it is closed to Sunnis.

docs.title: Playing the Imam
docs.text:
You are small, poor, devout and very hard to dislodge. Devotion pays for everything — tenets, the jihād, the Imam's House — so guard it. Your first Imam is old; look at the succession candidates early, because the next Imam is whoever scores best, and you may not like him.

  • Use the ground. Meet the Rasulids in mountains and hills, never on the Tihāma. A jihād for Ḏamār or Ḥajja (your cores) is the natural first war.
  • Decide what the lowlands are for. Taking Ta'izz, Zabīd or Aden triggers the Dīwān of the Lowlands. Dispersing the scribes keeps the imamate pure and the clergy content. Taking them up starts the road to a hereditary sultanate with a chancery, a tax base and both levy systems — at the price of devotion, stability and a generation of the jurists' resentment.
  • The Imam's House is a commitment. The tenet alone costs 120 religious influence, 75 devotion and 20 prestige; the proclamation another 50 devotion. Plan it over a reign.
  • Bayʿa grows slowly. Vassals and weaker Zaydī neighbours will swear; nobody stronger than you will. Each sworn member is both an ally bound to your wars and a payer of zakāt.

docs.title: How it connects
docs.text:
• The Zaydi Imamate religious aspect (+5% army morale, drift toward Jurisprudence) is given to every sworn member, and the imamate starts with Qiyām bi'l-Sayf, the rising by the sword, as well. These belong to the mod's wider treatment of Shia Islam; the Twelver and Ismaili commitments are described with the Commonwealth of Martyrs and the ṭarīqa orders.
  • Only the living imamate exists as an organisation. There is no organisation for the Twelver hidden Imam in the current build.
  • The chancery the imamate can capture is the same institution described under the Dīwān estate and buildings.
  • Levies and the light/heavy cavalry split: the military system.

See also: Persianate Sultanate, Government reforms, Military system, Demography and cultures, Commonwealth of Martyrs, Countries and tags, Known issues.

docs.title: Countries and tags
docs.text:
A reference to the countries the mod adds or changes at the 1337 start: what each is called in game, its tag, where it sits, how it is governed on day one, and which page of this wiki covers it. Countries the mod leaves exactly as the base game has them are listed only where they belong to one of the mod's organisations.

"Türk-leaning" and "Tāzīk-leaning" give the starting position on the Türk–Tāzīk axis: −25 or +25, with the matching set of starting privileges. Location counts are those owned on day one. A dash for the ruler means the game generates one.

docs.title: A note on names
docs.text:
Hamedān, Kāshān, Esfarāyen, Qom, Merv and Kuhistān take their country names from the city or district they hold, spelled as the game spells the place. Rulers are given here in their usual scholarly form. The game builds character names from its own name list, so a few read differently on screen — Ardashīr of Shabankara, for one, appears under the Greek form of his name.

See also: Starting the game, The Erānzamīn organisation, Demography and cultures, Ulus Chaghatay, Tariqa orders.

docs.title: Known issues and systems in testing
docs.text: The mod is under active development on Europa Universalis V 1.4.7. This page lists the systems that are new and have not yet been played through, and the faults already noticed in them. Everything below comes from reading the mod as it stands, not from a finished test campaign: treat it as a list of places to be careful, and report what you find on the Workshop page.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Built for 1.4.7. Earlier game versions will not load it correctly.
  • The mod replaces the base game's Ilkhanate situation, the Rise of the Ottomans situation, the scheduled appearance of Timur, the 1337 population of the Middle East and much of its political setup. It is not compatible with other mods that change the same things.

docs.title: The succession of Erānzamīn
docs.text:
• The timeout event The Dream Dies is set for a date after the situation has already ended, so it probably never appears.
  • Taking a province capital as a contender takes every location in the province, including land held there by a third party.
  • A country that becomes a contender after the start receives the contender actions but not the Contender modifier or the opening legitimacy event.
  • A contender who is also a member carries two nearly identical bonuses, so some of them (war score cost among them) count twice.
  • The tooltip on Consolidate the Diwan asks for a Tāzīk lean above 15; the real requirement is above 25.
  • Consolidate the Diwan and Mixed Settlement make the land core; Grant the Yurt only integrates it.
  • An Amīr Sultanate reached through The Fiction Expires does not shed Unsettled Legitimacy.
  • In the Custody of the Ulus the count of successions starts at one, so "two successions survived" is reached after a single real succession.

docs.title: The Matters and the audits
docs.text:
• Persia cannot be formed after a Matter of Tork closed by proclamation; the decision only recognises eradication or a defection war.
  • The Matter of Tazik is switched off. Türk-leaning regimes currently face no consolidation crisis of their own.
  • Change Approach locks as soon as any path is begun, although paths are meant to stack.
  • The Farr panel's end conditions read 90 and 25; the real thresholds are 95 and 40. The Farr counts victories in great battles but defeats only in skirmishes.
  • The Iranization bar is drawn out of 240 months although it completes at 120.

docs.title: Estates and the Maẓālim
docs.text:
• Muṣādara Right cannot be revoked once granted, which leaves the Mulk Protection Charter and Soyurghal Grants out of reach. Muṣādara always falls on a Dīwān minister, whatever its tooltip says.
  • Burghers hold no seat in the Majlis-e Mazalim, so their cases and petitions may never come up.
  • Parliament event rewards still pay in the 1.3 currencies rather than political influence.
  • Curtail the Umara gives +50% tax efficiency, almost certainly meant to be +5%.
  • Khāṣṣa Crown Demesne lists its cut to the Amirs' power twice.

docs.title: Buildings and goods
docs.text:
• The Kāshī Guild consumes goods but produces nothing.
  • The Qanāt Network's requirement tooltip is blank.
  • Unaudited Iqṭāʿ and Tuyul tooltips promise larger levies; they give smaller ones or none.

docs.title: The Shia world and Yemen
docs.text:
• Rise Against the Patron asks for no radicalisation, declares no war, and grants neither Zeal nor membership in the Movement.
  • Patronize An Order only works while the Sarbadar Phenomenon is running.
  • Capture the Court always installs the Ṣafavī school, whichever order did the capturing.
  • Ardabil starts without the base reform the other six orders hold.
  • A player cannot found a rival imamate, so the jihād against a "rival Imam" has no target. Two of the three Zaydi tenet groups do not yet change how the Imam is chosen.
  • Swear Bayʿa says Twelvers must recommit first; in fact it converts them.

docs.title: Ulus Chaghatay, the regencies and the Ṣāḥib-qirān
docs.text:
These systems were written in November 2026 and have been corrected after short tests, not after campaigns. Treat every number on their pages, and on Ulus and regency numbers, as a first setting. The mod's own files say as much; the points below are the ones they single out, followed by discrepancies found while writing this wiki.

Marked as unverified or provisional in the mod's files

  • All the regency's numbers are described as values to tune after watching AI play. None has been tuned that way yet.
  • The amir bar of 4.00 is provisional. 6.00 was found too high; 4.00 sits between the two readings seen on the 1337 map (5.25 on the first day, 3.5 after a month), and is to be retuned once those readings settle. Until then the first Chagatai succession may or may not open a regency.
  • "Tribesmen enfranchisement", lowered by Hereditary Tümens and Bound to the Tümen, is a modifier the mod defines as a test. The engine may ignore it; the rest of both privileges does not depend on it.
  • Marry into the Line attempts the marriage, but the engine may refuse it to a ruler who is already married. The regency counts the ruler as a son-in-law of the line either way, so the wife may not be visible.
  • Recall the Darughas weakens the nobles for ten years but cannot remove the Darugha's Seats themselves.
  • A Ṣāḥib-qirān's automatic conquest did not take unfortified country in a test, so occupied locations are now handed over by script as well. How the two interact everywhere is unchecked.
  • Sworn amirs did not join a war begun by Plan Invasion on their own, so that action now puts them into it. Wars the Ṣāḥib-qirān declares in the ordinary way rely on the subject type's own rule, which has not been confirmed.
  • Base events that name the historical Temür (his death, "the Lame", and several others) are not rewritten. Under a different conqueror they stay silent or read oddly.
  • The four carved tümens vanished on the first day in an early build for want of a Kurultai. Each now starts with one; the mod's notes still treat their survival past the first day as something to confirm.

Discrepancies between the text in game and what the script does

  • Claim the Khan says whoever takes the regent's capital takes the khan. That is true only from the regency's third stage. In the second stage the claim opens the war, but winning it costs the regent standing and does not move the khan.
  • The Office Hardens promises +10% per step to the heir's standing. The bar on the panel shows it; the poll at the regent's death, as written, does not apply it.
  • The bar "Regent's heir against the best rival" scores the heir by an older formula than the one the poll uses at the regent's death, so the bar can be a poor guide to the result.
  • The Khan Is Taken from Us promises a claim to take the khan back. The claim is given when an heir loses the khan at a regent's death, but not when the khan is taken by force or passes to a rival at the turn into the fourth stage.
  • An Amir Asks for Our Tümen still says half our weight would be counted as his. A pledge is the whole of it.
  • Client King of the Ulus is set on Badakhshan and Karategin at the start but is not on the organisation's own list of statuses, so the status and its small bonuses may not appear. Their membership, their reform and their exclusion from the amirs' reckoning do not depend on it.
  • The qubchur's description still reads "one part in a hundred"; the levy is 5%.
  • A raid by a non-Muslim chief, or by a Muslim chief on a Muslim realm of another rite, is neither a ghazā nor a raid on his own faith, and carries no price or reward of either kind.

docs.title: The steppe
docs.text:
• Two succession events (Too Many Sons of the Line and The Amirs Have Been Counting) still show placeholder text.
  • The Question of the Far Country fires for any distant area, not only poorly controlled ones.
  • The yam's description says flatland only; the bonus applies everywhere.
  • The Törü succession is seated only on the Golden Horde and Chagatai.
  • An ulus holder's loyalty is meant to be shaken when the khan who granted it dies; this is not yet in play.

docs.title: Rum and the Kurdish emirates
docs.text:
• Restore the Diwan of Rum shows −5 stability; it costs −15 (−10 where a chancery already stands).
  • Winning Shattered Rum still uses the base game's size test, which is larger than Anatolia.
  • The Chancery Within Reach is offered again for every great city a Kurdish emirate takes.
  • The Kurdish Emirate modifier's numbers are placeholders.

docs.title: The map and its people
docs.text:
• The retyping of protected communities is unfinished: the Jews of Iran and Yemen are done, but Syriac Christians and Armenians in Iraq, the Jazira and Azerbaijan are still typed as slaves, as in the base game.
  • The Jalayirids start without recognising the Syriacs of their own realm.
  • Kerman (KRM) shows a country history written for Karaman.
  • Three countries whose land has been reassigned (HLL, ASR, SBZ) are still on the Erānzamīn member list.

docs.title: Not in the mod yet
docs.text:
Mentioned in older descriptions or planned, but not present: the Matter of Tazik as a playable crisis, a Twelver Imamate organisation, the Mamluk and Delhi event chains beyond their opening events, demanding fealty between hordes, and a kuriltai (parliament) of Ulus Chaghatay itself.

See also: What changed in 1.4, Countries and tags, Ulus and regency numbers.
